title: História
blurb: Os grandes momentos da humanidade, dos primeiros agricultores à era digital.

lessons.title: Momentos de viragem da humanidade
lessons.summary: Cinco mudanças que criaram o mundo moderno, pela ordem em que aconteceram.

cards.title: A história humana num só dia
cards.text:
Comprime os cerca de 300 000 anos do Homo sapiens num único dia. Durante quase todo esse tempo, toda a gente vivia da caça e da recoleção.

A agricultura só começa por volta das 23:02. A escrita aparece às 23:36. A imprensa chega a menos de três minutos da meia-noite, e tudo o que veio depois da máquina a vapor cabe no último minuto.

deep.x: The trick of squeezing history into a day works because our minds can't feel the difference between 3,000 and 300,000 years. Turn the numbers into clock time and the proportions suddenly become obvious.

x: 300,000 years ÷ 1,440 minutes in a day
≈ 208 years per minute
Farming began about 12,000 years ago → 58 minutes before midnight → about 23:02

deep.x: What filled the rest of the day

For about 96% of our existence, people lived in small, mobile bands of perhaps 20–50, hunting, fishing and gathering plants. They were not primitive. They had the same brains as us, made jewellery, buried their dead, traded shells over hundreds of kilometres and painted caves.
Why the pace speeds up

Each turning point made the next one come faster. Farming fed more people; more people meant more inventors; writing and printing let ideas pile up instead of being forgotten. So the clock is crowded at the end not because recent people are cleverer, but because knowledge accumulates.

x: Farming: about 58 minutes before midnight
Writing: about 25 minutes before midnight
Everything since 1800, including electricity, cars and phones: roughly the last minute

deep.x: On the human clock, almost everything we call "history" happened in the last half-hour.
Portugal's Côa Valley holds thousands of rock engravings of horses, aurochs and ibex, many over 20,000 years old: art made by hunter-gatherers long before 23:02.

cards.title: A agricultura mudou tudo
cards.text:
Por volta de 10 000 a.C., as pessoas do Crescente Fértil (atuais Iraque, Síria e Turquia) começaram a semear trigo e cevada e a criar animais.

A agricultura tornou possíveis os excedentes de comida. Os excedentes podiam ser armazenados, trocados e taxados, e alimentavam quem não cultivava: oleiros, sacerdotes, soldados e reis. As aldeias cresceram até se tornarem as primeiras cidades.

deep.x: Farming wasn't one invention. Over many generations, people kept the seeds of plants that didn't scatter on the wind and the animals that were calmer to handle. Slowly, wild wheat, barley, goats and sheep became domesticated: dependent on humans, and far more productive.
It happened more than once

The Fertile Crescent was first, but people elsewhere invented farming independently, with their own crops. That tells us it was a common human response to a warmer, more stable climate after the last Ice Age.
The hidden costs

Early farmers often had a harder life than foragers. Skeletons show they were shorter, had more tooth decay and suffered from diseases caught from animals and crowded villages. A single bad harvest could mean famine. But farming fed far more people per square kilometre, so farmers outnumbered and slowly replaced most hunter-gatherers.

x: Farming reached Portugal around 5500 BCE, spreading along the Mediterranean coast
Megaliths such as the Almendres Cromlech near Évora were raised by early farming communities

deep.w: Farming made life easier
deep.r: It produced more food overall, but early farmers often worked longer and were less healthy than foragers

deep.x: Farming didn't make people richer at first; it made them more numerous, and numbers changed everything.

cards.title: A escrita começou como contabilidade
cards.text:
A escrita mais antiga que conhecemos vem da Suméria, no atual Iraque, por volta de 3200 a.C. Não era poesia. Eram contas: quem entregou quanta cevada, quantas ovelhas, quanta cerveja foi paga como salário.

Os escribas pressionavam marcas em forma de cunha no barro húmido com uma cana. Chamamos a esta escrita cuneiforme, do latim para 'cunha'.
cards.sketch: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g class="d"><rect class="s bgf" x="90" y="26" width="140" height="116" rx="18"/><path class="fi" d="M108 47 L120 52 L108 57 Z"/><path class="fi" d="M126 47 L138 52 L126 57 Z"/><path class="fi" d="M144 47 L156 52 L144 57 Z"/><path class="s" d="M178 44L178 60"/><path class="s" d="M185 44L185 60"/><path class="s" d="M192 44L192 60"/><path class="s" d="M199 44L199 60"/><path class="fi" d="M108 73 L120 78 L108 83 Z"/><path class="fi" d="M126 73 L138 78 L126 83 Z"/><path class="fi" d="M144 73 L156 78 L144 83 Z"/><path class="fi" d="M162 73 L174 78 L162 83 Z"/><path class="s" d="M178 70L178 86"/><path class="s" d="M185 70L185 86"/><path class="s" d="M192 70L192 86"/><path class="fi" d="M108 99 L120 104 L108 109 Z"/><path class="fi" d="M126 99 L138 104 L126 109 Z"/><path class="fi" d="M144 99 L156 104 L144 109 Z"/><path class="s" d="M178 96L178 112"/><path class="s" d="M185 96L185 112"/></g><text class="" x="160" y="166" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:16px">Uruk, ~3200 a.C.: cevada, ovelhas, cerveja</text><text class="a" x="270" y="60" text-anchor="start" style="font-size:15px">cunhas</text><text class="a" x="270" y="104" text-anchor="start" style="font-size:15px">contagens</text></svg>

deep.x: Long before writing, people in Mesopotamia used small clay tokens to count goods: a cone for a measure of grain, a cylinder for an animal. To make a contract tamper-proof, tokens were sealed in clay envelopes, with their shapes pressed on the outside. Eventually someone realised the marks alone were enough.
From accounts to literature

Early tablets mix numbers with pictures of goods. Over centuries the signs became abstract wedges, and many began to stand for sounds, so scribes could write names, laws, letters and stories. Epics like Gilgamesh came over a thousand years after the first receipts.

x: Cuneiform was used for about 3,000 years and for more than a dozen languages
Hundreds of thousands of tablets survive, because baked clay lasts
It was deciphered by European scholars in the 1800s

deep.x: Invented several times
The Phoenician alphabet, with a sign for each sound, was passed to the Greeks and then the Romans. The letters you're reading now descend from it.
One of the oldest known customer complaints is a clay tablet from Ur, around 1750 BCE, in which a man called Nanni grumbles to a merchant, Ea-nasir, about poor-quality copper.
Writing was invented to keep track of debts and taxes; stories came later.

cards.title: A imprensa
cards.text:
Por volta de 1450, em Mainz, Johannes Gutenberg juntou tipos móveis de metal, tinta à base de óleo e uma prensa adaptada das prensas de vinho. Um livro que levava meses a um escriba podia agora ser impresso às centenas.

Em 50 anos circulavam milhões de livros. As ideias espalhavam-se mais depressa do que as autoridades as conseguiam controlar, alimentando a Reforma e a revolução científica.
cards.sketch: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g class="d"><path class="s" d="M80 30L80 150"/><path class="s" d="M240 30L240 150"/><path class="s" d="M68 30L252 30"/><path class="s" d="M160 32L153 35.7L167 43L153 50.3L167 57.7L153 65L167 72.3L160 76"/><path class="s" d="M128 60L192 60"/><rect class="s bgf" x="110" y="78" width="100" height="16" rx="3"/><rect class="w" x="115" y="110" width="90" height="10" rx="0"/><rect class="s bgf" x="100" y="120" width="120" height="14" rx="3"/><path class="s" d="M56 150L264 150"/></g><text class="a" x="252" y="58" text-anchor="start" style="font-size:15px">parafuso</text><text class="a" x="252" y="120" text-anchor="start" style="font-size:15px">tipos e</text><text class="a" x="252" y="138" text-anchor="start" style="font-size:15px">papel</text><text class="" x="160" y="172" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:16px">Gutenberg, Mainz, ~1450</text></svg>

deep.x: Gutenberg didn't invent printing. China printed with woodblocks by the 800s, and Korea used metal movable type in the 1300s. His breakthrough was a complete system that suited an alphabet of a few dozen letters.
The system

x: A hand mould to cast thousands of identical letters quickly
A metal alloy of lead, tin and antimony that cast cleanly
Oil-based ink that stuck to metal
A screw press, like those used for grapes and olives

deep.x: Speed and price
His Bible, finished around 1455, was printed in about 180 copies; around 49 survive. By 1500 presses were working in more than 250 European towns, and books cost a fraction of a hand copy.
Why it mattered

Identical copies meant scholars across Europe could cite the same page, compare data and correct errors. Pamphlets let Luther reach hundreds of thousands of readers. Authorities tried to license and ban books, but they could not keep up.

deep.w: Gutenberg invented printing
deep.r: China and Korea printed centuries earlier; Gutenberg made it fast, cheap and practical for alphabets

deep.x: The press didn't just copy books faster; it made knowledge identical, cheap and hard to suppress.

cards.title: A Revolução Industrial
cards.text:
A partir de cerca de 1760, na Grã-Bretanha, máquinas movidas a água e depois máquinas a vapor alimentadas a carvão passaram a fazer a fiação, a tecelagem e a mineração. O trabalho saiu das casas e dos campos para as fábricas, e as pessoas mudaram-se para cidades em rápido crescimento.

Pela primeira vez na história, a produção por pessoa continuou a subir década após década. Também trouxe o trabalho infantil, a poluição e o início das emissões de CO₂ em grande escala.
cards.sketch: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g class="d"><path class="s bgf" d="M30 150 V102 L70 80 V102 L110 80 V102 L150 80 V150 Z"/><rect class="s bgf" x="160" y="44" width="20" height="106" rx="0"/><path class="dash" d="M170 38 q-12 -8 2 -16 q14 -8 6 -18"/><path class="s" d="M18 150L302 150"/><circle class="s" cx="250" cy="112" r="32"/><path class="s" d="M250 80L250 144"/><path class="s" d="M218 112L282 112"/><path class="s" d="M227 89L273 135"/><path class="s" d="M273 89L227 135"/><circle class="s bgf" cx="250" cy="112" r="6"/></g><text class="" x="90" y="70" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:16px">fábricas</text><text class="r" x="250" y="70" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:16px">energia a vapor</text><text class="" x="160" y="172" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:16px">Grã-Bretanha, desde ~1760</text></svg>

deep.x: Britain had a rare mix: lots of cheap coal, high wages that made machines worth buying, a big trading empire, patents, and canals to move heavy goods. Inventors had a reason to replace muscle with machines.
How it worked

Textiles came first. Spinning machines like the spinning jenny and Arkwright's water frame multiplied what one worker could produce. James Watt's engine, with a separate condenser, burned far less coal than earlier ones, so steam could power mills anywhere, not just beside rivers. Then came railways and steamships.
The costs

x: Children as young as five or six worked in mills and mines
Cities like Manchester grew fast, with crowded, dirty housing
Burning coal began the rise in atmospheric CO₂

deep.x: Portugal industrialised later, with textiles in the north and cork and canning in the south. Its first railway, Lisbon to Carregado, opened in 1856.

deep.w: The Industrial Revolution was a sudden explosion
deep.r: Growth was only about 1–2% a year, but it never stopped, and over two centuries that compounded into a revolution

deep.x: For the first time, living standards could rise every generation instead of being eaten up by more mouths.

cards.title: Fogo e ferramentas
cards.text: Muito antes da agricultura, os humanos dominaram o fogo, cozinharam os alimentos e fizeram ferramentas de pedra cada vez melhores. Cozinhar tornou a comida mais fácil de digerir e pode ter ajudado os nossos antepassados a desenvolver cérebros maiores.

deep.x: Tool-making is far older than our species. The oldest known stone tools, from Kenya, are about 3.3 million years old. Around 1.7 million years ago, Homo erectus began shaping symmetrical hand axes, a design used for over a million years.
Why cooking mattered

Cooking breaks down fibres and starches, kills germs and makes food softer, so we get more energy from it with less chewing. Some scientists argue this freed energy for a bigger, hungrier brain and allowed smaller guts and teeth. The idea is popular but still debated.
Fire did more than cook

x: Warmth let people live in colder places
Light extended the day for talking and making things
Fire scared off predators and could reshape landscapes
Heat let Neanderthals make glue from birch bark

deep.w: Stone Age tools were crude lumps of rock
deep.r: Later tools were precise blades, needles and spear-throwers that demanded years of skill

deep.x: Fire turned humans from animals that eat whatever they find into the only animal that processes its food.

cards.title: Para fora de África
cards.text: Os humanos modernos evoluíram em África e espalharam-se pelo mundo em vagas, chegando à Europa há cerca de 45 000 anos, à Austrália talvez há 50 000–65 000 anos e às Américas há pelo menos 15 000 anos.

deep.x: The oldest known Homo sapiens fossils, from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, are about 300,000 years old. For most of our history we lived only in Africa. Small groups left earlier, but the main dispersal that gave rise to today's non-African populations began roughly 60,000–70,000 years ago.
Dates, in years ago
Reaching Australia meant crossing open sea, so these people had boats. The Americas were reached from Siberia across a land bridge exposed when sea levels were lower in the Ice Age.
Meeting other humans
Our ancestors weren't alone. Neanderthals lived in Europe and western Asia, and Denisovans further east. Groups met and sometimes had children together.

x: Most people outside Africa carry about 1–2% Neanderthal DNA
Iberia was one of the last Neanderthal refuges
In 1998 the skeleton of a child, buried over 20,000 years ago, was found at Lapedo near Leiria

deep.x: Many scientists think the Lapedo child shows a mix of modern human and Neanderthal features, though this is still debated.
Every person alive today is descended from Africans, and many carry a little Neanderthal too.

cards.title: Cidades e Estados
cards.text: Com a agricultura vieram as primeiras cidades na Mesopotâmia, como Uruk e Ur, por volta de 4000–3000 a.C.: templos, reis, leis, impostos e soldados.

deep.x: Uruk, in southern Iraq, may have had 40,000 people or more by about 3000 BCE, an astonishing size at the time. Irrigation canals needed organising, harvests needed storing, and stores needed guarding. Out of these jobs grew officials, priests, soldiers and kings.
What made a state

x: A ruler with power to tax and command
Officials and records, which is why writing mattered
Laws written down and enforced
An army to defend and conquer

deep.x: Not only Mesopotamia

Cities also grew independently along the Nile, the Indus (Mohenjo-daro, around 2500 BCE), the Yellow River in China and later in Mexico and Peru. Each time, the pattern was similar: farming surplus, then cities, then kings and writing.

deep.w: "An eye for an eye" meant equal justice
deep.r: In Hammurabi's code, punishment depended on rank: blinding a nobleman cost an eye, blinding a commoner cost silver

deep.x: Cities and states grew from the problem of managing a surplus: someone had to count it, guard it and decide who got it.

cards.title: Dinheiro
cards.text: Antes das moedas, as pessoas trocavam bens ou usavam pesos-padrão de prata e de cereais. As primeiras moedas surgiram na Lídia (atual Turquia) por volta de 600 a.C. Mais tarde, a China inventou o papel-moeda.

deep.x: Money does three jobs: it lets you buy without swapping goods directly, it measures value, and it stores wealth for later. Long before coins, Mesopotamians used weighed silver to keep accounts; the shekel was originally a weight of about 8 grams.
Coins, then paper

Lydian kings stamped lumps of electrum, a natural gold and silver alloy, so no one had to weigh them. The idea spread to Greek cities and Persia. In China, merchants used paper receipts for heavy coins, and the Song government issued official paper money in the 1020s. Europe's first banknotes came from Stockholm in 1661.
Portugal's money

x: The **real** was used for centuries, so big sums were counted in thousands of réis
The escudo replaced it in 1911
The euro arrived in notes and coins in 2002, at 200.482 escudos per euro

deep.w: Before money, people bartered goods
deep.r: Historians and anthropologists find little evidence of barter economies; communities mostly ran on credit and debts, recorded or remembered

deep.x: Money is a shared promise: it works only because everyone trusts others will accept it.

cards.title: A era da internet

events.l: World Wide Web aberta ao público

cards.text: O momento de viragem mais recente: computadores, internet e smartphones ligaram a maior parte da humanidade em poucas décadas e mudaram a forma como trabalhamos, aprendemos e comunicamos.

deep.x: The internet began as ARPANET, a US research network that sent its first message in 1969. The shared language TCP/IP arrived in 1983, and in 1989–91 Tim Berners-Lee at CERN, near Geneva, created the World Wide Web, making it easy for anyone to publish and link pages.
Faster than any earlier turning point
Writing took thousands of years to spread and printing centuries. The internet reached most of humanity in about 30 years.
What changed

x: Work: email, remote work and global supply chains
Learning: almost any knowledge is a search away
Politics and news: anyone can publish, including misinformation
Daily life: maps, banking and shopping in your pocket

deep.x: Still, around a quarter to a third of people remain offline, mostly in poorer, rural regions.
Well over 95% of intercontinental data travels through undersea cables, not satellites. Several, such as EllaLink to Brazil, land on Portugal's coast.
The internet is the printing press again, but for everyone at once, at almost no cost per copy.

quiz.q: Para que servia a maior parte da escrita mais antiga?
options: Fazer contas de bens e pagamentos
quiz.explain: As tábuas sumérias mais antigas são sobretudo registos de cereais, gado e rações.

quiz.q: Porque é que a agricultura levou ao aparecimento de cidades?
options: Os agricultores gostavam de viver perto uns dos outros
Os excedentes de comida podiam alimentar quem não cultivava
Eram precisas cidades para guardar as ferramentas
quiz.explain: Os excedentes alimentares sustentavam especialistas, governantes e comerciantes, o que tornou possíveis as vilas e as cidades.

quiz.q: Onde e quando surgiu a prensa de Gutenberg?
quiz.explain: Gutenberg trabalhou em Mainz por volta de 1450. (Os tipos móveis já existiam antes na China e na Coreia, mas a prensa dele transformou a Europa.)

quiz.q: Onde evoluiu primeiro o Homo sapiens?
quiz.explain: Os humanos modernos espalharam-se a partir de África.

quiz.q: Onde foram cunhadas as primeiras moedas?

lessons.title: Antigo Egito
lessons.summary: Pirâmides, faraós e a dádiva do Nilo.

cards.title: A dádiva do Nilo
cards.text: A civilização egípcia cresceu ao longo do Nilo. Todos os anos o rio transbordava e deixava um lodo negro e fértil, que permitia aos agricultores cultivar trigo e cevada no meio do deserto.

deep.x: The Greek historian Herodotus called Egypt "the gift of the Nile", and he was right. Egypt gets almost no rain. Without the river, it would be desert like the land on either side.
Why the river flooded

Every summer, monsoon rains fell on the highlands of Ethiopia. The Blue Nile carried that water, and tonnes of mineral-rich silt, north. From about July to October the river spread over its banks; when it fell back, it left a fresh layer of black mud. Farmers sowed straight into it.
Floods meant taxes

A good flood meant a big harvest; a low one meant famine; a very high one could wash villages away. Officials measured the river with **nilometers**, stone steps or shafts marked with levels, and set taxes according to how high the water rose.

x: The river was also Egypt's highway: boats sailed south with the wind and drifted north with the current
Papyrus reeds from its banks became paper, rope and boats

deep.x: The annual flood stopped after the Aswan High Dam was completed in 1970. Egypt now relies on fertilisers, as the silt is trapped behind the dam.
Egypt was a narrow green ribbon in a desert, and the yearly flood decided whether its people ate.

cards.title: Três impérios
cards.text: A história egípcia abrange cerca de 3000 anos, normalmente dividida em Império Antigo, Médio e Novo, separados por períodos de desunião.

deep.x: Egyptian history is so long that the ancient Egyptians themselves could look back on ruins that were already old. Historians follow a priest called Manetho, who around 280 BCE grouped the rulers into about 30 dynasties. Modern scholars bundle these into stable "kingdoms" and messy "intermediate periods".
What each is known for
The gaps between

In the intermediate periods, central power broke down. Local governors ruled their own areas, harvests failed or foreigners took over. During the Second Intermediate Period, people from western Asia known as the Hyksos ruled the north and brought horses and chariots. The New Kingdom pharaohs who drove them out used those chariots to build an empire reaching into Syria and Nubia.

x: Famous New Kingdom rulers: Hatshepsut, Akhenaten, Tutankhamun, Ramesses II
After about 1070 BCE, Egypt was often ruled by Libyans, Nubians, Persians and finally Greeks

deep.x: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid.
Ancient Egypt lasted about 3,000 years, longer than the time from the Roman Empire to today.

cards.title: As pirâmides

items.l: a estrutura mais alta da Terra

cards.text: A Grande Pirâmide de Gizé foi construída para o faraó Quéops por volta de 2560 a.C., com cerca de 2,3 milhões de blocos de pedra. Foi a estrutura mais alta feita pelo ser humano durante quase 4000 anos.

deep.x: Pyramids grew out of earlier tombs. Kings were first buried under flat-topped benches of mud brick called mastabas. Around 2670 BCE, the architect Imhotep stacked six of them in stone for King Djoser: the Step Pyramid at Saqqara. Khufu's father, Sneferu, then experimented until he got smooth sides right.
The numbers

The Great Pyramid was about 146 m tall when finished (about 139 m today, after losing its smooth white casing and tip). Its base is about 230 m on each side, and the sides face north, south, east and west with an error of a small fraction of a degree.

x: 2.3 million blocks over about 20 years
≈ 115,000 blocks a year, ≈ 300+ a day
about one block every 2 minutes in a 10-hour working day

deep.x: Why so big?

The pyramid was a machine for eternity: it protected the king's body and helped him join the Sun god in the sky. Its shape may echo the sun's rays or the mound from which Egyptians believed creation began.

x: The average block weighs about 2.5 tonnes; some granite beams weigh much more
Most limestone was quarried right next to the site

deep.w: The pyramids were built by aliens or a lost civilisation
deep.r: Quarries, tools, ramps, workers' villages and papyrus logbooks all show how Egyptians did it

deep.x: The Great Pyramid held the height record for nearly 4,000 years, until an English cathedral spire beat it in 1311.

cards.title: Quem as construiu?

items.r: construídas por equipas organizadas e pagas

cards.text: Não foram escravos, como muitas vezes se diz, mas equipas organizadas de trabalhadores pagos e de agricultores que trabalhavam durante a época das cheias, alojados em aldeias próximas. Os seus túmulos e padarias já foram escavados.

deep.x: In the 1990s, archaeologists excavated a town just south of the Giza pyramids. They found bakeries, breweries, dormitories and huge numbers of cattle, sheep and goat bones: the workers ate well. Nearby, workers were buried in their own small tombs, with bread and beer for the afterlife, an honour unlikely for slaves.
How they were organised
Labour was arranged like a team sport, with crews and gangs that had names such as "Friends of Khufu", which they painted on stones.

A core of skilled craftsmen worked year-round. Thousands of farmers joined on rotation, especially during the flood months when fields were under water. This was a kind of labour tax, not free choice, but they were fed, housed and cared for; skeletons show healed broken bones.
A logbook from 4,500 years ago
In 2013, papyri were found at Wadi al-Jarf on the Red Sea. They include the diary of an inspector called Merer, who led a team moving limestone for the Great Pyramid.
Merer's diary is the oldest inscribed papyrus ever found, written during Khufu's reign.
The pyramids were built by a well-fed, well-organised state workforce, which is more impressive than slavery, not less.

cards.title: Hieróglifos

steps: Mesmo texto em grego e em escritas egípcias

cards.text: Os egípcios escreviam com hieróglifos: imagens que representavam sons e ideias. A Pedra de Roseta, com o mesmo texto em três escritas, permitiu a Champollion decifrá-los em 1822.

deep.x: Hieroglyphs mixed three kinds of signs. Some stood for whole words, some for sounds, and some were silent hints that told the reader what kind of word it was. A scribe might spell a word with sound signs, then add a picture of a man to show it was a person.
Faster scripts

Carving was slow, so scribes also wrote a joined-up cursive called hieratic with reed pens on papyrus, and later an even quicker script called Demotic. Only a small elite, perhaps a few per cent of people, could read.
Cracking the code

The stone, a priestly decree of 196 BCE, was found by French soldiers in 1799 and has been in the British Museum since 1802. Because scholars could read the Greek, they had a key. Thomas Young made progress, but Jean-François Champollion cracked it in 1822. He spotted that names in oval frames (cartouches), like Ptolemy and Cleopatra, were spelled with sound signs, and he knew Coptic, a late form of Egyptian.

deep.w: Hieroglyphs are just picture-writing
deep.r: Most signs stood for sounds; it was a full writing system for a spoken language

deep.x: The Rosetta Stone worked because one known language unlocked another; translation was the key.

cards.title: Múmias
cards.text: Os egípcios acreditavam que o corpo era necessário na vida depois da morte. Os embalsamadores retiravam os órgãos, secavam o corpo com sal de natrão durante cerca de 40 dias e envolviam-no em linho.

deep.x: The first Egyptian mummies were accidental: bodies buried in hot, dry sand dried out naturally. When elites began burying people in coffins and tombs, bodies rotted, so embalmers learned to dry them artificially.
The process

The brain was pulled out through the nose with a hook and thrown away; Egyptians thought it unimportant. The heart, seat of thought and feeling, was left in place. Natron, a natural salt from dry lake beds, sucked out the water. Hundreds of square metres of linen might be used, with protective amulets tucked between layers.
Where the organs went
Each organ went into a **canopic jar** protected by one of the four sons of Horus.

x: Full embalming was expensive; poorer people had simpler treatment
Millions of animals, from cats to ibises, were mummified as offerings

deep.x: In Europe from the Middle Ages to the 1700s, ground-up mummy, called "mumia", was sold by apothecaries as medicine.
Mummification was a drying process with a religious purpose: keeping the body ready for the soul.

cards.title: Faraós e deuses
cards.text: O faraó era visto como um deus vivo e a ligação entre o povo e o divino. Os egípcios adoravam muitos deuses: Rá, o Sol, Osíris, da vida depois da morte, Ísis, Hórus e Anúbis.

deep.x: "Pharaoh" comes from the Egyptian for "great house", meaning the palace, a bit like saying "the White House". The king's job was to keep **ma'at**: cosmic order, truth and justice. He built temples, made offerings and defeated enemies so that the Nile would flood and the Sun would rise.
Judgement after death
Egyptians believed the dead faced a test in the hall of Osiris.
The Book of the Dead, spells written on papyrus and placed in tombs, helped the dead say the right things.
An experiment in one god

Around 1350 BCE, Akhenaten promoted a single sun-disc god, the Aten, closed old temples and built a new capital. After his death, priests and his successors, including his son Tutankhamun, restored the old gods and tried to erase his memory.
Hatshepsut, a woman, ruled as pharaoh for about 20 years around 1470 BCE and was often shown with the king's false beard.
The pharaoh was the hinge between people and gods; if he kept order, the world kept turning.

cards.title: Tutankhamon
cards.text: Um rei-menino pouco importante, que morreu por volta dos 19 anos, Tutankhamon ficou famoso porque o seu túmulo foi encontrado quase intacto por Howard Carter em 1922, cheio de tesouros, incluindo a máscara de ouro.

deep.x: Tutankhamun became king aged about eight or nine, around 1332 BCE, and died about ten years later. DNA studies suggest he was Akhenaten's son. Born Tutankhaten, he changed his name to honour Amun as the old religion returned.
Why his tomb survived

Most royal tombs in the Valley of the Kings were robbed in ancient times. Tutankhamun's small tomb was entered by robbers soon after burial but resealed; later, workers' huts built over its entrance hid it. On 4 November 1922 Howard Carter, funded by Lord Carnarvon, found the steps.
How did he die?
Nobody is sure. Scans show a broken leg that may not have healed, malaria parasites and a bone disorder in his foot. Earlier theories of murder are now considered unlikely.

deep.w: The curse killed the discoverers
deep.r: Lord Carnarvon died of an infected mosquito bite in 1923, but most of the team lived long lives; Carter died in 1939

deep.x: Tutankhamun is famous not for what he did, but because his tomb is the only royal one found almost intact.

cards.title: A ciência egípcia
cards.text: Os egípcios criaram um calendário de 365 dias, uma geometria prática para voltar a medir os campos depois das cheias, uma medicina registada em papiro e uma engenharia notável.

deep.x: Egyptian science was practical: it served farming, building, medicine and religion. Much of what we know comes from a few surviving papyri.
The calendar

x: 12 months × 30 days = 360
+ 5 extra festival days = 365
the real year is about 365.24 days, so it slipped 1 day every 4 years

deep.x: When Julius Caesar reformed Rome's calendar in 46 BCE, he used advice from an astronomer in Alexandria and added a leap day. Egyptians also split day and night into 12 parts each, the origin of our 24 hours.
Maths and medicine
To find a circle's area, the Rhind papyrus says: take away a ninth of the diameter and square the rest.

x: Diameter 9
true area is about 63.6, less than 1% off

deep.x: The Edwin Smith papyrus describes injuries calmly, with examination, diagnosis and treatment, and some of its remedies, like honey on wounds, really work.
The pyramids' slopes were set with the "seked": how many palms the face moves in for each cubit it rises.
Egyptian science was built for jobs: re-measuring fields, counting days and healing wounds.

cards.title: Cleópatra
cards.text: Cleópatra VII, a última governante efetiva do reino ptolemaico, era de ascendência grega macedónia. Depois da sua derrota, ao lado de Marco António, o Egito tornou-se uma província romana em 30 a.C.

deep.x: After Alexander the Great conquered Egypt in 332 BCE, his general Ptolemy took it on Alexander's death and founded a dynasty. For about 300 years Egypt was ruled by Greek-speaking Macedonian kings and queens from Alexandria, a city of Greek culture with its famous library.
A ruler, not just a romance

Cleopatra was the first of her dynasty said to have learned the Egyptian language, and ancient writers say she spoke many others. Her goal was to keep Egypt independent as Rome swallowed the Mediterranean. She allied with Julius Caesar, with whom she had a son, and then with Mark Antony.
The end

Octavian, Caesar's adopted heir, defeated Antony and Cleopatra at the sea battle of Actium in 31 BCE. A year later both killed themselves; the story of the snakebite is traditional but uncertain. Octavian made Egypt his personal province, and its grain fed Rome.

deep.w: Cleopatra was famous mainly for her beauty
deep.r: Ancient writers stressed her intelligence, charm and conversation more than her looks

deep.x: Cleopatra was the last of the Greek kings of Egypt, and her defeat ended 3,000 years of independent pharaohs.

options: A cheia anual deixava lodo fértil

quiz.explain: O mesmo texto em três escritas.

lessons.title: Grécia Antiga
lessons.summary: Democracia, filosofia e os Jogos Olímpicos.

cards.title: Cidades-Estado
cards.text: A Grécia Antiga não era um só país, mas centenas de cidades-Estado (pólis) como Atenas, Esparta, Corinto e Tebas, que partilhavam a língua e os deuses mas muitas vezes estavam em guerra umas com as outras.

deep.x: Greece is a land of mountains, narrow valleys and islands. Communities were cut off from each other, so each grew into its own **polis**: a town with its farmland, its own laws, army, coins and gods. Historians count over 1,000 of them, most with only a few thousand people.
What united them
They called themselves Hellenes and everyone else "barbarians", people whose language sounded like "bar-bar".
Spreading across the sea
When land ran short, cities sent out colonies around the Mediterranean and Black Sea.
Rivalry often turned violent. The Peloponnesian War between Athens and Sparta and their allies (431–404 BCE) exhausted Greece.

deep.w: Ulysses founded Lisbon
deep.r: It's a legend; the name Olisipo is probably pre-Roman, and Greek colonies in Iberia were mostly on the Mediterranean coast

deep.x: Greece's geography made it a family of rival cities rather than a single nation.

cards.title: A democracia ateniense
cards.text: A partir de cerca de 508 a.C., os cidadãos atenienses votavam diretamente as leis na Assembleia. Mas só os homens adultos e livres contavam como cidadãos: as mulheres, os escravos e os estrangeiros estavam excluídos.

deep.x: In 508/507 BCE, the reformer Cleisthenes reorganised Athenians into new tribes that mixed people from city, coast and countryside, breaking the power of old noble families. The word democracy comes from **demos** (people) and **kratos** (power).
How it worked

The Assembly met on the Pnyx hill about 40 times a year, and some decisions needed 6,000 citizens present. Most officials were chosen by lot, because Athenians thought elections favoured the rich and famous. From the 450s, jurors were paid, so poorer citizens could take part.

x: Each citizen scratches a name on a pottery shard (ostrakon)
if at least 6,000 votes are cast
the most-named man is exiled for 10 years

deep.x: That's **ostracism**, a way to remove anyone who seemed too powerful.
Who was left out
Perhaps 30,000 adult male citizens, out of a population of roughly 250,000–300,000 in Attica. Women, slaves and foreign residents had no vote.
In Portugal, women first voted under restrictions in the 1930s; all adults could vote freely only after 1974.
Athens invented rule by citizens, even though its idea of "citizen" was very narrow.

cards.title: Filosofia
cards.text: Os pensadores gregos perguntavam como devemos viver e como funciona o mundo. Sócrates questionava tudo, Platão fundou a Academia e Aristóteles estudou tudo, da lógica à biologia.

deep.x: Philosophy means "love of wisdom". Around 600 BCE, thinkers in Ionia (today's western Turkey) began explaining the world through nature and reason rather than myths. Thales said everything came from water; Democritus later suggested everything was made of tiny, uncuttable "atoms".
Each was the teacher of the next.
Three giants

Socrates questioned people until their confident beliefs fell apart. Athens put him on trial for "corrupting the young" and executed him with poison hemlock. We know him through Plato's dialogues. Plato argued that true reality is a world of perfect ideas. Aristotle preferred observation: he classified hundreds of animals and created formal logic.
Later schools

x: Stoics: control what you can, accept what you can't
Epicureans: seek a calm, simple, pleasant life
Sceptics: suspend judgement when evidence is unclear

deep.x: Plato's Academy gave us the word "academy"; Aristotle's school, the Lyceum, gave Portuguese the word "liceu" for secondary school.
Greek philosophy's big idea was that the world, and how to live in it, can be understood by reasoning.

cards.title: As Guerras Persas
cards.text: O enorme império persa invadiu a Grécia duas vezes. Os gregos venceram em Maratona (490 a.C.), aguentaram o desfiladeiro das Termópilas tempo suficiente e ganharam a batalha naval de Salamina (480 a.C.).

deep.x: The Persian Empire stretched from Egypt to India. When Greek cities in Ionia rebelled in 499 BCE, Athens sent help. King Darius decided to punish it.
Marathon

About 10,000 Athenians and Plataeans charged the Persian landing force on the plain of Marathon. Herodotus says 192 Athenians and about 6,400 Persians died; the numbers may be exaggerated but the victory was real.
Thermopylae and Salamis

Ten years later Xerxes invaded with a huge army and fleet. At the narrow pass of Thermopylae, about 7,000 Greeks, including 300 Spartans under King Leonidas, held out for three days before being outflanked. Athens was evacuated and burned. Then the Athenian Themistocles lured the Persian fleet into the narrow straits of Salamis, where heavy Persian ships couldn't manoeuvre and Greek triremes rammed them.
Athens' fleet existed because, a few years earlier, Themistocles persuaded citizens to spend a rich new silver find on about 200 warships instead of sharing it out.

x: The modern marathon is 42.195 km
fixed at the 1908 London Olympics
inspired by the legend of a runner from Marathon to Athens

deep.x: A few small cities beat the world's largest empire by choosing where to fight.

cards.title: Os Jogos Olímpicos
cards.text: Os antigos Jogos Olímpicos realizavam-se em Olímpia de quatro em quatro anos desde 776 a.C., em honra de Zeus. As guerras paravam durante os jogos. Os Jogos Olímpicos modernos foram retomados em Atenas em 1896.

deep.x: For the first recorded Games, in 776 BCE, there was only one event: a sprint of one stadion, about 192 m at Olympia. Over time came longer races, wrestling, boxing, the pentathlon, chariot racing and the brutal pankration, a mix of boxing and wrestling with few rules.
Who took part

Competitors were free Greek men, and they competed naked. Married women weren't allowed to watch, but women had their own games for Hera, and rich women could win as owners of chariot teams. The official prize was an olive wreath, but home cities gave winners money, free meals and statues.
The revival

The French educator Pierre de Coubertin revived the Games; the first modern Olympics were held in Athens in 1896. Portugal's first gold came in 1984, when Carlos Lopes won the marathon in Los Angeles aged 37.

deep.w: Wars stopped for the Olympics
deep.r: The sacred truce protected athletes and spectators travelling to Olympia; wars elsewhere usually carried on

deep.x: The Olympics began as a religious festival with one foot race and grew into the world's biggest sporting event.

cards.title: Alexandre, o Grande
cards.text: Alexandre da Macedónia conquistou um império da Grécia ao Egito e à Índia, antes de morrer aos 32 anos, em 323 a.C. A língua e a cultura gregas espalharam-se por toda a região (a época helenística).

deep.x: Alexander was born in 356 BCE, son of Philip II, who had made Macedon the strongest power in Greece. He was taught by Aristotle and became king at 20 when his father was murdered.
Why he won

His army combined a phalanx of men with very long pikes and fast cavalry, which Alexander led himself. He beat the Persian king Darius III three times and took over the whole Persian Empire. In India his exhausted soldiers refused to go further, and he turned back.
After him
He died in Babylon, probably of illness, before turning 33. With no adult heir, his generals fought over the empire and split it.
The Hellenistic age

Greek became the common language from Egypt to Afghanistan. Greek-style cities, theatres and gymnasiums spread, mixing with Egyptian, Persian and Indian cultures. The New Testament was later written in this common Greek.
Alexander founded around 20 cities named Alexandria, and one, Bucephala, named after his horse.
In 13 years Alexander conquered an empire, and Greek culture outlived it by centuries.

cards.title: A ciência grega
cards.text: A geometria de Euclides, a física de Arquimedes, a medicina de Hipócrates e a medição do perímetro da Terra por Eratóstenes vieram todas do mundo grego.

deep.x: Greek thinkers tried to find general rules behind what they saw, and to prove them. That habit of proof is their great contribution.
Euclid and Archimedes

Euclid's Elements started from a few simple axioms and proved hundreds of results step by step. It was used as a textbook for over 2,000 years. Archimedes of Syracuse worked out the law of the lever and why things float, and he trapped π between two fractions using polygons.

x: Draw 96-sided polygons inside and outside a circle
compare their perimeters

deep.x: Medicine
Hippocrates and his followers taught that disease came from natural causes, not angry gods, and that doctors should observe patients closely. Doctors still refer to the Hippocratic Oath.
Alexandria
Under the Ptolemies, the Museum and Library of Alexandria paid scholars to research. Here Eratosthenes measured the Earth and Herophilus dissected human bodies.
The Antikythera mechanism, found in a shipwreck, is a bronze gear device from around 100 BCE that predicted eclipses: nothing as complex survives for over 1,000 years after.
The Greeks turned knowledge into proof: not just what works, but why it must be true.

cards.title: Medir a Terra
cards.text: Por volta de 240 a.C., Eratóstenes comparou o ângulo do Sol ao meio-dia em Siena e em Alexandria. A partir de uma diferença de 7° e da distância entre as cidades, estimou o perímetro da Terra com notável precisão.

deep.x: Eratosthenes, head of the Library of Alexandria, heard that at noon on midsummer's day the Sun shone straight down a well at Syene (modern Aswan): it was directly overhead. At the same moment in Alexandria, further north, a vertical stick cast a shadow.
The geometry
Because the Sun is so far away, its rays arrive parallel. So the angle of the shadow equals the angle between the two cities at Earth's centre.

x: Distance ≈ 5,000 stadia
with a stadion of about 157–185 m, that's about 39,000–46,000 km

deep.x: How good was it?
We don't know exactly how long his stadion was, so his accuracy is debated: somewhere between about 2% and 15% off. Either way, the method was sound.

deep.w: Before Columbus, people thought the Earth was flat
deep.r: Educated Europeans knew it was round since Greek times; the argument was about its size, and Columbus underestimated it

deep.x: King João II's advisers rejected Columbus' plan partly because they judged, correctly, that Asia was much further west than he claimed.
With a stick, a shadow and a known distance, Eratosthenes measured the planet without leaving Egypt.

cards.title: Teatro
cards.text: Os gregos inventaram a tragédia e a comédia como formas de teatro. Enormes teatros ao ar livre como o de Epidauro têm uma acústica tão boa que um sussurro no palco se ouve nas últimas filas.

deep.x: Greek theatre grew out of festivals for Dionysus, god of wine. At Athens' City Dionysia, playwrights competed for prizes. Around 534 BCE, Thespis is said to have stepped out of the chorus as the first actor, which is why actors are still called "thespians".
Tragedy and comedy
Plays used at most three speaking actors, all men, wearing masks to switch roles, plus a chorus that sang and danced. Tragedies explored fate, pride and justice; comedies mocked politicians by name.
The building

Epidaurus, built in the 300s BCE, seats about 14,000. Its rows of limestone seats seem to damp low background noise while reflecting voices. Guides love to demonstrate the acoustics with a coin dropped on stage; recent measurements show normal speech carries very well, though whether a true whisper reaches the top rows is debated.
Words from the stage

x: Scene from skene, the stage building
Orchestra from the dancing floor
Tragedy, possibly "goat song"

deep.x: The Greek word for actor, hypokritēs, gave us "hypocrite": someone playing a part.
The Greeks invented drama as a public event where a whole city watched itself.

cards.title: Palavras que ainda usamos
cards.text: Muitas palavras inglesas e portuguesas vêm do grego: democracia, filosofia, teatro, telefone, biologia, geografia, matemática.

deep.x: Greek was the language of learning in the ancient Mediterranean, and scholars kept borrowing from it. Many "Greek" words were actually built much later from Greek parts, like telephone in the 1800s.

x: tele (far) + phone (sound) = telephone
bio (life) + logia (study) = biology
geo (earth) + graphein (write) = geography

deep.x: In everyday Portuguese
Greek came into Portuguese through Latin, the Church and science.
Surprising origins

x: Igreja comes from ekklesia, the name of Athens' citizens' assembly
Idiot comes from idiōtēs, a private person who didn't take part in public life
Atom comes from atomos, "uncuttable", though we later split it
Alphabet is just the first two Greek letters, alpha and beta

deep.x: Escola and school come from scholē, which originally meant "leisure": the free time to think and learn.
Every time you say "democracia" or "telefone", you speak a little ancient Greek.

quiz.explain: As mulheres, os escravos e os estrangeiros não podiam.

lessons.title: China Imperial
lessons.summary: Dinastias, invenções e exames ao longo de mais de 3000 anos.

cards.title: Ossos oraculares

deep.x: The Shang ruled the Yellow River valley from roughly 1600 to 1046 BCE. Their last capital, near modern Anyang in Henan province, has produced more than 150,000 inscribed fragments, the earliest large body of Chinese writing.
How a divination worked

Diviners carved rows of small hollows into the back of a bone or shell. A heated rod pressed into a hollow made the surface crack with a sharp pop, and the shape of the crack was read as yes or no, lucky or unlucky.
What kings worried about

x: Will it rain? Will the millet harvest be good?
Should we attack this enemy?
Will the queen's childbirth be lucky?
Why does the king have toothache? Which ancestor is angry?

deep.x: One name that appears often is Fu Hao, a royal consort who also led armies. Her tomb, found intact at Anyang in 1976, held hundreds of bronzes and jades.
The bones were rediscovered around 1899, when scholars noticed carvings on "dragon bones" sold in pharmacies to be ground into medicine.

deep.w: Chinese characters have not changed in 3,000 years
deep.r: The writing system is continuous, but the shapes of characters changed greatly and thousands of new ones were added

deep.x: Chinese writing began as a conversation between kings and their ancestors, scratched into bone.

cards.text:
A escrita mais antiga da China sobrevive em ossos. Por volta de 1200 a.C., os reis da dinastia Shang perguntavam aos antepassados sobre colheitas, guerras e doenças, aquecendo omoplatas de boi e carapaças de tartaruga até racharem.

Os adivinhos liam as rachas e gravavam no osso a pergunta e, por vezes, o resultado. Esses sinais são os antepassados diretos dos caracteres chineses de hoje.

cards.title: O Primeiro Imperador

deep.x: Zheng became king of Qin at about 13 and spent some 25 years conquering the six other major states. The title he invented, huangdi, combined words used for legendary sages and gods, and every Chinese ruler used it until 1912. Many scholars think the Western name "China" comes from Qin.
One standard for everything

Standard axles mattered because carts wore deep ruts into dirt roads, and a cart of the wrong width could not use them. The old noble domains were replaced by commanderies run by officials the emperor could appoint and dismiss.
Harsh rule

Qin followed **Legalism**, a philosophy that kept people in line with strict laws and severe punishments. According to the historian Sima Qian, writing about a century later, the emperor ordered books burned in 213 BCE and scholars killed. Some historians think the account is exaggerated, but the regime was certainly feared. Hundreds of thousands of conscripts built roads, canals, walls and his tomb.
The Terracotta Army

In 1974 farmers digging a well near Xi'an found pieces of a clay soldier. Excavations revealed pits holding an estimated 8,000 life-size soldiers, plus horses and chariots, guarding the emperor in death.
Sima Qian wrote that the tomb held rivers of mercury. Soil tests over the mound have found unusually high mercury levels, one reason it has not been opened.
The Qin dynasty lasted only 15 years, but its standards and its idea of one emperor over one China lasted more than 2,000.

cards.text:
Após séculos de guerra entre estados rivais, o rei Zheng de Qin conquistou-os a todos e, em 221 a.C., proclamou-se Qin Shi Huang, o "Primeiro Imperador".

Governou através de funcionários nomeados em vez de nobres e impôs uma só escrita, uma só moeda e um só sistema de pesos. A sua dinastia caiu pouco depois da sua morte, mas a ideia de uma China única perdurou.

cards.title: As Grandes Muralhas

deep.x: A Chinese government survey published in 2012 counted every wall, trench and natural barrier from all periods and arrived at about 21,000 km, more than half the distance around the Equator. Many stretches are now low earth ridges that are easy to miss.
Building materials
Builders used whatever was nearby.

x: Rammed earth: soil pounded in layers inside wooden frames
In the Gobi desert: layers of gravel with reeds or tamarisk branches
Ming sections: fired bricks and cut stone, bonded with lime mortar

deep.x: Studies of Ming mortar found sticky rice soup mixed into the lime, which made it stronger and more water-resistant.
What walls were for

A wall could not stop a determined army, but it slowed raids, funnelled traffic through gates and let watchtowers pass warnings with fire at night and smoke by day. It also marked where settled farming China ended. In 1644 the Manchus came through the Shanhai Pass at its eastern end after a Ming general opened the gate to them.

deep.w: The Great Wall is visible from space with the naked eye
deep.r: It is very long but only a few metres wide and the colour of the land; China's first astronaut, Yang Liwei, said in 2003 that he could not see it

deep.x: The Great Wall is a 2,000-year collection of frontiers, each one a snapshot of where China's rulers drew their line.

cards.text:
A Grande Muralha não é uma muralha, mas muitas, construídas ao longo de cerca de 2000 anos por diferentes estados e dinastias para proteger as terras de cultivo dos cavaleiros da estepe do norte.

Os famosos troços de pedra e tijolo perto de Pequim são relativamente recentes: a maioria foi construída pela dinastia Ming, sobretudo no século XVI. As muralhas mais antigas eram sobretudo de terra batida.

cards.title: Os Han e a Rota da Seda

deep.x: In 138 BCE Emperor Wu sent an officer called Zhang Qian west to find allies against the Xiongnu, a nomadic confederation that raided Han lands. He was captured by the Xiongnu and held for about ten years, escaped, and returned around 125 BCE without an alliance but with something more valuable: detailed reports on the kingdoms of Central Asia.
Heavenly horses

Zhang Qian described tall, fast horses in the Ferghana valley, in today's Uzbekistan. Han cavalry needed them to fight the steppe riders, so the emperor sent armies thousands of kilometres to get them. Garrisons and watchtowers were then built along the Gansu corridor to protect the caravans.
Two empires that never met

The Romans knew the Chinese only as the Seres, the "silk people", and the Han knew Rome vaguely as Daqin. In 97 CE an envoy, Gan Ying, was sent to reach it; he got as far as the Persian Gulf or the Black Sea region and turned back. Goods, not people, made the whole journey, passing through Parthian and other middlemen.

items.l: people in the Han census of 2 CE

deep.x: A Chinese chronicle records that in 166 CE visitors claiming to represent the Roman emperor Andun, probably Marcus Aurelius, arrived by sea. They were most likely enterprising merchants.
Ideas on the road
Buddhism reached China from India along these routes in the 1st century CE. Monks, translators and pilgrims followed the merchants, and cave temples grew up at oasis towns such as Dunhuang.
The Han turned a military search for horses and allies into a lasting link between East and West.

cards.text:
A dinastia Han (206 a.C.–220 d.C.) governava aproximadamente tantas pessoas como o Império Romano, na mesma época. A maioria dos chineses ainda se diz Han.

Os exércitos e enviados Han abriram rotas pela Ásia Central. Por elas, a seda viajou para ocidente, enquanto cavalos, novas culturas e, mais tarde, o budismo chegaram a oriente.

cards.title: Os exames imperiais

deep.x: Confucius (551–479 BCE) taught that society works when rulers govern by moral example and everyone respects their duties: children to parents, subjects to rulers, friends to friends. Han emperors made his teachings state orthodoxy, and the Sui dynasty began formal exams in 605 CE. The system matured under the Song, when printed books made study more widely possible.
Days in a cell

At the provincial level, candidates were locked into tiny brick cells for about three days, with one board as a desk and another as a bed. The examination hall in Nanjing had about 20,000 cells. Answers were recopied by clerks before marking, so examiners could not recognise handwriting.
Very few winners

Pass rates at the higher levels were often only a few per cent. Men sat the exams again and again, some into old age. Cheating was a constant battle: museums hold silk undershirts covered in thousands of tiny handwritten passages from the classics.

deep.w: Anyone could rise through the exams
deep.r: In theory most men could sit them, but women were excluded and years of study cost money, so wealthy families had a big advantage

deep.x: Copied abroad

Korea and Vietnam adopted similar exams. European writers admired the idea of officials chosen by merit, and Britain's competitive civil-service exams, introduced from the 1850s, were partly inspired by the Chinese example.
China's exams made learning the road to power for over a thousand years, an early form of government by merit.

cards.text:
Durante cerca de 1300 anos, de 605 a 1905, a China escolheu muitos dos seus funcionários através de exames escritos sobre os clássicos confucianos, e não apenas pelo nascimento.

Os candidatos memorizavam centenas de milhares de caracteres de textos antigos e escreviam ensaios sobre como governar. Passar trazia prestígio, poder e riqueza a toda uma família.

cards.title: Quatro grandes invenções

deep.x: Paper

Early paper fragments date from the 2nd century BCE. In 105 CE a court official, Cai Lun, presented an improved recipe: mulberry bark, hemp, rags and old fishing nets, pulped, spread on a screen and dried. Papermaking reached Samarkand in the 700s, Baghdad soon after, and Europe through al-Andalus, where Xàtiva near Valencia was making paper by the 1100s.
Printing

Woodblock printing carved a whole page into one block. The oldest dated printed book, a Buddhist text called the Diamond Sutra, was printed in 868 and found in a cave at Dunhuang. Around 1040 an artisan called Bi Sheng made movable type from baked clay, but with thousands of characters to cast, whole-page blocks often stayed cheaper.
Compass

Chinese thinkers knew that lodestone points south and first used it for divination. In 1088 the scholar Shen Kuo described a magnetised needle, and by about 1100 sailors used one to navigate in cloudy weather.
Gunpowder
Alchemists searching for an elixir of long life noticed that mixing saltpetre, sulphur and charcoal could burn a house down. Fire arrows, bombs and rockets followed.
China produced many other inventions too, including cast iron, the wheelbarrow, porcelain and an earthquake detector built by Zhang Heng in 132 CE.
The four inventions spread knowledge, guided ships and changed warfare, and every one crossed Asia before reaching Europe.

cards.text:
O papel, a impressão, a bússola magnética e a pólvora são muitas vezes chamados as "quatro grandes invenções" da China. Cada uma espalhou-se depois para ocidente e mudou o mundo.

Em 1620, o filósofo inglês Francis Bacon escreveu que a impressão, a pólvora e a bússola tinham transformado o mundo mais do que qualquer império. Ele não sabia de onde vinham.

cards.title: Tang e Song

deep.x: Tang Chang'an had perhaps a million people in and around its walls, laid out on a grid of wide avenues with two great markets. Persians, Sogdians, Arabs, Koreans and Japanese lived there, and Buddhist temples stood near Zoroastrian, Manichaean and Christian ones. Japan copied its layout for its capitals at Nara and Kyoto.
Poets and an empress

Li Bai and Du Fu, still memorised by Chinese schoolchildren, wrote in the 700s. Wu Zetian became the only woman in Chinese history to rule as emperor in her own name, from 690 to 705. Then the An Lushan rebellion (755–763) devastated the empire, and the Tang never fully recovered.
The Song economy

x: Fast-ripening rice from Champa (now in Vietnam) allowed two harvests a year in the south
China's population passed 100 million
Sichuan merchants used paper notes; the state took over issuing them in 1024
Kaifeng and later Hangzhou may each have held around a million people

deep.x: Painters and scholars

Song scholar-officials, chosen by exam, also painted, wrote poetry and practised calligraphy. The long scroll *Along the River During the Qingming Festival*, painted in the 1100s, shows more than 800 people going about city life in minute detail.
Despite this wealth, the Song paid large yearly sums of silver and silk to northern neighbours to keep the peace, and still lost the north to the Jurchen in 1127.
Tang brought power and openness; Song brought wealth, cities and paper money that later amazed Marco Polo.

cards.text:
A dinastia Tang (618–907) governava a partir de Chang'an, talvez a maior cidade do mundo, cheia de mercadores, monges e enviados de toda a Ásia. Foi a idade de ouro da poesia chinesa.

A Song (960–1279) era militarmente mais fraca, mas mais rica: o cultivo de arroz disparou, as cidades cresceram e o governo emitiu o primeiro papel-moeda do mundo.

cards.title: As frotas de Zheng He

deep.x: Zheng He was born around 1371 into a Muslim family in Yunnan. Captured as a boy when Ming armies conquered the province, he was made a eunuch and served Prince Zhu Di. When the prince seized the throne as the Yongle Emperor, Zheng He became one of his most trusted commanders.
Treasure ships

Ming records describe the largest "treasure ships" as about 120–135 m long. Many historians think that is exaggerated and that 60–75 m is more likely, but even that dwarfed European ships of the time.
Where they went

x: Champa, Java, Sumatra and Malacca
Sri Lanka and Calicut in India
Hormuz, Aden and the Red Sea
Mogadishu and Malindi in East Africa

deep.x: In 1414 the fleet brought a giraffe from East Africa, via Bengal, to the Ming court. Courtiers presented it as a qilin, a mythical creature said to appear only under a wise ruler.
Why it stopped

After Yongle died in 1424, officials argued that the voyages were hugely expensive and brought back mainly luxuries. The real threat was the Mongols in the north, so money went to walls and to the new capital in Beijing. Later Ming governments even restricted private sea trade.

deep.w: Zheng He reached America in 1421
deep.r: This popular claim from a 2002 book has no evidence behind it and is rejected by historians

deep.x: In the early 1400s China had the greatest navy in the world, and chose to stop using it.

cards.text:
Entre 1405 e 1433, o almirante Ming Zheng He comandou sete enormes frotas através do oceano Índico, chegando à Índia, à Arábia e à África Oriental.

As viagens exibiam o poder Ming e recolhiam tributos. Depois pararam: a corte fechou-se sobre si mesma e a China deixou os oceanos a outros, décadas antes da chegada dos portugueses.

cards.title: A dinastia Qing

deep.x: The Manchus were a small minority ruling a vast Han majority. They kept many Ming institutions, including the exams, but required Chinese men to shave the front of the head and wear a long braid, the queue, as a sign of loyalty.
The high Qing

Kangxi (ruled 1661–1722) and his grandson Qianlong (1735–1796) had two of the longest reigns in Chinese history. Their campaigns brought Taiwan, Mongolia, Xinjiang and Tibet under Qing control, roughly setting the borders of modern China.
Trade on China's terms

From 1757 Western merchants could trade only at Canton (Guangzhou), through licensed Chinese firms. Europeans paid for tea, silk and porcelain mostly in silver. In 1793 a British embassy under Lord Macartney asked for wider access; Qianlong replied that China had no need of British goods.
Opium and unequal treaties
The treaties that followed opened more ports, gave foreigners legal privileges and fixed low tariffs. Chinese historians call the era that began then the "century of humiliation".
The Taiping Rebellion (1850–1864), led by a man who believed he was the younger brother of Jesus, became one of the deadliest wars in history, with an estimated 20–30 million deaths.
Portugal had a presence in Macau from 1557, long before Britain took Hong Kong. It was handed back to China on 20 December 1999, the last European colony in Asia.
The Qing built China's largest empire, then struggled to adapt when industrial powers arrived by sea.

cards.text:
Em 1644, os manchus, vindos do nordeste, tomaram Pequim e fundaram a Qing, a última dinastia da China. Com imperadores como Kangxi e Qianlong, quase duplicou de tamanho e enriqueceu.

No século XIX enfrentou potências ocidentais em ascensão, duas Guerras do Ópio, tratados desiguais e uma guerra civil devastadora, a Rebelião Taiping.

cards.title: O fim do império, 1912

deep.x: For almost half a century real power lay with the Empress Dowager Cixi, who dominated the court from 1861 until her death in 1908. She backed some modernisation, such as arsenals and shipyards, but in 1898 she crushed a burst of reforms by her nephew, the Guangxu Emperor, after only about a hundred days.
Shocks from abroad

The Boxers, a movement that blamed foreigners and Christians for China's troubles, besieged the foreign legations in Beijing in 1900. An army of eight foreign powers took the city, and China was forced to pay a vast indemnity.
Revolution

Revolutionary groups, many organised by Sun Yat-sen from exile, staged a series of failed uprisings. The one that worked began almost by accident: on 9 October 1911 a bomb went off by mistake in neighbouring Hankou, police found membership lists, and plotters in the Wuchang army rose the next day before they could be arrested. Province after province then declared independence from the Qing.
The last emperor

Puyi was allowed to live on in the Forbidden City until 1924. Japan later made him puppet ruler of Manchukuo, in north-east China. After years in Soviet and Chinese prisons he lived as an ordinary citizen in Beijing until his death in 1967, a story told in the 1987 film *The Last Emperor*.
Portugal had become a republic on 5 October 1910, so both countries ended their monarchies within about 16 months of each other.
The fall of the Qing did not end China's troubles: it opened decades of warlords, invasion and civil war.

cards.text:
Depois de derrotas frente às potências ocidentais e ao Japão, as reformas chegaram tarde demais. Em outubro de 1911, uma revolta militar em Wuchang espalhou-se pelas províncias.

A 1 de janeiro de 1912 foi proclamada a República da China e, em fevereiro, o imperador Puyi, de seis anos, abdicou. Mais de 2000 anos de governo imperial, iniciados pelo Primeiro Imperador em 221 a.C., tinham chegado ao fim.

quiz.q: Quem unificou a China em 221 a.C.?
quiz.explain: Adotou o novo título de "Primeiro Imperador".

quiz.q: Para que serviam os ossos oraculares Shang?
quiz.explain: Os adivinhos aqueciam-nos e liam as rachas.

quiz.q: Que dinastia construiu a maior parte da Grande Muralha de pedra e tijolo que hoje vemos?
Qual destas NÃO é uma das quatro grandes invenções da China?
quiz.explain: As quatro são o papel, a impressão, a bússola e a pólvora.

quiz.q: Quando abdicou o último imperador, Puyi?
quiz.explain: A República da China foi proclamada a 1 de janeiro de 1912.

lessons.title: O Império Romano
lessons.summary: De uma pequena cidade a senhora do Mediterrâneo, incluindo a Lusitânia.

cards.title: Reino, república, império
cards.text: Segundo a tradição, Roma foi fundada em 753 a.C. Foi governada por reis, depois tornou-se uma república dirigida por magistrados eleitos e pelo Senado, e mais tarde um império sob Augusto, a partir de 27 a.C.

deep.x: Legend says Rome was founded by Romulus, a twin raised by a she-wolf. Archaeology shows villages on Rome's hills from around that time, which merged into a town by a ford on the Tiber.
The republic
After expelling their last king, Romans hated the word "king" so much they built a system to stop any one man taking power. Power was shared and limited in time.
Around 450 BCE, Rome's laws were written down on the Twelve Tables so that everyone could know them.
Why it became an empire

Conquests brought slaves, loot and huge armies loyal to their generals rather than to the state. In the first century BCE, generals like Marius, Sulla, Pompey and Julius Caesar fought civil wars. Caesar's adopted heir Octavian won, kept the Senate and elections for show, and took the name Augustus. He held real power until his death in 14 CE.

deep.w: Julius Caesar was the first Roman emperor
deep.r: Caesar was dictator; Augustus was the first emperor. "Caesar" became a title, which gave us Kaiser and Tsar

deep.x: Rome kept the look of a republic long after one man held all the power.

cards.title: A dimensão do império
cards.text: No seu auge, por volta de 117 d.C., sob Trajano, o império estendia-se da Britânia à Mesopotâmia e do Reno ao Norte de África, com talvez 50–70 milhões de pessoas.

deep.x: At its largest, the Roman Empire covered about 5 million km² and every coast of the Mediterranean, which Romans called **Mare Nostrum**, "our sea".
What held it together

items: Latin in the west, Greek in east

deep.x: Local towns largely governed themselves, collected taxes and copied Roman life: baths, forums, theatres. In 212 CE, almost all free men in the empire were made Roman citizens.
Too big to hold
Trajan's conquests in Mesopotamia were given up by his successor Hadrian almost at once. Hadrian preferred fixed borders and built a wall across northern Britain from 122 CE.

x: Rome to Britain's Hadrian's Wall
about 2,000 km by road
roughly 6–8 weeks for an official messenger at normal pace

deep.x: The empire's population was perhaps a fifth to a quarter of all humans alive at the time.
Rome ruled a world, but the distances were so great that it depended on local elites wanting to be Roman.

cards.title: Lusitânia
cards.text: Grande parte do atual Portugal tornou-se a província romana da Lusitânia, com capital em Emerita Augusta (Mérida). O líder lusitano Viriato resistiu ferozmente a Roma até ser assassinado em 139 a.C.

deep.x: Romans first came to Iberia in 218 BCE, during their war with Carthage. Conquering the whole peninsula then took about 200 years, longer than anywhere else in the empire.
Viriato

Viriato was a Lusitanian, possibly a shepherd, who survived a Roman massacre of his people in 150 BCE. He led a guerrilla war, using the hills to ambush and defeat several Roman armies. Rome could not beat him in battle, so it bribed three of his companions to kill him in his sleep.
Two provinces
So the Minho and Trás-os-Montes were not actually in Lusitania, but in the region of Gallaecia, shared with today's Galicia.
Legend says Rome refused to pay Viriato's killers, declaring that "Rome does not pay traitors". It's a famous story, but the ancient sources are thin.
Lusitania became Roman slowly and painfully, and Viriato became Portugal's first national hero.

cards.title: O Portugal romano hoje
cards.text: Ainda podes ver o Portugal romano: o templo de Évora, as ruínas de Conímbriga, a ponte de Chaves e inúmeras estradas. O próprio português descende do latim.

deep.x: Roman Portugal is unusually easy to visit. Many sites are small, quiet and right in the middle of towns.
Conímbriga

Near Condeixa, it has some of the finest mosaics in Iberia: hunting scenes, sea creatures and geometric patterns. Its House of the Fountains still has working water features. The town was attacked by the Suebi in the 460s and slowly abandoned; its name passed to nearby Coimbra.
Everyday traces

x: Lisbon's Roman theatre, rediscovered after the 1755 earthquake
The Geira road in Gerês, with dozens of Roman milestones still standing
Villas like Milreu near Faro
Bracara Augusta's remains under Braga

deep.w: Évora's temple was dedicated to Diana
deep.r: That's a romantic 1600s story; it was most likely built for the cult of the emperor

deep.x: The fish-salting works at Tróia, making the fish sauce garum, are among the largest known in the Roman world.
Every Portuguese sentence is a Roman monument you carry with you.

cards.title: Estradas e aquedutos
cards.text: Os romanos construíram cerca de 80 000 km de estradas pavimentadas e aquedutos que levavam água por gravidade ao longo de grandes distâncias, usando declives suaves e arcos.

deep.x: Roman roads were built for armies first. They went as straight as possible, with stone milestones at every Roman mile (about 1.48 km). Major roads were layered for strength and drainage.
Aqueducts

An aqueduct is a gently sloping channel that lets gravity pull water from springs in the hills to a city. Most of it ran underground. Arches were used only to cross valleys, which is why they are the famous bit.

x: The aqueduct to Nîmes falls about 12.6 m over about 50 km
≈ 25 cm per km
a slope of only about 0.025%

deep.x: Rome itself had 11 aqueducts, supplying public fountains, baths and rich homes with water flowing day and night.
Some Roman bridges, like Chaves' Trajan Bridge, carried traffic for about 1,900 years.
Roman engineers moved water across whole regions using only gravity and patience.

cards.title: O betão romano
cards.text: Os romanos usavam cinza vulcânica num betão que durou 2000 anos, mesmo na água do mar. A cúpula do Panteão de Roma, terminada por volta de 125 d.C., continua a ser a maior cúpula de betão não armado.

deep.x: Roman concrete (**opus caementicium**) mixed lime, water and volcanic ash called pozzolana, from near Pozzuoli by Naples, with chunks of stone or brick. The ash reacts with lime to make a hard, durable binder, even underwater.
Why it lasts

Studies of Roman harbour walls show seawater seeping in slowly grows new mineral crystals that strengthen the concrete. Research in 2023 suggested small lumps of lime left in the mix could also dissolve and refill cracks: a kind of self-healing.
The Pantheon
The builders made the dome thinner and lighter near the top, using lighter stones such as pumice, and set coffers (sunken panels) into it to cut weight.

deep.w: Roman concrete is stronger than modern concrete
deep.r: Modern concrete is far stronger; Roman concrete can be more durable in certain conditions, especially with no steel to rust

deep.x: Roman concrete wasn't magic; it was chemistry that keeps working for centuries.

cards.title: O direito romano
cards.text: O direito romano, mais tarde compilado sob o imperador Justiniano, é a base dos sistemas de direito civil na Europa e na América Latina, incluindo o de Portugal.

deep.x: Rome produced professional legal experts, the jurists, who wrote opinions on real cases. Their reasoning about contracts, property, inheritance and families became a huge body of law.
Justinian's collection
In Constantinople, Emperor Justinian ordered all of it organised. The result, later called the **Corpus Juris Civilis**, had four parts.
Rediscovery

In the west it was largely forgotten until a copy of the Digest resurfaced in Italy in the late 1000s. Scholars at Bologna studied it, and lawyers trained in Roman law spread across Europe, including Portugal.

x: Legal terms like "contrato", "obrigação" and "usufruto" come from Roman law
Ideas such as legal persons, written contracts and property rights shaped modern economies

deep.x: Brazil, Mozambique and Angola inherited civil law through Portugal, so Roman legal ideas reach well beyond Europe.
Rome's armies vanished, but its legal reasoning still governs contracts in Lisbon and São Paulo.

cards.title: Os filhos do latim
cards.text: O latim deu origem ao português, ao espanhol, ao italiano, ao francês e ao romeno. Cerca de 60% do vocabulário inglês também vem do latim, diretamente ou através do francês.

deep.x: Ordinary Romans spoke **Vulgar Latin**, the everyday language of soldiers, traders and settlers. After the empire broke up, regions drifted apart until their speech became separate languages.
Same word, different paths
Portuguese often keeps features others lost, and dropped others: Latin "luna" became "lua", and "colorem" became "cor".
Portuguese emerges
In the Middle Ages, Galician-Portuguese was spoken across the northwest of Iberia, including the Minho. Among the oldest Portuguese documents is King Afonso II's will, from 1214.
English, too

English is a Germanic language, but after the Norman conquest of 1066 it absorbed thousands of French words, and scholars later borrowed straight from Latin. Everyday short words are mostly Germanic; the longer, formal ones are often Latin.
Galician and Portuguese were essentially one language in the Middle Ages and are still largely mutually understandable today.
Portuguese is Latin that kept changing for 2,000 years in the mouths of ordinary people.

cards.title: A queda do Ocidente

events.l: império divide-se em Oriente e Ocidente

cards.text: O império do Ocidente enfraqueceu com guerras civis, problemas económicos e a pressão dos povos germânicos. Em 476, o último imperador do Ocidente foi deposto. O império do Oriente (bizantino) durou até 1453.

deep.x: The empire faced crises long before 476: civil wars, plagues, inflation and invasions in the 200s. Emperors responded by splitting the work. In 330 Constantine founded a new capital, Constantinople, and after 395 East and West had separate emperors.
Why the West fell
The East was richer, more urban and easier to defend. It survived and is known today as the Byzantine Empire, until the Ottoman Turks took Constantinople in 1453.
In Iberia
In 409, Germanic peoples crossed into Iberia. The Suebi set up a kingdom in the northwest with its capital at Braga, which lasted until the Visigoths absorbed it in 585.

deep.w: Rome fell suddenly in 476
deep.r: It was a slow transformation; many people barely noticed, as Roman towns, law and Church carried on

deep.x: A German historian once collected 210 different explanations that have been offered for Rome's fall.
The western empire didn't crash in a day; it faded into the kingdoms that became medieval Europe.

cards.title: O cristianismo
cards.text: O cristianismo espalhou-se pelo império apesar das perseguições. O imperador Constantino legalizou-o em 313 e, em 380, tornou-se a religião oficial.

deep.x: Christianity began among the followers of Jesus, executed in Jerusalem around 30 CE. Missionaries such as Paul spread it along Roman roads and sea routes, first to Jewish communities and then to others, especially in cities.
Persecution and tolerance

Christians refused to sacrifice to the Roman gods and the emperor, which looked like disloyalty. Persecutions were occasional, but some, like Diocletian's from 303, were severe. Constantine, after a victory he credited to the Christian God, legalised Christianity with his co-emperor in 313. Under Theodosius it became the state religion in 380.
Built on Roman foundations
In Portugal, Braga became an important bishopric; its archbishops later called themselves "primate of the Spains".
Portuguese weekdays (segunda-feira, terça-feira…) avoid the pagan god names other languages use; tradition credits the 6th-century bishop Martinho de Dume, in Braga.
Christianity used the empire's roads, cities and language to spread, and then outlived the empire itself.

quiz.q: Como se chamava, em grande parte, o Portugal romano?
Que líder lusitano resistiu a Roma?
Quando terminou o Império Romano do Ocidente?
quiz.explain: O último imperador do Ocidente foi deposto em 476.

lessons.title: A Idade Média
lessons.summary: Castelos, mosteiros, cavaleiros e peste.

cards.title: Mil anos
cards.text: A Idade Média vai, grosso modo, da queda de Roma (476) até ao final do século XV. O nome foi criado mais tarde por pensadores do Renascimento, que a viam como um intervalo entre a Antiguidade e a sua própria época.

deep.x: Italian writers like Petrarch, in the 1300s, saw a glorious ancient past, then a long gloomy time, then a revival in their own day. The term "Middle Ages" (medium aevum) took hold in the 1400s–1600s for that middle period.
Three stages

Historians usually split the period. The early centuries saw fewer and smaller towns in the west. After about 1000, population, trade, towns and building boomed, until famine and plague struck in the 1300s.
When did it end?
There's no single date. Historians choose different markers depending on what they study.
The whole story of how Portugal was born, from county to kingdom to Aljubarrota, happened in the Middle Ages.
"Middle Ages" is a label invented by people who looked down on it; the period itself was a thousand years of change.

cards.title: Feudalismo
cards.text: A terra era a principal fonte de riqueza. Os reis concediam terras aos senhores em troca de serviço militar; os camponeses trabalhavam a terra dos senhores em troca de proteção.

deep.x: After Rome's fall, there was little money and few strong states. Rulers paid for soldiers with the one thing they had: land. A lord promised loyalty and service; in return his lord granted him a **fief**, land plus the peasants who worked it.
Life on the manor

Serfs weren't slaves, but they were tied to the land. They farmed their own strips and owed the lord work, often several days a week, plus payments in grain, eggs or money. They also paid a tithe to the Church.
Portugal was different

Portuguese kings stayed strong, partly because the Reconquista made them war leaders. Many towns received a **foral**, a royal charter setting out their rights and taxes, which limited what lords could demand.

deep.w: Feudalism was a neat pyramid everywhere
deep.r: It was messy and varied by region; the word "feudalism" was coined centuries later, and historians debate how useful it is
