deep.x: In a world without much money, land was how you paid for loyalty.

cards.title: A Igreja

items: Catedrais construídas ao longo de séculos

cards.text: A Igreja Católica era a instituição mais poderosa da Europa Ocidental: tinha terras, dirigia escolas e hospitais, mantinha vivo o saber nos mosteiros e moldava o dia a dia.

deep.x: The Church touched everything: birth (baptism), marriage, death and burial. Bells marked the hours, saints' days set the calendar, and the parish priest was often the only local person who could read.
Monasteries

Monks following the Rule of St Benedict, written around 530, divided the day between prayer, work and study. In scriptoria they copied Latin texts, including pagan classics that might otherwise have been lost. Monasteries also ran farms, schools and guest houses for travellers.

x: Alcobaça, founded in 1153 by Cistercian monks, was given land by Afonso Henriques
Its monks drained marshes and spread new farming techniques

deep.x: Wealth and power

x: A farmer harvests 200 sacks of grain
tithe = one-tenth
20 sacks go to the Church

deep.x: Its wealth also caused scandals and calls for reform, which would eventually lead to the Reformation.
In 1054 the Latin west and Greek east excommunicated each other, splitting Catholic and Orthodox churches; the split still exists.
The medieval Church was church, school, hospital, landlord and record office all at once.

cards.title: Castelos
cards.text: Os castelos eram residências fortificadas e bases militares. Portugal tem centenas, muitos construídos ou reconstruídos durante a Reconquista: Guimarães, Almourol, Óbidos, Marvão.

deep.x: Castles spread across Europe from the 900s, as local lords needed strongholds. Early ones were earth mounds with wooden towers. From the 1100s, stone castles with tall keeps and thick walls became common.
Built to make attackers suffer

x: Battlements let defenders shoot and then duck
Arrow slits were narrow outside, wide inside
Gates had drawbridges, portcullises and holes above to drop things through

deep.x: Portugal's castles
Many frontier castles were built by the Templars under Gualdim Pais, who also founded Tomar in 1160. King Dinis rebuilt dozens along the border with Castile.
The end of castles

Gunpowder cannons, common from the 1400s, smashed high walls. Engineers replaced castles with low, thick, star-shaped forts. The fortifications of Elvas, a UNESCO site, are among the largest of this kind in the world.
Since King Dinis gave it to his wife Isabel in 1282, the town of Óbidos was traditionally a wedding gift to Portuguese queens.
Castles were built for a world of swords and arrows, and cannons made them romantic ruins.

cards.title: Cruzadas
cards.text: A partir de 1096, exércitos cristãos lançaram cruzadas para conquistar Jerusalém e a Terra Santa. Os cruzados também ajudaram Afonso Henriques a conquistar Lisboa em 1147, a caminho do Oriente.

deep.x: In 1095, Pope Urban II called on western knights to help the Byzantine Empire against the Seljuk Turks and to take Jerusalem. Fighters were promised forgiveness of sins.
The siege of Lisbon

In 1147 a fleet of crusaders from England, Flanders and the Rhineland stopped in Porto on their way to the Holy Land. The bishop of Porto persuaded them to help Afonso Henriques besiege Lisbon, in return for loot.
An Englishman, Gilbert of Hastings, became Lisbon's first bishop after the conquest.
Consequences
In Iberia, popes granted crusade status to the Reconquista, and military orders like the Templars and the Order of Avis received land for defending the frontier.

deep.w: The crusades were only about faith
deep.r: Faith mattered, but so did land, plunder, trade, family honour and politics, as Lisbon showed

deep.x: Lisbon became Portuguese partly because crusaders heading east took a profitable detour.

cards.title: A Peste Negra
cards.text: A peste varreu a Europa a partir de 1347, transportada por pulgas dos ratos e transmitida entre pessoas. Em poucos anos matou talvez entre um terço e metade da população europeia.

deep.x: The plague is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, which lives in wild rodents. It arrived in Europe in 1347 on ships from the Black Sea and spread along trade routes, reaching Portugal in 1348.
Three forms

x: Bubonic: swollen, painful lymph nodes (buboes); many died within a week
Pneumonic: in the lungs, spread by coughing, almost always fatal
Septicaemic: in the blood, killing fastest of all

deep.x: Some researchers now think human fleas and lice also spread it between people, helping explain how fast it moved.
Responses

Nobody knew about bacteria. People blamed bad air, the stars or God's anger. Some groups whipped themselves in public; others attacked Jewish communities, falsely accused of poisoning wells. Ragusa (Dubrovnik) and then Venice developed isolation for arriving ships.

x: Ships made to wait 30 days, later 40
Italian "quaranta giorni" = 40 days
→ the word "quarantine"

deep.x: The plague kept returning for centuries; one of the last big western European outbreaks hit Marseille in 1720.
The Black Death was the deadliest pandemic in European history, and quarantine was one of its lasting lessons.

cards.title: Depois da peste
cards.text: Com tantos trabalhadores mortos, os sobreviventes podiam exigir salários mais altos e mais liberdade. A servidão enfraqueceu na Europa Ocidental e novas ideias ganharam raízes.

deep.x: The plague killed people but left land, tools and buildings intact. Suddenly there were too few workers for the work, and labour became valuable.
Lords fight back
Governments tried to force wages back to pre-plague levels. In Portugal, King Fernando's **Lei das Sesmarias** of 1375 ordered idle land to be farmed and pushed labourers back to the fields.
A divided Europe

Ordinary survivors in the west often ate more meat, drank more ale and wore better clothes than their grandparents. Some economists argue high wages encouraged labour-saving inventions in later centuries.
A darker mood
Art turned to death: skeletons dancing with kings and peasants, the "dance of death", reminded everyone that death came for all.

deep.w: Things went back to normal after the plague
deep.r: Society changed for good: in western Europe, peasants gained freedoms that lords could never fully take back

deep.x: When labour became scarce, ordinary people gained bargaining power for the first time in centuries.

cards.title: Catedrais góticas
cards.text: A partir do século XII, os arcos quebrados, as abóbadas de nervuras e os arcobotantes permitiram erguer catedrais altas e luminosas, com enormes vitrais. O Mosteiro da Batalha é uma obra-prima portuguesa.

deep.x: Gothic began at the abbey of Saint-Denis near Paris in the 1140s. Builders wanted churches full of light, which they saw as a symbol of God. The problem: big windows weaken walls. Gothic engineering solved it.
Height records
Builders pushed too far sometimes: part of Beauvais' vault collapsed in 1284.
Batalha

Begun in 1386, the Monastery of Batalha was designed first by Afonso Domingues, then by a master called Huguet. Its Founder's Chapel holds the tombs of João I and Philippa of Lancaster. Its "Unfinished Chapels" were never roofed.

x: Stained-glass windows taught Bible stories to people who couldn't read
Many cathedrals took over a century to build; Cologne's was finished only in 1880

deep.x: Notre-Dame in Paris burned in 2019 and reopened in December 2024 after a huge restoration.
Gothic builders turned stone into light by pushing its weight outside the walls.

cards.title: Universidades
cards.text: As primeiras universidades da Europa surgiram em Bolonha (1088), Paris e Oxford. A universidade portuguesa foi fundada em Lisboa em 1290 e mais tarde fixou-se definitivamente em Coimbra, em 1537.

deep.x: A medieval university wasn't a campus; it was a **universitas**, a guild of students or teachers who organised to protect their interests, like any trade guild. At Bologna, students hired and fined their professors.
What students learned
Teaching was in Latin. Students started with the seven liberal arts, then could move to higher faculties.
Teaching was by lecture, where a master read and explained a text, and by disputation, a formal debate on a question. Degrees were bachelor, master and doctor, titles still used today.
Portugal's university
King Dinis founded a "Estudo Geral" in Lisbon in 1290. It moved between Lisbon and Coimbra several times before King João III settled it in Coimbra for good in 1537.
In Coimbra's 18th-century Joanina Library, a colony of small bats eats insects that would damage the old books; staff cover the tables at night.
The university began as a medieval guild, and its degrees, gowns and debates are still with us.

cards.title: O mundo medieval não foi "obscuro"

items: Moinhos de vento e de água

cards.text: A Idade Média trouxe moinhos de vento, óculos, relógios mecânicos, a bússola na Europa, universidades e grande arte. A ideia de "idade das trevas" é hoje vista como demasiado simplista.

deep.x: The label "Dark Ages" came from Renaissance writers who admired ancient Rome, and from later critics of the Church. Today historians see the period as one of real invention and growth.
Farming advances

x: The heavy plough turned heavy northern soils
The horse collar let horses pull without choking
Three-field rotation left only a third of land fallow, not half

deep.x: These raised food production and helped Europe's population roughly double between 1000 and 1300.
Culture
Medieval Europe produced Dante, Chaucer, Gothic cathedrals and the universities. In Iberia, poet-kings wrote songs: King Dinis was one of the finest troubadour poets in Galician-Portuguese.
The 1086 Domesday survey of England counted about 5,600 watermills, roughly one for every few hundred people.
The Middle Ages were dark only to those who weren't looking.

quiz.q: O que matou talvez um terço da Europa no século XIV?
Quem ajudou Afonso Henriques a conquistar Lisboa em 1147?
Onde se fixou definitivamente a universidade portuguesa em 1537?
quiz.explain: Andou entre Lisboa e Coimbra antes de se fixar.

lessons.title: Al-Andalus
lessons.summary: A Península Ibérica muçulmana e a idade de ouro islâmica.

cards.title: 711: uma nova era na Península Ibérica

events.l: maior parte da Península sob domínio muçulmano

cards.text: Em 711, exércitos muçulmanos vindos do Norte de África atravessaram para a Península Ibérica e, em poucos anos, controlavam a maior parte do território, incluindo o atual Portugal. Chamaram-lhe al-Andalus.

deep.x: In 711 a commander called **Tariq ibn Ziyad** crossed the strait from North Africa with an army of perhaps 7,000–12,000 men, most of them Berbers rather than Arabs. The rock where he landed still carries his name: Jabal Tariq, "Tariq's mountain", which became Gibraltar.
Why it was so fast

The Visigothic kingdom was divided. Its king, Roderic, had just taken the throne in a disputed succession, and his rivals may even have helped the invaders. Roderic died at the Battle of Guadalete, and many towns surrendered by treaty, keeping their property and religion in exchange for tribute.
Who ruled

At first al-Andalus was a far-western province of the Umayyad caliphate, ruled from Damascus. When the Umayyads were overthrown in 750, a surviving prince, Abd al-Rahman I, escaped to Iberia and set up an independent emirate in Córdoba in 756.

x: The far north, around Asturias, was never conquered
Tradition dates the first Christian victory to Covadonga, around 722
The name al-Andalus may echo the Vandals, but its origin is still debated

deep.w: The Arabs swept in and replaced the population
deep.r: Most people stayed; over generations many converted and learnt Arabic, while a small Arab and Berber elite ruled

deep.x: The conquest of 711 was quick because a divided kingdom gave way, not because Iberia was emptied and refilled.

cards.title: Córdova
cards.text: No século X, Córdova era uma das maiores e mais sofisticadas cidades da Europa, com ruas pavimentadas, iluminação, banhos, bibliotecas e a grande mesquita.

deep.x: Under Abd al-Rahman III, who declared himself caliph in 929, Córdoba became the capital of the richest state in western Europe. Population estimates vary widely, from about 100,000 to several hundred thousand, but it was certainly far bigger than Paris or London at the time.
The Great Mosque

Building began in 785 and was enlarged by later rulers until it held a forest of more than 800 columns, topped by striped red-and-white double arches. Some columns were reused from Roman and Visigothic buildings.
City life

x: Running water from restored Roman aqueducts and many public baths
Markets selling silk, leather, paper and ivory
The library of caliph al-Hakam II, said to hold hundreds of thousands of books (the number is probably exaggerated)
A palace-city, Madinat al-Zahra, built just outside town

deep.x: The philosophers Averroes (Ibn Rushd) and Maimonides, a Muslim and a Jew, were both born in Córdoba in the 1120s–1130s.
For about a century, Córdoba was the place western Europe looked to for luxury, learning and power.

cards.title: Três religiões
cards.text: Muçulmanos, cristãos e judeus viviam lado a lado no al-Andalus, sendo cristãos e judeus minorias protegidas mas sujeitas a impostos. A convivência era real, mas não havia igualdade, e variou ao longo do tempo.

deep.x: Islamic law treated Christians and Jews as **dhimmis**, "protected people" of the Book. They could keep their religion, property and own courts, but paid a special tax (the jizya) and faced limits: no new churches, no public processions, no authority over Muslims.

items.b: ruling faith, a minority at first

deep.x: A changing picture

Over centuries, conversion slowly turned Muslims into the majority. Some Christians and Jews rose high: the Jewish doctor Hasdai ibn Shaprut served as a diplomat for Abd al-Rahman III. But tensions flared too. In the 850s about 48 Christians in Córdoba were executed after deliberately insulting Islam, and in 1066 a mob in Granada killed many Jews.
Harder times

From the late 1000s, rulers from North Africa, the Almoravids and then the Almohads, were far stricter. Maimonides' family fled Córdoba in the 1140s. The Christian kingdoms, for their part, later forced Jews and Muslims to convert or leave.

deep.w: Al-Andalus was a paradise of tolerance
deep.r: It allowed more diversity than most of Europe then, but within a clear hierarchy, and conditions changed a lot over time

deep.x: Al-Andalus offered protection, not equality, and that was unusual enough for its time.

cards.title: A idade de ouro islâmica
cards.text: Mais ou menos entre os séculos VIII e XIII, sábios de Bagdade, do Cairo e de Córdova traduziram e alargaram o conhecimento grego, persa e indiano em matemática, astronomia, medicina e filosofia.

deep.x: From the 700s the Abbasid caliphs in Baghdad paid for the translation of Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic. A centre often called the **House of Wisdom** gathered scholars. They didn't just copy; they tested, corrected and added.
Big names

Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine was still a textbook in European universities in the 1600s. Ibn al-Haytham showed that we see because light enters the eye, not because the eye sends out rays, and insisted on testing ideas with experiments.
Paper made it possible

Papermaking reached the Islamic world from China in the 700s; Baghdad had paper mills by about 800. Cheap paper made books far more common than in Christian Europe. One of Europe's first paper mills worked at Xàtiva, near Valencia, under Muslim rule.
The route to Europe
After Castile took Toledo in 1085, translators there turned Arabic books into Latin. Gerard of Cremona alone translated dozens of works, including Ptolemy's astronomy and Ibn Sina.
Many star names, like Aldebaran, Betelgeuse and Rigel, come from Arabic.
Much of the "rediscovery" of Greek science in medieval Europe arrived by way of Arabic.

cards.title: Os números que usamos
cards.text: Os algarismos 0–9 vieram da Índia, chegaram à Europa através do mundo árabe e chamam-se algarismos indo-árabes. A palavra "algoritmo" vem do nome de al-Khwarizmi.

deep.x: Indian mathematicians developed a system with just nine digits plus a sign for zero, where a digit's **place** sets its value. By 628 the astronomer Brahmagupta was writing rules for calculating with zero as a number.
Why place value wins
Roman numerals have no zero and no place value, so written sums are awkward. With Hindu-Arabic digits you can add, multiply and keep accounts on paper, which merchants and bankers loved.

x: 1,888 in Roman numerals
MDCCCLXXXVIII
13 symbols instead of 4

deep.x: The man behind the words

Al-Khwarizmi wrote a book explaining Indian reckoning around 825. Its Latin translation began "Algoritmi dicit…", "Al-Khwarizmi says…", and his name became **algorithm**. His other book, on "al-jabr" (restoring), gave us **algebra**.
Change was slow. Some European cities, worried about fraud, banned the new digits in official accounts in the 1200s, because a 0 could easily be changed into a 6 or 9.
In Portuguese a digit is an **algarismo**, a word that comes straight from al-Khwarizmi's name.
The numbers on every price tag travelled from India through Baghdad and al-Andalus before reaching Portugal.

cards.title: Agricultura e rega
cards.text: Os agricultores muçulmanos introduziram ou difundiram na Península Ibérica culturas como a laranja, o limão, o arroz, a amêndoa e a cana-de-açúcar, juntamente com sistemas de rega como a nora.

deep.x: Al-Andalus drew on farming know-how from across the Islamic world, from Persia to Egypt. Andalusi agronomists like Ibn al-Awwam wrote detailed manuals on grafting, soils and watering.
Lifting water

The **nora** is a wheel with clay pots (alcatruzes) tied to it. Turned by a donkey or a mule, it lifts water from a well and tips it into channels (acéquias). Small dams (açudes) held river water back. Portuguese farmers used noras well into the 20th century.
Summer crops
Many new crops needed water in the hot, dry summer. Irrigation let farmers grow a second harvest, so the same field fed more people. That supported bigger towns like Córdoba and Seville.

deep.w: The Arabs brought the sweet orange
deep.r: They brought the bitter orange; the sweet orange arrived around 1500, partly via Portuguese traders, which is why Greeks call it "portokali"

deep.x: Valencia's Water Tribunal, which settles irrigation disputes every Thursday by the cathedral door, is said to go back to Andalusi times.
Irrigation turned dry southern Iberia into a garden that could grow crops all year.

cards.title: O árabe no português
cards.text: O português tem centenas de palavras de origem árabe, muitas vezes começadas por "al-": azeite, arroz, alface, almofada, açúcar, aldeia, armazém. "Oxalá" vem de "se Deus quiser".

deep.x: After Latin, Arabic gave Portuguese more words than any other language in the Middle Ages, with estimates from several hundred to around a thousand. Most are **nouns** for things that were new or traded: food, farming, building, trade and government.
Why so many start with "a"
"Al" means "the" in Arabic. Portuguese speakers heard it as part of the word. Before certain consonants Arabic changes al- to as-, az- or ar-, which is why we get açúcar and arroz.
What didn't change
Grammar, verbs and everyday basics like "pai", "água" and "comer" stayed Latin. Arabic added vocabulary, not structure. Even "fulano", meaning "so-and-so", comes from Arabic fulan.

deep.w: Every word starting with "al-" is Arabic
deep.r: Many aren't: almoço comes from Latin, and alto from Latin altus

deep.x: Spanish and Portuguese often share the same Arabic words, while Italian or French use Latin ones: "azeite" but "olio", "huile".
Portuguese is Latin in its bones, with Arabic woven into its kitchen, house and market.

cards.title: Nomes de lugares
cards.text: Muitos lugares portugueses têm nomes árabes: o Algarve (al-gharb, "o ocidente"), Alcácer, Alfama, Albufeira, Fátima (um nome muçulmano).

deep.x: Place names are like fossils: they keep old languages long after people stop speaking them. Southern Portugal is especially rich in Arabic names.
Rivers and towns

The Arabic **wadi**, "river" or "valley", turns up as "Ode-" or "Guadi-": Odemira, Odeceixe, Odivelas and the Guadiana, which mixes wadi with the Roman river name Anas. Coimbra's Arco de Almedina comes from al-madina, "the town".
Fátima

Fatima was the name of the Prophet Muhammad's daughter, popular among Muslims. A local legend says a Moorish girl named Fátima was captured by a Christian knight, married him and converted, taking the name Oureana, which gave nearby Ourém its name. It's a legend, but the place name is real evidence of the Muslim past.

deep.w: The north has no Arabic place names
deep.r: They are rarer, since Muslim rule there was shorter, but some exist, like Alfândega da Fé

deep.x: Lisbon's Mouraria neighbourhood is where Muslims were made to live after the city's conquest in 1147.
Read a map of the Algarve and you're reading Arabic.

cards.title: A Reconquista
cards.text: Os reinos cristãos do norte foram avançando para sul ao longo de quase 800 anos. Portugal concluiu a sua reconquista com o Algarve em 1249; Espanha, com Granada, em 1492.

deep.x: The word **Reconquista** ("reconquest") was coined much later and is debated by historians, because it suggests a single planned campaign. In reality it was nearly 800 years of advances, truces, alliances and civil wars on both sides.
How the frontier moved

When al-Andalus split into small rival kingdoms (taifas) after 1031, Christian kings forced them to pay tribute called parias. North African dynasties then came in twice to reunite the south and push back. The great Christian victory at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212 broke Almohad power.
Allies across faiths
El Cid, Castile's hero, also fought for the Muslim king of Zaragoza. Alfonso VI of Castile took a Muslim princess, Zaida of Seville, as a partner, and Muslim rulers often hired Christian soldiers.

x: almost eight centuries

deep.x: Portugal finished its reconquest 243 years before Spain, which is one reason it was free to look to the sea earlier.
The Reconquista was a long, messy shifting of borders, not a single crusade.

cards.title: Silves e Mértola

items: Traçado das ruas de Alfama, Lisboa

cards.text: Silves foi a capital do Algarve sob domínio muçulmano, e a igreja de Mértola foi em tempos uma mesquita. Ambas ainda mostram o seu passado islâmico nas muralhas, nas ruas e nos museus.

deep.x: Silves

Called **Xelb** (Shilb), Silves was the main city of the Algarve under Muslim rule, famous for its poets and gardens. Its red sandstone castle still looms over the town, and an Almohad cistern inside it once stored water for a siege. Sancho I took the city in 1189 with crusaders' help, lost it two years later, and Portugal took it for good in the 1240s.
Mértola

Mértola sits on a steep hill above the Guadiana, which was a river port for Roman and Islamic traders. In 1144 a Sufi leader, Ibn Qasi, launched a revolt from here. The main church was the town mosque. It still has the **mihrab**, the niche facing Mecca, and the forest of columns inside echoes a mosque's prayer hall.

x: Mértola calls itself a "Vila Museu", with small museums of Islamic art and ceramics
It holds an Islamic Festival every two years
Silves has an archaeology museum built around a deep Islamic well

deep.x: Al-Mu'tamid, a poet-king of Seville born in Beja, governed Silves as a young man and later wrote longingly about its palace.
In Silves and Mértola, al-Andalus isn't in a textbook; you can walk through it.

quiz.q: Como chamavam os muçulmanos à Península Ibérica?
A palavra "algoritmo" vem…
Quando concluiu Portugal a sua reconquista?

lessons.title: O Império Mongol
lessons.summary: Como cavaleiros da estepe construíram o maior império terrestre da história, e o que deixaram para trás.

cards.title: Temujin torna-se Gengis Khan

deep.x: Our main source for his early life is *The Secret History of the Mongols*, written in the 13th century by someone close to the ruling family. It tells of a hard youth: a captured boy who escaped from a wooden collar, a young husband whose wife Börte was kidnapped by a rival clan and rescued with the help of allies.
Breaking the old tribes

Steppe politics had been built on clans and tribes that changed sides constantly. Temüjin replaced them with an army and society organised in units of ten, mixing people from different tribes so that loyalty went to the khan, not to a clan chief.
Rule by merit and law

x: Commanders were promoted for loyalty and ability, not birth; some former enemies became generals
A body of laws, the Great Yasa, governed the army and nobility, though no full text survives
Mongolian was first written in a script borrowed from the Uyghurs, still used in Inner Mongolia
Religious leaders of many faiths were often exempt from taxes

deep.x: The meaning of "Chinggis", usually written Genghis in English, is still debated: suggestions include "firm", "fierce" and "universal".
His burial place was kept secret and has never been found. According to tradition, the ground was ridden over by horses to hide it.
Genghis Khan's first conquest was of the steppe itself: he turned quarrelling clans into one disciplined people.

cards.text:
Temujin nasceu por volta de 1162 na estepe mongol. Depois de o pai ter sido envenenado, a família foi abandonada e viveu na pobreza, a caçar marmotas e a apanhar raízes.

Com alianças, lealdade e guerra, uniu as tribos rivais da estepe. Em 1206, uma grande assembleia proclamou-o Gengis Khan, soberano de todo o "povo das tendas de feltro".

cards.title: Arqueiros a cavalo

items: Arco compósito de corno e madeira

deep.x: The Mongol bow was a composite: a wooden core, horn on the belly and sinew on the back, glued together and curved against its natural bend. That stored far more energy than a simple wooden bow of the same size, which mattered on horseback, where a long bow would be clumsy.
Born in the saddle

Mongol children learned to ride at about three or four and hunted from horseback as they grew. Great organised hunts, in which thousands of riders slowly closed a ring around game, trained the same skills as war: keeping formation over huge distances and closing in on command.
Tactics

x: Light cavalry harassed with arrows; heavier cavalry with lances finished the job
Flags, drums and later lanterns passed signals between units
The feigned retreat drew enemy knights out of formation, into waiting archers
Captured Chinese and Persian engineers built catapults for sieges

deep.w: The Mongols won through huge numbers
deep.r: They were often outnumbered; speed, discipline, scouting and planning mattered more

deep.x: A stone inscription from about 1225 records a shot by Genghis Khan's nephew of more than 500 m, though how it was measured is uncertain.
The horse archer turned the open steppe into a weapon: fast, hard to catch and able to strike from a distance.

cards.text:
O exército mongol era formado por arqueiros montados. Cada cavaleiro levava um potente arco compósito e conseguia disparar com precisão a galope, de pé nos estribos.

Cada guerreiro tinha vários cavalos e trocava de montada para os manter frescos. Unidades rápidas e disciplinadas conseguiam cercar o inimigo, retirar de propósito para o atrair a uma armadilha e voltar a carregar.

cards.title: Um exército em movimento

deep.x: Each soldier was expected to bring his own horses, weapons and food. Officers inspected kit before campaigns, and a missing item could be punished. Because the horses grazed on grass, even in winter by pawing through snow, the army needed no fodder carts, though it did need good pasture and often campaigned in the seasons that offered it.
Planning ahead

Campaigns were prepared years in advance. Merchants and spies gathered information on roads, rivers, rulers and rivalries, and scouts rode far ahead of the main army. Several columns would march separately over hundreds of kilometres and meet at an agreed place and time.
Surrender or else

The Mongols used terror as a weapon. Cities that surrendered usually paid tribute and were spared; cities that resisted could be destroyed and their people killed, as at Nishapur and Merv in 1221 and Baghdad in 1258. Reports of these massacres made other cities think twice.
Skilled workers were often spared and sent east, which is how Persian weavers and Chinese engineers ended up far from home.
In an emergency, a rider could open a small cut in his horse's vein, drink some blood and close it again, as Marco Polo and others reported.
Speed was the Mongols' secret weapon, and speed came from an army that carried almost nothing.

cards.text:
Os exércitos mongóis levavam pouco e viviam dos seus animais e da terra. Os cavaleiros tinham coalho seco, carne seca e leite de égua fermentado, e os rebanhos viajavam com eles.

Sem lentas carroças de abastecimento, deslocavam-se muito mais depressa do que os inimigos, atravessavam desertos e montanhas e apareciam onde ninguém os esperava.

cards.title: O maior império terrestre

viz.unit: área no auge, milhões de km² (aprox.)

deep.x: Genghis Khan's armies took northern China's capital, near today's Beijing, in 1215. After a Central Asian ruler killed Mongol envoys and merchants, they destroyed the Khwarazmian Empire in 1219–1221. His sons and grandsons kept going.
Europe's narrow escape

In 1241 Mongol armies crushed a Polish-German force at Legnica and the Hungarian army at Mohi. Then they withdrew. News had arrived that the Great Khan Ögedei had died, and the princes rode home to choose a successor. Whether they would have pushed further west remains one of history's great "what ifs".
Where the advance stopped

x: 1260: defeated by the Mamluks of Egypt at Ain Jalut, in today's Israel
1274 and 1281: two invasions of Japan wrecked by storms, later called kamikaze, "divine wind"
Jungle and heat in Vietnam and Java defeated steppe cavalry

deep.x: The human cost was enormous. Estimates of deaths caused by the conquests run into the tens of millions, though all such figures are uncertain.

deep.w: The Mongol Empire was bigger than any other ever
deep.r: The British Empire was larger in total, but the Mongol Empire is the largest single unbroken land empire

deep.x: A people of perhaps a million riders came to rule a huge part of Eurasia within about 70 years.

cards.text:
No seu auge, por volta de 1270, o Império Mongol estendia-se da Coreia à Hungria e da Sibéria ao golfo Pérsico, cerca de 24 milhões de km².

É o maior império terrestre contínuo da história. Só o Império Britânico, espalhado pelos oceanos, foi maior no total. E, no entanto, os próprios mongóis talvez não fossem mais do que um milhão de pessoas.

cards.title: O yam, rede de postos

deep.x: The system was expanded and organised under Ögedei in the 1230s. Stations were set roughly a day's ride apart for ordinary travellers, with smaller posts in between for urgent riders. Local households were assigned to supply horses, food and labour, a heavy duty that was sometimes resented.
The paiza

A paiza was a metal or wooden tablet engraved with the khan's order. Its holder could demand horses, food and guides. In effect it was both a passport and a credit card, and misusing one was a serious crime.
How fast?

Riders on urgent business wore bells so the next station could prepare a horse before they arrived. Reports suggest they could cover around 200 km or more in a day, though such figures are hard to check.
More than mail

The yam carried envoys, merchants with permits, tax records and military orders, and it let a khan in Mongolia keep track of governors thousands of kilometres away. Marco Polo described it with amazement, claiming there were tens of thousands of horses kept ready.
The Russian word "yamshchik", a coachman, comes from the Mongol yam, and the Russian postal relay system long kept its outline.
The yam was the Mongol Empire's nervous system, carrying the khan's word across a continent.

cards.text:
Para governar tais distâncias, os mongóis construíram o yam, uma rede de postos de muda por todo o império, com cavalos frescos, comida e alojamento para os mensageiros oficiais.

Os mensageiros que levavam uma placa de metal chamada paiza podiam trocar de cavalo em cada posto e cavalgar dia e noite, levando notícias muito mais depressa do que alguma vez antes.

cards.title: Pax Mongolica

deep.x: The khans actively favoured trade. They lent money to merchant partnerships, cut tolls on main routes and protected caravans. In return, trade brought in taxes and luxury goods for the Mongol elite.
Who travelled

x: Franciscan friars sent by the Pope, such as John of Plano Carpini (1245) and William of Rubruck (1253)
Rabban Bar Sauma, a Christian monk from China, who visited Rome, Paris and the English king in the 1280s
Merchants from Venice and Genoa
Muslim scholars, doctors and administrators in China

deep.x: Ideas in motion

In 1267 the Persian astronomer Jamal al-Din brought instruments and calendars to Kublai Khan. In Persia, the minister Rashid al-Din, a Jewish-born convert to Islam, compiled a *Compendium of Chronicles* with the help of Chinese, Mongol and European informants, often called the first attempt at a history of the whole world.
William of Rubruck described a religious debate in 1254 at the Mongol capital, Karakorum, between Christians, Muslims and Buddhists, organised by the Great Khan Möngke.

Ordinary people felt the effects too. Spices, silks and cotton became more widely available in Persian and Italian markets, and Italian merchants wrote handbooks for the long journey east, listing routes, costs and how to change money along the way.
The Mongols conquered with great brutality, then made Eurasia's trade routes safer than they had ever been.

cards.text:
Terminadas as conquistas, os mongóis passaram a controlar a maior parte das rotas da Rota da Seda. Durante cerca de um século, aproximadamente de 1250 a 1350, mercadores e viajantes podiam atravessar a Eurásia sob um mesmo chapéu político.

Os historiadores chamam-lhe Pax Mongolica, a "paz mongol". Mercadorias, ideias, tecnologias e pessoas circularam entre a China, a Pérsia e a Europa como nunca antes.

cards.title: Kublai Khan

deep.x: Kublai's claim to the throne was contested by his younger brother Ariq Böke, who had the support of many traditional Mongols. Kublai won the civil war in 1264, but parts of the family never accepted him, and the empire began to split.
A Mongol emperor of China
Kublai adopted Chinese court rituals and gave his dynasty a Chinese name, Yuan, meaning "origin". He kept the Mongols on top, however, ranking his subjects in an unofficial hierarchy.
Two capitals
Dadu was the winter capital, built on a grand grid plan. Shangdu, the summer capital on the steppe to the north, was known in the West as Xanadu and became a byword for fabulous luxury.
Projects and failures

x: Extended the Grand Canal to supply Dadu with rice from the south
Commissioned a new script for all the empire's languages, the 'Phags-pa script, in 1269
Two invasions of Japan, in 1274 and 1281, ended in disaster
Expeditions to Vietnam and Java also failed

deep.x: After Kublai, the Yuan weakened through floods, famine, inflation of paper money and rebellions. In 1368 the Ming drove the Mongols back to the steppe.

deep.w: The Yuan were a foreign dynasty China rejected entirely
deep.r: China kept much of the Yuan's legacy, including Beijing as capital and the province system

deep.x: Kublai Khan was both a Mongol conqueror and a Chinese emperor, and his capital is still China's capital.

cards.text:
Kublai, neto de Gengis Khan, tornou-se Grande Khan em 1260 e fundou a dinastia Yuan na China em 1271. Em 1279 tinha conquistado os Song, tornando-se o primeiro soberano não chinês de toda a China.

A sua capital, Dadu, deu origem à atual Pequim. Governou com uma mistura de funcionários mongóis, centro-asiáticos e chineses e usou papel-moeda em todo o império.

cards.title: Marco Polo

deep.x: Marco's father Niccolò and uncle Maffeo had already met Kublai on an earlier trip. The khan asked them to come back with Christian scholars. They returned in 1271 with the teenage Marco instead, travelling overland through Persia and Central Asia.
What he described

According to his account he served the khan on missions around the empire. The family finally left by sea, escorting a Mongol princess to marry the ruler of Persia, and reached Venice in 1295 after about 24 years away.
Did he really go?

Some scholars have doubted it. Chinese records do not mention him, and his book says nothing of tea, chopsticks or the Great Wall. But most historians now think he did go, because many details check out, such as the salt tax figures, paper money and the princess's voyage, which matches Persian records.
A best-seller before printing

The book was copied by hand into Latin, French, Italian and other languages, and about 150 manuscripts survive, each slightly different. Many readers treated it as a collection of tall tales, and in Italian it was nicknamed *Il Milione*, perhaps mocking its "million" marvels.
Christopher Columbus owned a copy of Marco Polo's book and filled its margins with notes. It is still kept in Seville.
Marco Polo's book gave Europe its first detailed picture of China, and inspired explorers looking for a way to reach it by sea.

cards.text:
O mercador veneziano Marco Polo viajou até à corte de Kublai Khan com o pai e o tio, ficou cerca de 17 anos e regressou a Veneza em 1295.

Mais tarde, prisioneiro de guerra em Génova, ditou a sua história a um escritor de romances. *A Descrição do Mundo* deslumbrou a Europa com relatos de papel-moeda, cidades enormes e pedras que ardiam.

cards.title: Peste nas rotas comerciais

deep.x: In 2022 scientists studied DNA from people buried in 1338–1339 in two Christian cemeteries near Lake Issyk-Kul, in today's Kyrgyzstan. Their gravestones mention a "pestilence", and the bacteria found were close to the ancestor of the Black Death strains. The disease almost certainly started in wild rodents in this region.
The siege of Caffa

In 1346 a Golden Horde army besieged the Genoese trading port of Caffa in Crimea. An Italian writer, who was not there himself, claimed the attackers catapulted corpses over the walls to spread the disease. Whether or not that happened, Genoese ships leaving Caffa and other Black Sea ports carried infected rats, fleas and people.

deep.w: The Mongols started the Black Death on purpose
deep.r: Even if bodies were thrown at Caffa, plague spread along many routes with rodents, fleas and travellers

deep.x: A shock to the Mongol world

items: Cities of the Golden Horde hit

deep.x: The plague killed huge numbers in the Middle East and the Mongol lands, not only in Europe. Trade fell, tax income shrank, and the open routes of the Pax Mongolica closed as the khanates fought each other and broke up.
Historians still debate whether the plague also struck China in the 1330s and 1340s. Chinese records describe terrible epidemics in those years, but they do not say clearly which disease it was.
The connected world the Mongols created carried disease as easily as silk.

cards.text:
A Peste Negra terá começado na Ásia Central na década de 1330. As mesmas rotas comerciais da era mongol que transportavam seda e especiarias ajudaram a levar a bactéria da peste para ocidente.

Em 1346 tinha chegado ao mar Negro, onde mercadores italianos comerciavam com a Horda Dourada mongol. Os seus navios levaram-na depois para o Mediterrâneo.

cards.title: Divisão e legado

deep.x: Each khanate adapted to the people it ruled. The Ilkhans of Persia became Muslims after Ghazan converted in 1295, and the Golden Horde followed under Özbeg in the early 1300s. The Yuan in China leaned towards Tibetan Buddhism.
Successor states

x: Timur (Tamerlane) built a new empire in Central Asia in the late 1300s, claiming Mongol links
Babur, descended from both Timur and Genghis Khan, founded the Mughal Empire in India; "Mughal" means Mongol
The Crimean Khanate, a Golden Horde successor, lasted until 1783

deep.x: What remained
Moscow rose as tax collector for the Golden Horde before throwing it off. Beijing stayed China's capital. Iran's Ilkhans encouraged Persian painting and history writing.
A 2003 genetic study suggested that about 0.5% of men worldwide share a Y-chromosome lineage that may trace back to Genghis Khan's family, though the link is debated.
In Mongolia today Genghis Khan is a national hero, on banknotes and the airport's name, while in Iran, Russia and China he is remembered far more darkly.
The Mongols also left new administrative habits behind: censuses, relay posts and the use of paper money spread through the lands they had ruled, and China's system of provinces dates from the Yuan.
The Mongol Empire lasted barely a century as one state, but it rewired Eurasia for centuries afterwards.

cards.text:
Depois de 1260, o império dividiu-se em quatro canatos governados por diferentes ramos da família de Gengis Khan, muitas vezes em guerra entre si.

Foram-se desfazendo ou sendo absorvidos, mas os mongóis deixaram uma marca profunda: na Rússia, na China e no Irão, no comércio entre Oriente e Ocidente e na própria ideia de um mundo ligado de ponta a ponta.

quiz.q: Em que ano foi Temujin proclamado Gengis Khan?
quiz.explain: Uma grande assembleia, o kurultai, deu-lhe o título.

quiz.q: O que era o yam mongol?
options: Uma rede de postos de muda
quiz.explain: Os cavaleiros trocavam de cavalo em postos por todo o império.

quiz.q: Que cidade construiu Kublai Khan como sua capital?
quiz.explain: Desde então, Pequim tem sido a capital da China durante a maior parte do tempo.

quiz.q: Onde terá começado a Peste Negra?
quiz.explain: O ADN de sepulturas de 1338–39 no Quirguistão aponta para lá.

lessons.title: Maias, astecas e incas
lessons.summary: Três grandes civilizações das Américas, as suas cidades, ciência e culturas agrícolas, e a conquista que pôs fim à sua independência.

cards.title: Assentes no milho e na batata

deep.x: Maize descends from teosinte, a wild grass of the Balsas river valley in south-west Mexico. About 9,000 years ago people began choosing seeds from the best plants. The earliest cobs were only a few centimetres long; over thousands of years farmers bred them into large ears that cannot even seed themselves without human help.
The three sisters

Mesoamerican farmers often grew maize, beans and squash together in a field called a milpa. The maize stalk supports the climbing beans, the beans add nitrogen to the soil, and squash leaves shade out weeds and keep moisture in.
Cooking with lime

Maize was soaked and cooked with lime or wood ash, a process now called **nixtamalisation**. It softens the grain for tortillas and releases niacin, a B vitamin. When maize spread to Europe without this step, poor people who lived mainly on it developed a disease called pellagra.
Potatoes of the Andes

Potatoes were domesticated near Lake Titicaca, on today's border of Peru and Bolivia, perhaps 7,000–10,000 years ago. Andean farmers grow thousands of varieties at different altitudes. They also invented chuño: potatoes frozen at night, trodden to squeeze out water and dried in the sun, which keeps for years.
In the Maya creation story, the *Popol Vuh*, the gods finally succeed in making human beings out of maize dough.
Every great American civilisation rested on a crop that farmers had spent thousands of years shaping.

cards.text:
As civilizações das Américas cresceram a partir de plantas ali domesticadas milhares de anos antes. O milho veio de uma gramínea selvagem do México; a batata, dos altos Andes.

Estas plantas alimentavam cidades, exércitos e sacerdotes, tal como o trigo e o arroz na Eurásia. Hoje, o milho e a batata estão entre os alimentos mais importantes da Terra.

cards.title: Cidades maias

deep.x: Maya cities were not packed inside walls like European towns. A ceremonial centre of temples and palaces was surrounded by houses, gardens, fields and reservoirs spreading over many square kilometres.
Hidden by the forest

In 2018 archaeologists used **lidar**, laser scanning from aircraft, to look through the forest of northern Guatemala. It revealed more than 60,000 previously unknown structures: houses, causeways, terraces, canals and defensive walls. Population estimates for the Maya lowlands at their peak rose to several million people.
The ballgame

Almost every city had a ball court. Players kept a heavy solid rubber ball in the air using their hips, never their hands. The game could be sport, ritual or both, and sometimes ended in sacrifice. Mesoamericans were making rubber from tree sap thousands of years before Europeans.
The Classic collapse

In the 800s and 900s, many southern cities were abandoned. Lake sediments show a series of severe droughts, which came on top of warfare between cities, deforestation and growing populations. Northern cities such as Chichén Itzá flourished for a while longer.

deep.w: The Maya disappeared
deep.r: Cities were abandoned, but the people stayed; millions of Maya live in the region today

deep.x: The Maya world was a network of rival cities, much like ancient Greece, set in tropical forest.

cards.text:
Os maias construíram centenas de cidades no que é hoje o sul do México, a Guatemala, o Belize e as Honduras, com pirâmides em degraus, palácios, praças e campos de jogo da bola.

Nunca foram um único império. Cidades-estado rivais como Tikal e Calakmul, cada uma governada por um rei divino, combateram-se e aliaram-se durante séculos.

cards.title: A escrita maia

deep.x: Maya scribes could write the same word in several ways: with one word sign, with syllable signs spelling it out, or with a mixture. This flexibility made the script beautiful but hard to crack.
Burned books

Maya books, called codices, were folded screens of bark paper coated with fine plaster. Spanish missionaries saw them as works of idolatry. In 1562, at Maní in Yucatán, the friar Diego de Landa burned dozens of them.
Only four codices are known to survive, named after the cities where they ended up. The fourth, in Mexico, was confirmed as genuine in 2016.
Cracking the code

x: 1950s: the Soviet scholar Yuri Knorozov argued many signs stood for syllables
1960: Tatiana Proskouriakoff showed that monuments recorded the lives of real rulers
1970s onwards: teams worked out the dynasties of Palenque and other cities

deep.x: Who wrote

Scribes were high-ranking specialists, sometimes members of royal families, and painted vases show them at work with brushes and shell ink pots. Texts were meant to be seen as well as read: on a single monument, carving and writing form one design.
Landa, who burned the books, also wrote down what he thought was the Maya "alphabet". It was confused, but it later gave decipherers a vital clue.
Maya inscriptions turned silent ruins into history, with names, dates and quarrels of real kings.

cards.text:
Os maias desenvolveram o sistema de escrita mais completo das Américas antigas, com sinais para palavras inteiras e sinais para sílabas.

Gravavam-no em monumentos de pedra, pintavam-no em cerâmica e escreviam livros em papel de casca de árvore. Após anos de trabalho, os investigadores conseguem hoje ler a maioria dos textos que sobreviveram: registam reis, guerras, nascimentos e rituais.

cards.title: A Contagem Longa e o zero

deep.x: The Maya tracked time with interlocking cycles. A sacred calendar of 260 days ran alongside a solar year of 365 days. The two came back into line only every 52 years, a period known as the Calendar Round.
How the Long Count works
The Long Count counted days in place-value units, mostly in twenties. A date was written as five numbers, largest unit first.

x: k'in: 1 day
winal: 20 days
tun: 360 days
k'atun: 7,200 days, about 20 years
b'ak'tun: 144,000 days, about 394 years
= 1,386,478 days since the start, a date in 683 CE

deep.x: Zero

A place-value system needs a sign for "nothing in this place". The oldest known Long Count dates, from the 1st century BCE in southern Mexico, already imply a zero. Only a few cultures, including Babylon and India, ever invented such a placeholder.

deep.w: The Maya predicted the end of the world in 2012
deep.r: 21 December 2012 simply completed a large cycle of 13 b'ak'tun; Maya texts mention dates thousands of years later

deep.x: Maya astronomers built a calendar of astonishing precision, with a zero at its heart.

cards.text:
Os números maias usavam apenas três sinais: um ponto para o um, uma barra para o cinco e uma concha para o zero. Contavam em vintenas, não em dezenas.

Com eles mantinham vários calendários, incluindo a Contagem Longa, que numerava os dias a partir de um ponto inicial em 3114 a.C. Precisava de um verdadeiro zero, que os maias inventaram independentemente da Índia.

cards.title: Tenochtitlan

deep.x: According to legend, the Mexica were told to settle where they saw an eagle on a cactus eating a snake. That scene is now on the flag of Mexico. In 1428 Tenochtitlan joined two neighbouring cities in a Triple Alliance that came to dominate central Mexico, collecting tribute from hundreds of towns.
A city on water

x: Three causeways linked the island to the shore
An aqueduct brought fresh water from springs at Chapultepec
Canals served as streets for thousands of canoes
The Templo Mayor, a double pyramid, stood at the centre

deep.x: How chinampas worked

Farmers staked out long rectangles in the shallow lake, piled up layers of vegetation and mud, and planted willow trees at the edges whose roots held the soil. Canals kept the fields watered and brought fresh mud. Seedlings were raised in nurseries and transplanted.
Sacrifice and markets

The Mexica believed the gods needed human blood to keep the sun moving, and they sacrificed prisoners of war. Excavations since 2015 near the Templo Mayor have uncovered racks and towers holding hundreds of skulls. Yet daily life centred on trade: Cortés wrote that the market of Tlatelolco drew tens of thousands of people a day, using cacao beans as small change.
Chinampas are still farmed at Xochimilco in Mexico City, a UNESCO World Heritage site, while the rest of the city sits on the drained lake bed and is slowly sinking.
Tenochtitlan was one of the world's great cities, built on water and fed by fields made by hand.

cards.text:
Os mexicas, mais conhecidos como astecas, fundaram Tenochtitlan por volta de 1325 numa ilha do lago Texcoco. Em 1519 poderia ter mais de 200 000 habitantes, mais do que qualquer cidade de Espanha.

Era alimentada pelas chinampas: campos estreitos erguidos com lodo do lago, separados por canais. Podiam dar várias colheitas por ano.

cards.title: A rede de estradas inca

deep.x: The Inca called their empire Tawantinsuyu, "the four parts together". It expanded rapidly from the 1430s under Pachacuti and his successors, absorbing many peoples in less than a century.
Roads through the mountains

The road system, the Qhapaq Ñan, had two main routes, one in the highlands and one along the coast, linked by cross-roads. Builders cut stairways into cliffs, paved wet ground and built drainage channels. Since 2014 it has been a UNESCO World Heritage site shared by Peru, Ecuador, Bolivia, Colombia, Chile and Argentina.
Runners and storehouses

Chasqui runners waited at small posts a few kilometres apart and ran messages, quipus and light goods to the next post. Spanish chroniclers wrote that fresh fish could reach Cusco from the coast in about two days. Tambos along the roads stored food, cloth and weapons for travelling armies and officials.
Grass bridges
Over deep gorges, villagers wove suspension bridges from grass ropes. Each community was responsible for its own bridge.
The Q'eswachaka bridge in southern Peru is still rewoven by local communities every year in a few days, a tradition recognised by UNESCO.
The Inca ran an empire without money, wheels or writing, held together by roads, runners and labour.

cards.text:
O Império Inca, governado a partir de Cusco, foi o maior das Américas, estendendo-se ao longo dos Andes do Equador ao Chile. Uma rede de estradas de cerca de 30 000 km mantinha-o unido.

Os incas não tinham transporte com rodas nem cavalos. As estradas eram percorridas por pessoas a pé, caravanas de lamas e corredores de estafeta que passavam mensagens de posto em posto.

cards.title: Quipu: nós que contam

deep.x: A quipu usually has a thick main cord with dozens or even hundreds of thinner cords hanging from it, made of cotton or llama and alpaca wool. Specialists called quipucamayocs made and read them, and could report figures to officials from memory with their help.
Reading the numbers
Knots near the bottom of a cord are units, higher up are tens, then hundreds. An empty space means zero. Long knots with several turns show units from 2 to 9.

x: Top cluster: 3 single knots = 300
Middle: no knot = 0 tens
Bottom: long knot of 5 turns = 5
Cord reads 305

deep.x: Cracked and uncracked

In 1912 the American scholar Leland Locke showed how quipus record numbers. Some cords add up to totals on other cords, like a spreadsheet. But some quipus do not fit a simple numerical pattern, and several researchers think they may hold names or stories.
About 1,000 quipus survive, many in museums. In 1583 a church council in Lima ordered some to be destroyed as idolatrous.
Some Andean villages still keep old quipus and bring them out at community ceremonies, though the knowledge to read them fully has been lost.
Quipus show that a state can keep detailed accounts with string, and they still hold secrets.

cards.text:
Os incas não tinham escrita no sentido habitual. Os funcionários mantinham registos com quipus: feixes de cordões coloridos atados com nós.

A posição e o tipo de cada nó representavam um número, num sistema de base dez. Os quipus registavam censos, impostos e o conteúdo dos armazéns por todo o império. Se alguns também registavam palavras ainda é debatido.

cards.title: Machu Picchu

deep.x: The site was a retreat for the emperor and his court, with temples, palaces, houses for servants and about 200 buildings in all. Perhaps several hundred people lived there, rising to more when the ruler visited. Radiocarbon dating published in 2021 suggests it was in use from about 1420, a little earlier than once thought.
Stone without mortar

The finest walls are made of granite blocks cut to fit so tightly that a knife blade will not slip between them. In an earthquake the blocks shift slightly and settle back, which is one reason the walls still stand in a seismic zone.
Engineering hidden below

x: Terraces held up the steep slopes and gave space for crops
Layers of stone and gravel under them drained the heavy rain
Stone channels carried spring water to a chain of fountains

deep.x: Lost city?
Bingham presented it as a "lost city", but farmers were living and working on the terraces when he arrived, and a local farmer had written his name on a wall in 1902.

deep.w: Machu Picchu is the ancient name of the site
deep.r: Researchers have argued from old documents that the Inca probably called it Huayna Picchu, after the nearby peak

deep.x: Machu Picchu survived because the conquerors never found it, and today its biggest challenge is the number of visitors.

cards.text:
Machu Picchu foi construída por volta de 1450 como propriedade real do soberano inca Pachacuti, numa crista muito acima do rio Urubamba, no Peru.

Os espanhóis nunca a encontraram. Tornou-se mundialmente famosa depois de o explorador americano Hiram Bingham a visitar em 1911, guiado por agricultores locais que já a conheciam bem.

cards.title: Conquista e epidemias

deep.x: Cortés landed in 1519 with about 500 soldiers. He was helped by Malintzin, a Nahua woman who became his interpreter and adviser, and by the Tlaxcalans, enemies of the Mexica, who supplied tens of thousands of warriors. The final siege of Tenochtitlan in 1521 was fought mostly by indigenous armies.
Disease ahead of the soldiers

People in the Americas had never been exposed to smallpox, measles or influenza, so they had no immunity. Smallpox struck Tenochtitlan in 1520 and killed the new Aztec ruler, Cuitláhuac. It reached the Andes even before the Spanish did, killing the Inca ruler Huayna Capac around 1527 and probably his heir.

steps: Two sons fight a civil war

deep.x: Cajamarca

At Cajamarca in 1532 Pizarro, with fewer than 200 men, ambushed Atahualpa's escort and took him prisoner. Atahualpa filled a room with gold and silver as ransom, but was executed in 1533. Inca resistance continued from Vilcabamba until 1572; the last independent Maya kingdom fell only in 1697.
The great dying

Repeated epidemics over the 1500s, including the mysterious cocoliztli of 1545 and 1576, cut native populations by perhaps 80–90% in many regions. The figures are estimates and debated, but the catastrophe is not.

deep.w: A few hundred Spaniards defeated empires alone
deep.r: Indigenous allies did most of the fighting, and epidemics had already shattered both empires

deep.x: The conquest of the Americas was decided as much by germs and local alliances as by Spanish weapons.

cards.text:
Pequenas forças espanholas conquistaram os impérios asteca e inca em poucos anos: Hernán Cortés tomou Tenochtitlan em 1521 e Francisco Pizarro capturou o soberano inca Atahualpa em 1532.

O aço, os cavalos e as armas de fogo ajudaram, mas duas coisas pesaram mais: milhares de aliados indígenas que odiavam o domínio asteca ou inca, e doenças novas como a varíola, que mataram um número enorme de pessoas.

cards.title: O legado hoje

deep.x: Quechua, the language of the Inca administration, is the most widely spoken indigenous language family in the Americas and has official status in Peru and Bolivia. In Guatemala, people of Maya descent make up a large part of the population, and about 30 Maya languages are still spoken across the region.
Words we borrowed
Traditions that blended

x: The Day of the Dead in Mexico mixes indigenous and Catholic customs, and is UNESCO-listed
Inti Raymi, the Inca festival of the sun, has been re-enacted in Cusco every June since 1944
Milpa farming of maize, beans and squash continues across Central America

deep.x: Rediscovering the past

Archaeology keeps changing the picture. In 1978 electricity workers digging in central Mexico City struck a huge carved stone of the goddess Coyolxauhqui, leading to the excavation of the Templo Mayor. Lidar surveys keep finding new Maya settlements under the forest.
Indigenous peoples across the region also face poverty, discrimination and pressure on their land, and many communities campaign to keep their languages taught in schools and used in public life.
Mexico's national flag shows the eagle and cactus from the founding legend of Tenochtitlan, and Peru's tourism draws heavily on Inca sites.
The Maya, Aztec and Inca worlds live on in languages, foods, festivals and the faces of millions of their descendants.

cards.text:
Os impérios caíram, mas os seus povos não desapareceram. Milhões ainda falam quíchua, línguas maias e náuatle, e as tradições indígenas moldam a vida do México à Bolívia.

O resto do mundo herdou as suas culturas, do milho, da batata e do tomate às malaguetas, ao cacau e à baunilha, e palavras como chocolate, tomate, abacate e lama.

quiz.q: Que civilização inventou um calendário de Contagem Longa com um zero?
quiz.explain: As suas datas contavam os dias a partir de 3114 a.C.

quiz.q: O que eram as chinampas?
options: Parcelas de cultivo erguidas num lago

quiz.q: Para que usavam os incas os quipus?
quiz.explain: Nós em posições definidas representavam números.

quiz.q: Que fator matou a maioria dos indígenas depois da conquista?
quiz.explain: Não tinham imunidade às doenças do Velho Mundo.

lessons.title: O Renascimento
lessons.summary: O renascer da arte, da ciência e das ideias.

cards.title: Um renascer

steps: Estudar a natureza e as pessoas

cards.text: O Renascimento começou em Itália entre os séculos XIV e XV. Os eruditos redescobriram textos gregos e romanos, os artistas estudaram a natureza e o corpo humano, e o indivíduo passou a ser celebrado.

deep.x: The word comes from the Italian **rinascita**, used by the painter-biographer Giorgio Vasari in 1550. "Renaissance" as the name of a whole period only caught on in the 1800s, with historians such as Jacob Burckhardt.
Why Italy?

x: Rich, independent cities competing for prestige
Roman ruins everywhere, a daily reminder of a great past
Contact with Byzantine scholars who knew Greek
Wealth from trade and banking to pay for it all

deep.x: Hunting for lost books

Scholars searched monastery libraries for forgotten Latin texts. Petrarch found letters by Cicero in Verona in 1345. In 1417 Poggio Bracciolini found Lucretius' poem On the Nature of Things, with its ancient ideas about atoms. Greek scholars, some fleeing the Ottoman advance, brought Plato and other authors little read in the West.

deep.w: The Middle Ages were dark and the Renaissance a clean break
deep.r: Medieval scholars already read Aristotle and built universities; the Renaissance grew out of them, and Petrarch's "dark ages" was partly self-promotion

deep.x: The Renaissance was Europe looking back to Greece and Rome in order to move forward.

cards.title: Florença e os mecenas

steps: Riqueza da banca e do comércio

cards.text: Florença liderou o movimento, financiada por famílias ricas como os Médici, que patrocinavam artistas, arquitetos e eruditos. A riqueza da banca e do comércio pagava a arte.

deep.x: Florence, a city of perhaps 40,000–60,000 people after the Black Death, grew rich on wool cloth and banking. Its gold coin, the **florin**, first struck in 1252, was trusted across Europe.
The Medici

Giovanni di Bicci de' Medici founded the family bank in 1397, with branches from London to Rome; the Pope was a key client. His son Cosimo and great-grandson **Lorenzo the Magnificent** ran Florence in practice without holding a crown.
Why pay for art?

Patrons wanted to show piety, outshine rivals and, for bankers accused of usury, perhaps ease their conscience. Contracts often set exactly what was to be painted and even how much costly blue (ultramarine, made from ground lapis lazuli) to use.
Competition

Guilds commissioned work too. In 1401 the cloth merchants held a contest for new bronze doors for the Baptistery. Lorenzo Ghiberti beat Filippo Brunelleschi, and later spent 27 years on a second pair, nicknamed the "Gates of Paradise".
Brunelleschi built the cathedral dome without the usual wooden frame underneath, using a herringbone brick pattern so each ring held itself up.
In Florence, bankers' money turned rivalry into masterpieces.

cards.title: Perspetiva
cards.text: Artistas como Brunelleschi desenvolveram a perspetiva linear por volta de 1420: as linhas paralelas encontram-se num ponto de fuga, o que faz as pinturas planas parecerem tridimensionais.

deep.x: Medieval painters often made the most important figures biggest, not the nearest ones. Around 1415–1420, **Filippo Brunelleschi** showed how to make a painting match what the eye really sees.
The experiment

He painted the Baptistery on a panel and drilled a small hole through it. Standing in the cathedral doorway, a viewer looked through the hole from the back at a mirror held in front. Lowering the mirror revealed the real building, lined up exactly with the painting.
Written down

In 1435 Leon Battista Alberti explained the method in his book On Painting, so any artist could learn it. Masaccio's Holy Trinity fresco in Florence, from about 1427, is one of the first surviving paintings to use it fully: a painted chapel seems to open into the wall.
apparent size ∝ 1 ÷ distance

x: A person 1.8 m tall at 10 m
the same person at 20 m
looks half as tall in the picture

deep.w: Nobody before 1420 painted depth
deep.r: Roman wall paintings in Pompeii show depth convincingly; what was new was an exact, geometric rule

deep.x: Perspective turned painting into a window, built with geometry.

cards.title: Leonardo da Vinci
cards.text: Pintor da Mona Lisa e da Última Ceia, Leonardo (1452–1519) também encheu cadernos com anatomia, máquinas voadoras, engenharia e estudos sobre a água, um verdadeiro "homem do Renascimento".

deep.x: Leonardo was born in 1452 in Vinci, near Florence, the son of a notary and a young woman not married to him. He trained in Verrocchio's workshop, then worked for the Duke of Milan, and died in 1519 at Amboise in France, as a guest of King Francis I.
Finished little, studied everything

Fewer than 20 paintings are generally accepted as his. He painted The Last Supper with an experimental mix on dry plaster instead of true fresco, so it began flaking within his lifetime. The Mona Lisa, probably Lisa Gherardini, wife of a Florentine merchant, stayed with him for years as he kept reworking it.
The notebooks
More than 7,000 pages survive. Left-handed, he wrote in mirror script, from right to left.
His anatomical drawings, based on dissecting dozens of bodies, were remarkably accurate, but stayed unpublished for centuries, so they barely influenced medicine at the time.

deep.w: Leonardo invented working helicopters and tanks
deep.r: They were sketches and ideas; most were never built and many wouldn't have worked as drawn

deep.x: The Mona Lisa became world-famous partly because it was stolen from the Louvre in 1911; it was recovered in Florence two years later.
Leonardo's genius was curiosity: he looked at everything, though he finished little.

cards.title: Miguel Ângelo
cards.text: Miguel Ângelo (1475–1564) esculpiu o David e pintou o teto da Capela Sistina, deitado em andaimes durante quatro anos. Também projetou a cúpula da Basílica de São Pedro, em Roma.

deep.x: Michelangelo Buonarroti saw himself as a sculptor first. At about 24 he carved the Pietà in St Peter's, the only work he signed. In 1501, aged 26, he began **David** from a huge block of marble other sculptors had abandoned.
The Sistine ceiling, 1508–1512

Pope Julius II pushed him into a job he didn't want. He painted in true fresco: wet plaster laid each morning, painted before it dried, so each day's patch (a giornata) had to be finished at once. The centre shows scenes from Genesis, including the Creation of Adam.
He even wrote a comic poem about the pain: neck twisted, beard pointing at the sky, paint dripping on his face.
A long life
He took over St Peter's at 71 and designed its dome, which was finished in 1590, after his death, by Giacomo della Porta. He died in 1564, aged 88, still working.
Michelangelo and Leonardo were once both asked to paint huge battle scenes in the same hall in Florence; neither finished.
Michelangelo made marble seem alive and turned a chapel ceiling into a universe.

cards.title: Humanismo
cards.text: Os humanistas acreditavam no estudo dos textos clássicos, na boa escrita e no potencial do ser humano. Erasmo de Roterdão foi a sua voz mais famosa no norte da Europa.

deep.x: The **studia humanitatis**, the "humanities", were five subjects: grammar, rhetoric, poetry, history and moral philosophy. Humanists wanted to read the classics in good original texts and write elegant Latin, and believed education made better citizens.
Reading critically

Going back to sources, **ad fontes**, could be explosive. In 1440 Lorenzo Valla showed that the "Donation of Constantine", a document used to support the Pope's claim to land, was a forgery: its Latin was centuries too late.
Erasmus

Erasmus of Rotterdam (about 1466–1536) was Europe's best-known scholar. He published a Greek New Testament in 1516 with a new Latin translation, and mocked corrupt clergy in his satire In Praise of Folly. He wanted reform, but never left the Catholic Church.
A Portuguese humanist
Damião de Góis, a diplomat and chronicler, befriended Erasmus and stayed in his house in 1534. Back in Portugal he was later tried by the Inquisition and died soon after, in unclear circumstances.

deep.w: Humanists rejected religion
deep.r: Nearly all were Christians; they wanted purer texts and better morals, including in the Church

deep.x: Humanism trusted that careful reading and good education could improve both people and society.

cards.title: O estilo manuelino
cards.text: O gótico tardio próprio de Portugal, com o nome do rei D. Manuel I, decora os edifícios com cordas, esferas armilares, criaturas marinhas e corais, celebrando as viagens. O Mosteiro dos Jerónimos e a Torre de Belém são exemplos famosos.

deep.x: Manuel I reigned from 1495 to 1521, when spices from India made Lisbon one of Europe's richest ports. The name "Manueline" was coined only in the 1800s, but the style is unmistakable: late-Gothic buildings covered in carving of the sea.

items.b: the Order that paid for voyages

deep.x: Where to see it

The Jerónimos was begun around 1501, largely funded by a tax on the spice trade, with architects Diogo de Boitaca and then João de Castilho. Vasco da Gama and Camões lie there. Both it and the Belém Tower survived the 1755 earthquake and became a UNESCO site in 1983.
Look closer

The Belém Tower (1514–1520) has a stone rhinoceros under one turret, often linked to the animal sent from India to Lisbon in 1515, famous from Albrecht Dürer's print. Tomar's chapter-house window is a riot of ropes, corks, roots and coral.
The armillary sphere from Manueline buildings is still on the Portuguese flag today.
Manueline buildings are the Age of Discovery carved in stone: Gothic bones dressed in rope and coral.

cards.title: Os Lusíadas
cards.text: Luís de Camões publicou Os Lusíadas em 1572, um poema épico sobre a viagem de Vasco da Gama e a história de Portugal, inspirado nas epopeias clássicas. O dia nacional de Portugal, 10 de junho, assinala a sua morte.

deep.x: Luís de Camões (about 1524–1580) lived the adventure he wrote about. He lost an eye fighting in North Africa and spent about 17 years in Asia, in Goa and probably Macau. Tradition says he swam ashore from a shipwreck in the Mekong delta holding his manuscript.
A classical epic

It opens with "As armas e os barões assinalados", echoing Virgil's Aeneid, which begins with arms and a hero. As in Homer and Virgil, the gods take sides: Venus helps the Portuguese, Bacchus works against them.
More than praise

The poem tells Portuguese history while following Gama's voyage, but it also has doubts. The Old Man of Restelo, at the departure from Belém, condemns the thirst for glory that empties the country. Camões ends by addressing young King Sebastião, urging him on to great deeds; Sebastião would die in Morocco six years later.

deep.w: 10 June is Camões's birthday
deep.r: It marks his death, on 10 June 1580; it's now the Day of Portugal, Camões and the Portuguese Communities

deep.x: Os Lusíadas turned a sea voyage into Portugal's founding epic, with a voice of doubt built in.

cards.title: A imprensa espalha o Renascimento
cards.text: A prensa de Gutenberg (por volta de 1450) permitiu que os livros e as novas ideias se espalhassem depressa. Veneza tornou-se uma capital da impressão; o primeiro livro impresso em Portugal surgiu em 1487, em hebraico, em Faro.

deep.x: Around 1450 in Mainz, Johannes Gutenberg combined metal letters cast in a mould, an oil-based ink and a press adapted from wine presses. His Bible of about 1455 was printed in roughly 180 copies; about 49 survive.
Venice
By 1500 Venice had more printers than any other city. Aldus Manutius printed Greek and Latin classics in small, cheap formats and introduced italic type in 1501, the ancestor of the pocket paperback.

x: About 250 European towns had presses by 1500
they printed perhaps 10–20 million copies
all in about 50 years

deep.x: In Portugal

Jewish printers led the way. In 1487 Samuel Gacon printed the Pentateuch in Hebrew in Faro. In Leiria, in 1496, Abraham d'Ortas printed the astronomical tables of **Abraham Zacuto**, which Portuguese navigators used to work out latitude at sea.
Only one copy of the Faro Pentateuch is known to survive; it is in the British Library in London.
Printing turned rare ideas into common property, and fast.

cards.title: A ciência do Renascimento
cards.text: A observação cuidadosa dos artistas alimentou a ciência: a anatomia rigorosa de Vesálio (1543) e o universo centrado no Sol de Copérnico (1543) surgiram no mesmo ano.

deep.x: Artists measured bodies and light; navigators measured stars and coasts. That habit of careful observation fed directly into science.
1543: two books

**Andreas Vesalius**, a 28-year-old professor at Padua, published a huge illustrated anatomy, with woodcuts probably from Titian's workshop. Doctors had followed the Roman physician Galen, who mostly dissected animals. Vesalius showed many of his errors: the human jaw is one bone, not two, for example.
Portugal's contribution

Pedro Nunes, royal cosmographer, showed that a ship on a fixed compass bearing follows a spiral line, not a great circle. He also invented the **nónio**, a scale for reading tiny fractions of a degree. Garcia de Orta's book on the medicinal plants of India was one of the first European works on tropical medicine.
Old authority, new eyes
Neither Galen nor Ptolemy was thrown out overnight. But each time careful observation contradicted the ancients, trust slowly shifted from old books to evidence.
Duarte Pacheco Pereira wrote around 1505 that experience is "the mother of things", a slogan for science before the Scientific Revolution.
When people started trusting their own eyes over ancient books, science began to change.
