lessons.title: Entre as guerras
lessons.summary: Repúblicas, a Grande Depressão e ditaduras.

cards.title: Os loucos anos 20
cards.text: Depois da guerra, os anos 1920 trouxeram o jazz, o cinema, a rádio, os automóveis e a euforia das bolsas nos EUA, além de novas liberdades para as mulheres, incluindo o direito de voto em muitos países.

deep.x: After the horror of the war and the 1918 flu, many people, especially in American and European cities, wanted to enjoy life. The USA had come out of the war as the world's largest economy and its biggest lender. Mass production made new goods affordable for ordinary families for the first time.
The consumer society

Henry Ford's assembly line cut the time to build a car from over 12 hours to about an hour and a half. About 15 million Model Ts were made by 1927. Buying on credit, "pay as you go", spread to cars, radios and furniture, and advertising grew into an industry.
New freedoms for women
Young women called "flappers" cut their hair short, wore shorter skirts, smoked and danced in public, shocking their parents. More women worked in offices and shops.
The other side

Not everyone roared. American farmers suffered from falling prices, racial segregation was harsh, and the ban on alcohol (Prohibition, 1920–33) fed organised crime. In Germany the decade began with hyperinflation, and in Portugal it was a time of political chaos.
The 1920s created the modern consumer lifestyle, built on new technology, mass culture and credit.
In Portugal, Carolina Beatriz Ângelo voted in 1911, the first woman to vote in southern Europe, using a loophole for literate heads of household; the law was then changed to exclude women.

cards.title: O crash de 1929
cards.text: Em outubro de 1929, a bolsa de Nova Iorque afundou. Os bancos faliram, o comércio encolheu e o desemprego disparou em todo o mundo: a Grande Depressão.

deep.x: Through the 1920s, share prices on Wall Street soared. Many investors bought shares "on margin", paying perhaps only 10% themselves and borrowing the rest, betting prices would keep rising. When prices began to fall, lenders demanded their money, forcing sales that pushed prices down further.
Black Thursday and Black Tuesday
On 24 October 1929 panic hit the market; on 29 October, "Black Tuesday", it collapsed. But the crash was only the beginning. The Dow Jones index kept sliding for almost three years.

x: Sept 1929 peak: Dow ≈ 381
July 1932 low: Dow ≈ 41
Fall ≈ 89%

deep.x: From crash to Depression

x: About 9,000 American banks failed between 1930 and 1933, wiping out savers
US unemployment rose to about 25% in 1933
Countries raised tariffs to protect their industries, starting with the USA in 1930, so world trade shrank by about two-thirds in value
US banks called back loans from Europe, spreading the crisis, especially to Germany

deep.x: Portugal and the crisis

Portugal's mostly rural and fairly closed economy was hit less than industrial countries, though emigration to Brazil and the USA collapsed and exports suffered. The crisis helped Salazar argue that strict budgets and strong rule were needed.
The crash turned into a Great Depression because banks, trade and spending collapsed together, each making the others worse.

deep.w: The Depression was caused only by the stock crash
deep.r: Bank failures, tight money, the gold standard and trade wars did most of the damage

cards.title: A União Soviética
cards.text: Depois da revolução de 1917, os bolcheviques criaram a União Soviética. Sob Estaline, a coletivização forçada e as purgas mataram milhões, incluindo na fome da Ucrânia (Holodomor) de 1932–33.

deep.x: The Bolsheviks seized power in November 1917 and won a brutal civil war (1918–21). In 1922 they created the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR). After Lenin's death in 1924, Joseph Stalin outmanoeuvred his rivals and by about 1928 held supreme power.
Industry at any cost

Stalin's Five-Year Plans built steel works, dams and whole new industrial cities at enormous speed. Output of coal, steel and electricity rose sharply, which later helped the USSR survive Hitler's invasion. But the plans relied on forced labour and fear.
Collectivisation and famine

Peasants were forced to give up their land and animals to join collective farms. Those labelled "kulaks", supposedly rich peasants, were deported or shot. Grain was seized for the cities and for export even as harvests failed.

In Ukraine, the Holodomor ("death by hunger") killed roughly 3.5–5 million people; Kazakhstan lost perhaps a third or more of its Kazakh population. Ukraine and many other countries recognise the Holodomor as a genocide.
The Great Terror
Party members, army officers, engineers and ordinary people were arrested on invented charges, forced to confess and shot or sent to Gulag labour camps.
Stalin turned the USSR into an industrial power through terror, famine and forced labour that killed millions of its own people.
Soviet censors routinely erased purged officials from photographs, so that people "disappeared" from history as well as from life.

cards.title: O fascismo em Itália
cards.text: Mussolini tomou o poder em 1922 e construiu um Estado de partido único, com censura, culto da personalidade e nacionalismo agressivo: o fascismo.

deep.x: Italy was on the winning side in 1918, but many Italians felt cheated: the peace gave them less territory than promised, and the economy was in trouble. Strikes and factory occupations in 1919–20 frightened landowners and industrialists, who feared a communist revolution.
The march on Rome

Benito Mussolini, a former socialist journalist, founded the fascist movement in 1919. His "blackshirt" squads beat and killed socialists and burned union offices. In October 1922, as fascists gathered to march on Rome, King Victor Emmanuel III refused to use the army against them and asked Mussolini to form a government.
What fascism meant

In 1924 the socialist deputy Giacomo Matteotti, who denounced fascist violence, was murdered. Within two years opposition parties were banned. In 1929 Mussolini made peace with the Pope, creating the Vatican City state. In 1935–36 Italy invaded Ethiopia, using poison gas.
A model for others

x: The name comes from the "fasces", a bundle of rods carried in ancient Rome as a symbol of authority
Fascist movements copied Mussolini across Europe, from Germany to Spain
Salazar admired some of his methods but kept his own distance from fascist mass politics

deep.x: Fascism was born in Italy: a violent, nationalist movement that took power legally and then destroyed democracy from within.

deep.w: Mussolini made the trains run on time
deep.r: It was mostly propaganda; much railway improvement predated him

cards.title: A ascensão de Hitler
cards.text: Na Alemanha, a Depressão ajudou o partido nazi a crescer. Hitler tornou-se chanceler em 1933 e rapidamente destruiu a democracia, perseguiu judeus e opositores e rearmou o país.

deep.x: Adolf Hitler, an Austrian-born former corporal, led a small party of extremists that tried and failed to seize power in Munich in 1923. In prison he wrote Mein Kampf, setting out his racism and plans for conquest. For most of the 1920s the Nazis were a fringe party.
How the Depression helped

With six million unemployed, many voters turned to parties promising radical change: the Nazis and the communists. The Nazis blamed Versailles, communists and Jews, and promised jobs, order and national pride. They never won a majority in a free election.
From chancellor to dictator
Conservative politicians persuaded President Hindenburg to appoint Hitler chancellor on 30 January 1933, believing they could control him. They were wrong.

After a fire at the parliament building, civil liberties were suspended. The Enabling Act let Hitler make laws without parliament. Unions and other parties were abolished, and the first concentration camp opened at Dachau in March 1933.
Persecution and rearmament

x: Jews were boycotted, expelled from jobs and, from 1935, stripped of citizenship
On Kristallnacht in November 1938, synagogues burned across Germany
Conscription returned in 1935 and military spending soared, which reduced unemployment

deep.x: Hitler came to power through elections and a backroom deal, then used legal powers to destroy democracy in months.

deep.w: Hitler was elected by a majority of Germans
deep.r: The Nazis' best free result was 37%; he was appointed by elites who thought they could use him

cards.title: A Primeira República Portuguesa
cards.text: A monarquia caiu a 5 de outubro de 1910. A Primeira República separou a Igreja do Estado e alargou o ensino, mas foi instável: 45 governos em 16 anos.

deep.x: By 1910 the monarchy had lost much of its support, weakened by the 1890 Ultimatum, debt and the assassination of King Carlos and his heir in 1908. On 4 October 1910 republicans and rebel sailors rose in Lisbon. The next morning, 5 October, the Republic was proclaimed from the balcony of Lisbon's city hall, and King Manuel II sailed into exile in England.
Big ambitions
Republicans wanted a modern, secular, educated nation. About 70–75% of adults could not read, so schools were a priority. The new flag in green and red and the anthem "A Portuguesa" date from 1911.
Why it struggled

x: Clashes with the Catholic Church alienated much of the rural population
Voting was limited, mostly to literate men, so few took part
The First World War brought debt, hunger and the CEP disaster
Coups, bombs and strikes were frequent; in 1918 President Sidónio Pais was assassinated, and in 1921 the prime minister was murdered

deep.x: The First Republic modernised laws and symbols that last to this day, but never achieved stable government.
Today's 5 October public holiday, the flag and the national anthem all come from the First Republic.

cards.title: Começa o Estado Novo
cards.text: Depois de um golpe militar em 1926, o ministro das Finanças António de Oliveira Salazar tornou-se presidente do Conselho em 1932 e criou o Estado Novo, um regime autoritário e corporativo, com censura e uma polícia política (PVDE, mais tarde PIDE).

deep.x: On 28 May 1926 General Gomes da Costa marched from Braga, and the military took power with little resistance; many Portuguese were tired of chaos. But the generals could not fix the finances. In 1928 they appointed António de Oliveira Salazar, an economics professor from Coimbra, as finance minister, with a veto over every ministry's spending.
The "New State"

Salazar balanced the budget within a year, which won him prestige. As prime minister from 1932, he introduced a constitution in 1933, approved in a plebiscite in which abstentions were counted as votes in favour.
How it controlled society

x: The censors' "blue pencil" cut newspapers, books, plays and films
The political police (PVDE, renamed PIDE in 1945) used informers, torture and prison
In 1936 a prison camp opened at Tarrafal in Cape Verde, where dozens of prisoners died
Corporatism replaced free unions with state-run bodies; strikes were illegal
Youth were enrolled in the Mocidade Portuguesa

deep.x: Fascist or not?
Historians debate the label. Salazar preferred a quiet, Catholic, rural order and distrusted mass mobilisation, but his regime was clearly authoritarian.
The Estado Novo traded freedom for order, and lasted 48 years, from the 1926 coup to 1974.
Salazar rarely travelled abroad and never flew in an aeroplane, a symbol of his inward-looking rule.

cards.title: A Guerra Civil de Espanha
cards.text: De 1936 a 1939, a república espanhola combateu os nacionalistas de Franco, apoiados pela Alemanha e pela Itália. Franco venceu e governou Espanha até 1975. O regime português apoiou Franco.

deep.x: Spain became a republic in 1931. Its reforms on land, the Church and the army divided the country. In February 1936 a left-wing Popular Front won elections. In July, army generals, including Francisco Franco, launched a coup. It succeeded in some regions and failed in others, and Spain split in two.
A rehearsal for world war

Germany sent the Condor Legion of aircraft and pilots, and Italy sent tens of thousands of soldiers. The Soviet Union sold weapons to the Republic, and about 35,000–40,000 foreign volunteers fought in the International Brigades. Britain and France stayed out under a non-intervention policy that in practice hurt the Republic.
Portugal's role

Salazar feared a left-wing Spain would spread revolution to Portugal. He let supplies reach Franco through Portugal, sent volunteers known as "Viriatos" and backed the nationalists diplomatically. After the massacre in Badajoz in 1936, some refugees who fled across the border were handed back to Franco's forces. In 1939 the two dictatorships signed the Iberian Pact of friendship.
The cost
Estimates of the dead range up to about 500,000, including mass executions on both sides. Some 450,000 refugees fled to France in early 1939, and Franco's repression continued for years.
The Spanish Civil War was a brutal national conflict and a testing ground for the weapons and alliances of the Second World War.
Picasso painted Guernica in 1937 in response to the bombing of the Basque town; the painting returned to Spain only in 1981, after democracy was restored.

cards.title: O New Deal
cards.text: Nos EUA, o New Deal de Roosevelt criou obras públicas, segurança social e regulação bancária para combater a Depressão, alargando o papel do Estado.

deep.x: Franklin D. Roosevelt became US president in March 1933, at the depth of the Depression. A quarter of workers were jobless, and banks were closing across the country. He promised "a new deal for the American people" and launched a burst of laws in his first hundred days.
What it created

x: The Civilian Conservation Corps employed about 3 million young men planting forests and building parks
The Tennessee Valley Authority built dams that brought electricity to poor rural areas
The SEC was created to police the stock market

deep.x: Did it work?

Unemployment fell from about 25% in 1933 to about 14% in 1937, then rose again when spending was cut too soon. Full recovery came only with massive spending for the Second World War. Economists still argue about which policies helped most.
A lasting change

The New Deal established that national governments are responsible for protecting people from economic disaster. In 1936 the economist John Maynard Keynes argued that governments should spend more in slumps, an idea that shaped policy for decades.
The New Deal saved American democracy in a time of crisis by making government a safety net, not just a referee.
Roosevelt's radio "fireside chats" explained his policies directly to millions of listeners in their homes.

cards.title: A política de apaziguamento
cards.text: A Grã-Bretanha e a França tentaram evitar a guerra cedendo às exigências de Hitler, aceitando a anexação da Áustria e, em Munique, em 1938, de parte da Checoslováquia. Não resultou.

deep.x: Appeasement meant avoiding war by meeting what seemed like reasonable demands. Many in Britain felt Versailles had been too harsh, and almost everyone dreaded a repeat of the trenches. Britain and France were also slow to rearm and worried about their empires.
Munich, 1938

Hitler demanded the Sudetenland, a border region of Czechoslovakia with many German speakers. On 29–30 September 1938, Britain's Neville Chamberlain and France's Édouard Daladier met Hitler and Mussolini in Munich and agreed to hand it over. Czechoslovakia was not invited. Chamberlain returned promising "peace for our time".
Why it failed

In March 1939 Hitler seized the rest of Czechoslovakia, showing that his aims went far beyond German-speaking lands. Britain and France now guaranteed Poland. In August Hitler and Stalin signed a non-aggression pact, secretly dividing eastern Europe between them.
The lesson drawn

items.r: Some leaders read them as weakness

deep.x: Ever since, "Munich" and "appeasement" have been used as warnings, sometimes too quickly, whenever leaders debate standing up to an aggressor.
Appeasement failed because Hitler wanted not fair borders but conquest, and each concession made him bolder.

deep.w: Chamberlain was a fool who believed Hitler completely
deep.r: He was also rearming, especially the air force, which helped Britain survive in 1940

O que começou em outubro de 1929?
options: A Grande Depressão, com o crash de Wall Street
quiz.explain: Os mercados afundaram em Nova Iorque.

lessons.title: A Segunda Guerra Mundial
lessons.summary: 1939–1945, o conflito mais mortífero da história.

cards.title: Começa a guerra

events.l: caem Dinamarca, Noruega, Países Baixos, França

cards.text: A Alemanha invadiu a Polónia a 1 de setembro de 1939; a Grã-Bretanha e a França declararam guerra. Em meados de 1940, a Alemanha já tinha conquistado grande parte da Europa Ocidental, incluindo a França.

deep.x: On 1 September 1939 German forces invaded Poland, using a staged "Polish attack" on a German radio station as an excuse. Britain and France declared war two days later. On 17 September the Soviet Union invaded Poland from the east, as secretly agreed with Hitler. Poland was crushed within about five weeks.
Blitzkrieg

Germany's "lightning war" combined fast tank columns, motorised infantry, dive-bombers and radio communication to break through and encircle the enemy. In May 1940 German tanks crossed the Ardennes forest, which the French thought impassable, and raced to the Channel.
The fall of France

x: About 338,000 British and French soldiers were evacuated from Dunkirk, many in small civilian boats
Paris fell on 14 June; France signed an armistice on 22 June
The north was occupied; a collaborating regime ruled the south from Vichy
Charles de Gaulle called on the French to resist from London

deep.x: Britain alone

From July to October 1940 the Luftwaffe tried to destroy the Royal Air Force before an invasion. Radar and fighter pilots from Britain, the Commonwealth, Poland and Czechoslovakia won the Battle of Britain, though bombing of cities, the Blitz, went on into 1941.
In 1939–40 speed and surprise gave Germany control of most of western Europe, leaving Britain alone to fight on.

deep.w: Germany won because it had more and better tanks
deep.r: France and Britain had as many tanks; Germany won through tactics, surprise and concentration

cards.title: Uma guerra mundial
cards.text: Em 1941, a Alemanha invadiu a União Soviética e o Japão atacou Pearl Harbor, levando os EUA a entrar na guerra. Os combates estenderam-se à Europa, a África, à Ásia e aos oceanos.

deep.x: On 22 June 1941 Germany broke its pact with Stalin and invaded the Soviet Union with over three million soldiers, the largest invasion in history. Hitler wanted living space, grain and oil in the east, and planned to starve and enslave its people. German armies reached the edge of Moscow before winter and Soviet counter-attacks stopped them in December.
Japan and the Pacific

Japan had been at war in China since 1937. Wanting oil and raw materials, and facing a US oil embargo, it struck the US fleet at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, on 7 December 1941, killing about 2,400 Americans. Within months Japan conquered the Philippines, Malaya, Singapore, Indonesia and Burma. Four days after Pearl Harbor, Hitler declared war on the USA.
The turning points
At Stalingrad a whole German army of about 300,000 men was surrounded; around 91,000 survivors surrendered in February 1943. From then on the Red Army advanced westward.
1941 turned a European war into a global one, pitting Germany and Japan against the combined resources of the USSR, the USA and the British Empire.
Japan also occupied Portuguese Timor from 1942 to 1945; tens of thousands of Timorese died during the occupation.

cards.title: O Holocausto
cards.text: A Alemanha nazi assassinou sistematicamente cerca de seis milhões de judeus, além de ciganos, pessoas com deficiência, prisioneiros soviéticos, opositores políticos e outros, em guetos, fuzilamentos em massa e campos de extermínio como Auschwitz.

deep.x: The Holocaust (in Hebrew, the Shoah) was the systematic, state-organised murder of about six million Jews, around two-thirds of Europe's Jews. It grew out of Nazi racial ideology, which cast Jews as an enemy race to be removed from Europe.
How it happened

After the invasion of the USSR, mobile killing units shot Jews in their hundreds of thousands; at Babi Yar near Kyiv, over 33,000 were shot in two days in September 1941. In January 1942, at the Wannsee conference, officials coordinated the "Final Solution". Jews from across Europe were deported by train to camps in occupied Poland, built to kill with gas.
Other victims

x: Roma and Sinti, perhaps 200,000–500,000
Disabled people, killed in "euthanasia" programmes
About 3 million Soviet prisoners of war, mostly by starvation
Polish elites, political opponents, gay men, Jehovah's Witnesses

deep.x: How it was possible

It required the work or silence of many thousands of ordinary people: clerks, railway workers, police, neighbours. Some resisted: Jews rose up in the Warsaw Ghetto in 1943, and individuals across Europe hid people at great risk.
The Holocaust shows that genocide is a process built step by step by a modern state, with many hands involved.
Soviet soldiers liberated Auschwitz on 27 January 1945; that date is now International Holocaust Remembrance Day.

cards.title: Aristides de Sousa Mendes

steps: Sousa Mendes passa milhares de vistos

cards.text: Em junho de 1940, o cônsul português em Bordéus, Aristides de Sousa Mendes, desobedeceu às ordens de Salazar e passou milhares de vistos a refugiados, muitos deles judeus. Foi castigado e morreu pobre; hoje é homenageado como Justo entre as Nações.

deep.x: In June 1940, as German armies swept through France, hundreds of thousands of refugees fled south to Bordeaux, desperate for visas to cross Spain and leave from Lisbon. Salazar's government had instructed consuls, in a circular of November 1939, not to grant visas to Jews, stateless people and other "undesirables" without approval from Lisbon.
A crisis of conscience

Aristides de Sousa Mendes, born in 1885 in Cabanas de Viriato, was a Catholic diplomat with 14 children. After meeting refugees, including the rabbi Chaim Kruger, he reportedly spent days in turmoil. Then he decided to grant visas to everyone who needed them, free of charge, working day and night with his family and staff, and also issued visas in Bayonne.
The price

Salazar recalled him, and a disciplinary process stripped him of his career. He lived his last years in poverty and died in Lisbon in 1954. How many he saved is debated: figures of up to 30,000 are often quoted, while documented visas number in the thousands.
Recognition
One official who chose conscience over orders saved thousands of lives, at the cost of his own career and comfort.
According to the Sousa Mendes Foundation, people who received his visas included the authors of the Curious George children's books.

cards.title: Portugal neutral

items: Bases dos Açores para os Aliados (1943)

cards.text: Portugal manteve-se oficialmente neutral, vendendo tungsténio (volfrâmio) aos dois lados. Lisboa tornou-se um centro de espiões e uma porta de saída para refugiados que fugiam para as Américas. Em 1943, deixou os Aliados usar bases nos Açores.

deep.x: Salazar's priority was to keep Portugal and its empire out of the war and his regime intact. Portugal was Britain's oldest ally, but also ideologically close to Franco and wary of communism. The result was a careful "collaborative neutrality", leaning to whichever side could hurt Portugal most at the time.
The wolfram rush

Tungsten (volfrâmio) hardens steel for armour-piercing shells and tools, and Portugal had some of Europe's richest deposits, such as at Panasqueira. Germany and Britain competed to buy it, prices soared, and poor villagers in the Beiras and Trás-os-Montes dug it by hand. Germany paid partly in gold, some of it looted. Under Allied pressure, Portugal stopped exports in June 1944.
Lisbon, waiting room of Europe

Tens of thousands of refugees passed through Lisbon, waiting for ships or the Pan Am flying boats to New York. Estoril's hotels and casino were full of exiled royals, diplomats and spies from both sides.
The Azores

In 1943, citing the old alliance, Portugal allowed Britain and then the USA to use air bases in the Azores. Planes from there helped close the mid-Atlantic "air gap" where U-boats had been sinking convoys.
Portugal stayed out of the war by bargaining with both sides, and Lisbon became the last open door out of occupied Europe.
The double agent Juan Pujol García, codenamed Garbo, began his career in Lisbon, sending invented reports to the Germans; later his deceptions helped protect the D-Day landings.

cards.title: O Dia D
cards.text: A 6 de junho de 1944, as forças aliadas desembarcaram na Normandia, na maior invasão por mar da história, abrindo uma frente ocidental enquanto os soviéticos avançavam a leste.

deep.x: For years Stalin had demanded a second front in western Europe. On 6 June 1944 it came: Operation Overlord, the Allied invasion of Normandy, led by General Dwight Eisenhower. Bad weather had already delayed it by a day.
Five beaches

Paratroopers landed overnight to seize bridges and crossroads. At Omaha Beach, the Americans suffered heavy losses under German guns. Total Allied casualties on the first day were around 10,000, including about 4,400 dead.
Fooling Hitler

The Allies built a fake army in south-east England, with inflatable tanks, dummy radio traffic and double agents, to convince the Germans the main landing would come at Calais. Even after 6 June, Hitler kept forces waiting there for weeks.
Two fronts
Weeks later the Soviets launched Operation Bagration, destroying a whole German army group in Belarus. Germany was now squeezed from west and east. Paris was liberated on 25 August 1944.
D-Day succeeded through overwhelming resources, careful planning and deception, opening the front that, with the Soviet advance, crushed Germany.

deep.w: D-Day was mainly an American operation
deep.r: It was a joint effort: British, Canadian, American, French, Polish and other forces took part, with Britain as the base

cards.title: O fim na Europa
cards.text: As tropas soviéticas tomaram Berlim; Hitler suicidou-se; a Alemanha rendeu-se a 8 de maio de 1945 (Dia da Vitória na Europa).

deep.x: By early 1945 Germany was collapsing. A last German offensive in the Ardennes, the Battle of the Bulge, had failed in the winter. Allied bombers pounded German cities. Western armies crossed the Rhine in March, while the Red Army drove through Poland towards Berlin.
The fall of Berlin

About 2.5 million Soviet soldiers attacked Berlin, defended by a mix of soldiers, old men and teenagers. As street fighting closed in, Hitler killed himself in his bunker on 30 April. Berlin surrendered on 2 May. Two days earlier, Mussolini had been caught and shot by Italian partisans.
Surrender

Germany's unconditional surrender was signed at Reims on 7 May and took effect on 8 May. A second signing in Berlin ended late that night, already 9 May in Moscow, which is why Russia celebrates Victory Day on 9 May.
What the armies found

As they advanced, Allied troops liberated concentration camps such as Bergen-Belsen, Buchenwald and Dachau. Images of starving survivors shocked the world. Europe was in ruins, with millions of displaced people on the move.
The war in Europe ended with Germany completely occupied, its leaders dead or captured and its cities in ruins.
In Lisbon, crowds took to the streets to celebrate the Allied victory, a celebration that many also used as a quiet protest against Salazar's dictatorship.

cards.title: As bombas atómicas
cards.text: Os EUA lançaram bombas atómicas sobre Hiroxima (6 de agosto de 1945) e Nagasáqui (9 de agosto), matando bem mais de 100 000 pessoas. O Japão rendeu-se a 15 de agosto, formalmente a 2 de setembro.

deep.x: In 1939 scientists warned that Nazi Germany might build an atomic bomb. The USA launched the Manhattan Project, which at its peak employed about 130,000 people. The first bomb was tested in New Mexico on 16 July 1945.
Hiroshima and Nagasaki

On 6 August 1945 a uranium bomb destroyed Hiroshima. On 9 August a plutonium bomb hit Nagasaki. Most victims were civilians. Many died instantly; others died from burns, injuries and radiation in the following months.
Why Japan surrendered

On 8 August the Soviet Union declared war on Japan and invaded Manchuria. On 15 August Emperor Hirohito announced surrender on the radio, the first time most Japanese had heard his voice. The formal surrender was signed on the battleship USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay on 2 September.
A debate that continues

Historians still argue about how much the bombs, rather than the Soviet attack, caused the surrender. Survivors, the hibakusha, campaigned for decades against nuclear weapons. No nuclear weapon has been used in war since.
Two bombs ended the deadliest war in history and began the nuclear age, in which a single weapon could destroy a city.
Conventional fire-bombing of Tokyo in March 1945 killed around 100,000 people in one night, comparable to Hiroshima.

cards.title: O custo
cards.text: A Segunda Guerra Mundial matou cerca de 70–85 milhões de pessoas, na maioria civis. A União Soviética e a China sofreram as maiores perdas.

deep.x: About 70–85 million people died in the Second World War, roughly 3% of the world's population of around 2.3 billion. Unlike the First World War, most of the dead were civilians, killed by bombing, massacres, genocide, hunger and disease.
Proportion matters

Poland lost about 17% of its pre-war population, the highest share of any country, including some 3 million Polish Jews. The Soviet Union lost about one in seven of its people. By comparison, Britain and the USA each lost about 0.3–1% of theirs.
Why so many civilians?
After the guns fell silent

x: Tens of millions were displaced; about 12 million Germans were expelled from eastern Europe
Cities such as Warsaw, Dresden and Hiroshima had been largely destroyed
Millions of widows and orphans faced poverty

deep.x: The Second World War killed more people than any other conflict, and most of them were civilians.

deep.w: The Western Allies did most of the fighting against Germany
deep.r: Most German military losses were on the Eastern Front against the Soviet Union

cards.title: Depois da guerra
cards.text: A Organização das Nações Unidas foi fundada em 1945, os criminosos de guerra foram julgados em Nuremberga e a Europa ficou dividida entre democracias ocidentais e Estados controlados pelos soviéticos.

deep.x: The victors tried to build a world that would not repeat the 1930s. Even before the war ended, they designed new international institutions for peace, money and justice.
The United Nations

The UN Charter was signed in San Francisco in June 1945 by 50 countries, with Poland added soon after as the 51st founding member. The UN came into existence on 24 October 1945. Its Security Council has five permanent members, the USA, USSR (now Russia), Britain, France and China, each with a veto.
Justice at Nuremberg

The Nuremberg trials introduced the principle that "following orders" is no excuse, and charged leaders with crimes against peace, war crimes and crimes against humanity. In 1948 the UN adopted a convention against genocide, a word coined in 1944.
A divided Europe

Germany and Berlin were split into four occupation zones. Soviet-backed communist regimes took over eastern Europe, while the USA's Marshall Plan helped rebuild the west. The wartime allies became Cold War rivals.
After 1945 the world built new institutions for peace and justice, but split into two hostile camps almost immediately.
Portugal applied to join the UN in 1946 but was blocked by Soviet vetoes; it was admitted only in 1955, together with Spain and others.

quiz.q: Que cônsul português salvou milhares de refugiados em 1940?
O que aconteceu a 6 de junho de 1944?
options: O desembarque do Dia D na Normandia

quiz.q: O que vendeu Portugal aos dois lados durante a Segunda Guerra Mundial?
quiz.explain: Um metal vital para blindagens e ferramentas.

lessons.title: A Guerra Fria
lessons.summary: Superpotências, medo nuclear e um mundo dividido, 1947–1991.

cards.title: Duas superpotências
cards.text: Depois de 1945, os EUA e a União Soviética tornaram-se superpotências rivais com sistemas opostos: democracia capitalista contra regime comunista de partido único. Nunca se enfrentaram diretamente.

deep.x: The Second World War left Europe and Japan in ruins and only two countries strong enough to shape the world. The USA had the bomb, the biggest economy and a navy on every ocean. The Soviet Union had the largest army and controlled eastern Europe, where the Red Army had stopped in 1945. Wartime allies quickly became rivals.
How the rivalry hardened

In 1947 President Truman promised to help any country resisting communism, a policy called **containment**. The Marshall Plan then sent about 13 billion dollars of aid to rebuild western Europe. Moscow refused it for itself and its satellites, and Europe split along that line.
Why "cold"?

x: Neither side could risk a direct war once both had nuclear weapons
They competed instead through spies, propaganda, sport, science and allies
Each believed its system would eventually win the whole world

items: Aid to win over new nations

deep.x: The Cold War was a 44-year contest of two systems, fought everywhere except in a direct war between the two giants.
The term "cold war" was popularised in 1947 by the American journalist Walter Lippmann; George Orwell had used it two years earlier.

cards.title: A Cortina de Ferro
cards.text: A Europa ficou dividida. Churchill falou de uma "cortina de ferro" em 1946. A Alemanha foi dividida e, em 1961, a Alemanha de Leste construiu o Muro de Berlim para impedir as pessoas de fugirem para ocidente.

deep.x: On 5 March 1946, in Fulton, Missouri, Winston Churchill said an "iron curtain" had descended across Europe "from Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic". Behind it, Soviet-backed communists took over Poland, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Romania and Bulgaria by 1948, often through rigged elections and arrests.
Germany cut in two

Defeated Germany was divided into four occupation zones, and so was Berlin, deep inside the Soviet zone. In 1948 Stalin blocked all roads and railways into West Berlin. The western allies answered with an airlift: for almost a year, planes flew in food and coal.
The Wall

By 1961 roughly 3 million East Germans had fled west, many of them young and skilled, mostly through Berlin. On the night of 13 August 1961 East German troops strung barbed wire across the city; it became a concrete wall with watchtowers and a "death strip".

x: About 155 km of barriers surrounded West Berlin
At least 140 people were killed at the Wall
Families and friends were separated for 28 years

deep.x: The Berlin Wall was built not to keep enemies out but to keep a country's own people in.

deep.w: The Wall only divided Berlin
deep.r: It encircled West Berlin completely; the whole inner German border was also fenced and mined

cards.title: A corrida às armas nucleares
cards.text: Os dois lados construíram dezenas de milhares de armas nucleares. A doutrina da "destruição mútua assegurada" significava que qualquer guerra nuclear destruiria ambos.

deep.x: The USA dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945. The Soviet Union tested its own bomb in 1949, years earlier than Washington expected, partly thanks to spies. From then on each side raced to build more, and more powerful, weapons.
Bigger and bigger

The hydrogen bomb (USA 1952, USSR 1953) used fusion and could be a thousand times more powerful than the Hiroshima bomb. In 1961 the Soviets tested the "Tsar Bomba", about 50 megatons, the largest explosion ever made by humans.
Too many to use

Rockets meant a warhead could cross the world in about 30 minutes. Both sides kept missiles on land, bombers in the air and submarines hidden at sea, so that even after a surprise attack they could still strike back. This is **mutually assured destruction** (MAD): if attacking guarantees your own ruin, nobody attacks.
Deterrence worked by making nuclear war pointless, but it left humanity one mistake away from catastrophe.
In 1983 Soviet officer Stanislav Petrov judged a satellite warning of US missiles to be a false alarm and did not report it as an attack. He was right: sunlight on clouds had fooled the system.

cards.title: A Crise dos Mísseis de Cuba
cards.text: Em outubro de 1962, os EUA descobriram mísseis soviéticos em Cuba. Durante 13 dias, o mundo esteve à beira de uma guerra nuclear, até a URSS aceitar retirá-los e os EUA retirarem discretamente mísseis da Turquia.

deep.x: Fidel Castro took power in Cuba in 1959 and moved towards Moscow. After a failed US-backed invasion at the Bay of Pigs (1961), Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev secretly sent nuclear missiles to the island, about 150 km from Florida. He also wanted to answer US missiles placed in Turkey, next to the USSR.
Thirteen days

President John F. Kennedy rejected an immediate air strike and chose a naval "quarantine" around Cuba. Soviet ships approached, then turned back. On 27 October, the most dangerous day, a US spy plane was shot down over Cuba and secret talks raced against the military's plans.
The deal
Because the Turkish part stayed secret, Kennedy looked like the clear winner and Khrushchev lost face; he was removed in 1964.
Lessons learned

x: A direct "hotline" linked Washington and Moscow from 1963
The Partial Test Ban Treaty (1963) stopped tests in the air and sea
Both sides saw how fast misunderstanding could lead to war

deep.x: The crisis was the closest the world has come to nuclear war, and it ended through compromise, not victory.
On 27 October, officers on Soviet submarine B-59 considered firing a nuclear torpedo; officer Vasili Arkhipov is credited with refusing to agree.

cards.title: Guerras por procuração
cards.text: As superpotências combateram indiretamente, apoiando lados opostos noutros conflitos: Coreia, Vietname, Afeganistão e guerras em África, incluindo Angola depois de 1975.

deep.x: A proxy war is one where big powers fight through others: they supply weapons, money, advisers and sometimes troops, while avoiding a direct clash with each other. Most Cold War deaths happened this way, far from Washington and Moscow.
Korea and Vietnam

In Korea, the communist North invaded the South in 1950. A US-led UN force fought North Korea and China. The war ended in 1953 with an armistice, not a peace treaty, and the peninsula is still divided near where it began. In Vietnam, the USA had over 500,000 troops at its 1969 peak; about 58,000 Americans and probably well over a million Vietnamese died before Saigon fell in 1975.
Afghanistan and Angola

The Soviet Union invaded Afghanistan in 1979; the USA, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia armed the mujahideen fighters. After about 15,000 Soviet deaths, Moscow withdrew in 1989. In Angola, after independence from Portugal in 1975, the MPLA government was backed by the USSR and tens of thousands of Cuban troops, while UNITA had US and South African support.
The Cold War stayed "cold" in Europe partly because it ran hot in Asia, Africa and Latin America.

deep.w: Proxy wars were just superpower puppet shows
deep.r: Local causes mattered; outside money mostly made existing wars longer and deadlier

cards.title: A corrida espacial
cards.text: A URSS lançou o Sputnik (1957) e Iuri Gagarin, o primeiro ser humano no espaço (1961). Os EUA levaram os astronautas da Apollo 11 à Lua a 20 de julho de 1969.

deep.x: On 4 October 1957 the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, a 58 cm metal ball that beeped radio signals as it circled Earth every 96 minutes. Americans were shocked: a rocket that could reach orbit could also carry a warhead to any city.
Soviet firsts

The USSR led for years: the first animal in orbit (the dog Laika, 1957), the first man (Yuri Gagarin, 108 minutes, 12 April 1961), the first woman (Valentina Tereshkova, 1963) and the first spacewalk (Alexei Leonov, 1965).
America's answer

The USA created NASA in 1958 and in 1961 Kennedy set the goal of landing a man on the Moon by the end of the decade. On 20 July 1969 Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on the Moon while Michael Collins orbited above. Hundreds of millions watched on television.
The space race was a propaganda contest that also gave the world satellites we now depend on every day.
In 1975 an American Apollo and a Soviet Soyuz docked in orbit and their crews shook hands: a symbol of détente.

cards.title: Portugal na NATO
cards.text: Apesar de ser uma ditadura, Portugal foi membro fundador da NATO em 1949, em grande parte por causa da base estratégica dos Açores. As guerras coloniais, a partir de 1961, criaram tensões com os aliados.

deep.x: On 4 April 1949, twelve countries signed the North Atlantic Treaty in Washington. Portugal was one of them, even though it was a dictatorship that held no free elections. Western leaders valued geography and anti-communism more than democracy.
Why the Azores mattered

The Lajes air base on Terceira sits roughly midway between North America and Europe. Planes could refuel there, and aircraft could hunt submarines across the Atlantic. Britain had used it from 1943, and the USA wanted it for the long term.

items: Used in the 1973 Middle East airlift

deep.x: Friction over Africa

When the colonial wars began in 1961, the Kennedy administration voted against Portugal at the United Nations and limited arms sales. Salazar answered with defiance, speaking of a nation "proudly alone". Allies criticised the wars, yet NATO-supplied equipment still ended up in Africa.

After the 1974 revolution, Washington briefly feared Portugal might fall under communist influence. Democracy won, and Portugal has been an active member ever since, with troops in missions from Bosnia to the Baltic.
Portugal's place in NATO came from its geography, not its politics.
The Azores also hosted the 2003 summit where the leaders of the USA, UK and Spain met before the invasion of Iraq.

cards.title: Desanuviamento e reformas
cards.text: Nos anos 1970, as tensões diminuíram com tratados de controlo de armamento. Nos anos 1980, as reformas de Mikhail Gorbachev, a glasnost (transparência) e a perestroika (reestruturação), afrouxaram o controlo soviético.

deep.x: **Détente** is French for "relaxation". By the late 1960s both superpowers were spending huge sums on weapons, and the USSR had caught up in missiles. Leaders such as Richard Nixon and Leonid Brezhnev decided limits were safer than an endless race.
Freeze and thaw

The 1975 Helsinki agreements accepted Europe's borders but also committed the East to human rights, which dissidents then used against their own governments. Détente collapsed after the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979; the early 1980s brought new missiles and fear.
Gorbachev's gamble

Mikhail Gorbachev became Soviet leader in 1985, aged 54. The economy was stagnating, the Afghan war was draining it and oil prices were falling. The Chernobyl disaster in 1986, first hidden from the public, convinced him that secrecy was dangerous.
In 1987 he and Ronald Reagan signed the INF treaty, the first to scrap a whole class of nuclear missiles: about 2,700 were destroyed.
Gorbachev meant to save the Soviet system by reforming it; his reforms let people reject it.

deep.w: Reagan's arms build-up alone won the Cold War
deep.r: Economic decline, Gorbachev's choices and people's protests all mattered

cards.title: Cai o Muro
cards.text: A 9 de novembro de 1989, o Muro de Berlim abriu. Os governos comunistas da Europa de Leste caíram em poucos meses, a Alemanha reunificou-se em 1990 e a União Soviética dissolveu-se em dezembro de 1991.

deep.x: In 1989 the Soviet bloc unravelled, country by country. Gorbachev made clear that Soviet troops would not crush reform, as they had in Hungary in 1956 and Czechoslovakia in 1968. Without that threat, the communist regimes had little support of their own.
An accidental opening

On 9 November 1989, East German spokesman Günter Schabowski announced new travel rules at a press conference. Asked when they began, he shuffled his notes and said, in effect, "immediately". Crowds rushed to the checkpoints that night, and overwhelmed guards opened the gates.
The end of the USSR

Hardliners tried to overthrow Gorbachev in August 1991, but crowds in Moscow, led by Boris Yeltsin, resisted. The coup failed and the republics left one by one. On 25 December 1991 Gorbachev resigned, and the Soviet flag over the Kremlin came down.
Romania was the exception: dictator Nicolae Ceaușescu was overthrown in a bloody uprising and executed on 25 December 1989.
In 1989, people in the streets, not armies, brought down the communist regimes of eastern Europe.
Pieces of the Berlin Wall now stand in dozens of countries as memorials; one is at the Sanctuary of Fátima.

cards.title: Legado

items: Alargamento da NATO e da UE
Origem da internet e do GPS

cards.text: A Guerra Fria moldou fronteiras, alianças, tecnologias como a internet e o GPS (ambas nascidas da investigação militar) e conflitos que ainda hoje ecoam.

deep.x: The Cold War ended without the nuclear war everyone feared, but it left marks everywhere: on maps, in alliances, in technology and in the way we think about security.
Technology born from rivalry

GPS was built by the US military; after a Korean airliner strayed into Soviet airspace and was shot down in 1983, Reagan announced it would be opened to civilians. Today it guides your phone and every delivery van.
Borders and alliances

x: NATO grew from 12 members to 32, including Finland (2023) and Sweden (2024)
Korea remains divided, with the world's most fortified border
Germany's east is still poorer on average than its west

deep.x: Echoes today

Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 revived Cold War-style tensions: sanctions, arms deliveries and nuclear threats. Arms-control treaties from the era have mostly lapsed. Historians argue about whether NATO expansion, Russian imperial ambition or both explain the new confrontation.
The Cold War is over, but its technologies, alliances and unfinished conflicts still shape daily life.

deep.w: The internet was designed to survive a nuclear war
deep.r: ARPANET was built to share computers; survivability research only influenced it

quiz.q: Quando caiu o Muro de Berlim?
quiz.explain: A Alemanha reunificou-se no ano seguinte.

quiz.q: Quem foi o primeiro ser humano no espaço?
Porque é que o Portugal da ditadura foi membro fundador da NATO?
options: A base dos Açores tinha importância estratégica

lessons.title: O mundo desde 1945
lessons.summary: Descolonização, globalização e novos desafios.

cards.title: O fim dos impérios
cards.text: Entre 1945 e 1975, a maioria das colónias da Ásia e de África tornou-se independente: a Índia e o Paquistão (1947), a Indonésia, o Gana (1957), dezenas de nações africanas por volta de 1960 e as colónias portuguesas em 1974–75.

deep.x: In 1945 European countries still ruled much of Africa and Asia. Within thirty years nearly all of it was independent. The war had weakened Britain, France and the Netherlands, colonised peoples had fought for them and expected freedom in return, and both superpowers opposed old-style empires.
Peaceful and violent paths
Some independence came through negotiation, as in Ghana under Kwame Nkrumah. Some came through long wars: Indonesia against the Dutch, Algeria against France (1954–62), and the Portuguese colonies.
Partition

British India split into mainly Hindu India and mainly Muslim Pakistan in August 1947. Borders drawn in weeks set off mass migration and killings: perhaps 10–20 million people moved and hundreds of thousands to a million or more died.
A changed world

v.unit: member states of the United Nations

x: Many new states kept colonial borders that cut across ethnic groups
Some joined the Non-Aligned Movement (1961), refusing to pick a Cold War side
Economic ties with former rulers often continued long after the flags changed

deep.x: In one generation, empires that took centuries to build were dismantled, and most of humanity came to live in independent states.
In 1960 alone, 17 African countries became independent, most of them former French colonies.

cards.title: Direitos civis

events.l: Lei dos Direitos Civis dos EUA

cards.text: Vários movimentos combateram a discriminação: o movimento dos direitos civis nos EUA, liderado por Martin Luther King Jr., o fim do apartheid na África do Sul com a eleição de Nelson Mandela em 1994, e os movimentos pelos direitos das mulheres em todo o mundo.

deep.x: After 1945, people who were denied equal rights because of race or sex used the language of democracy and human rights, written into the 1948 Universal Declaration, against their own governments.
The US movement

In the American South, segregation laws kept Black citizens in separate schools, buses and restaurants, and stopped most from voting. In 1955 Rosa Parks refused to give up her bus seat in Montgomery, Alabama; the boycott that followed lasted over a year and made Martin Luther King Jr. a national leader.
King's method was non-violent protest: marches, sit-ins and boycotts that exposed the brutality of segregation on television. He was assassinated in 1968.
Apartheid

South Africa's white minority government classified everyone by race from 1948. International sanctions, boycotts and resistance inside the country forced change. Nelson Mandela became president in the first all-race election in 1994.
Women's rights
Civil rights were won by ordinary people who organised, protested and refused to accept unequal laws.

deep.w: Civil rights were granted by kind leaders
deep.r: They were won through years of protest, often at great personal cost

cards.title: A integração europeia

events.l: Comunidade do Carvão e do Aço

cards.text: A partir da comunidade do carvão e do aço de 1951, a cooperação europeia cresceu até se tornar a UE: um mercado único, livre circulação e, para muitos membros, o euro.

deep.x: After two world wars started in Europe, French minister Robert Schuman proposed on 9 May 1950 to pool coal and steel, the raw materials of war, under a shared authority. If France and Germany ran these industries together, war between them would become "materially impossible".
From six to 27

The six founders were France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg. The UK, Ireland and Denmark joined in 1973; ten countries mostly from the former Soviet bloc joined in 2004. The UK left in 2020, the only country ever to do so.
What it means day to day

x: Free movement of goods, services, money and people
No border checks in the Schengen area
Roaming without extra charges since 2017
The euro, used by 21 of the 27 countries since Bulgaria joined in 2026

deep.x: The EU began as a way to make war impossible and grew into a shared market and political union of about 450 million people.
9 May is celebrated as Europe Day, the anniversary of the Schuman Declaration.

cards.title: A ascensão da China
cards.text: Depois da era de Mao, as reformas de Deng Xiaoping, a partir de 1978, abriram a economia chinesa. Centenas de milhões de pessoas saíram da pobreza e a China tornou-se o centro industrial do mundo.

deep.x: Under Mao Zedong (1949–76), China's economy was run by central plans and political campaigns. The Great Leap Forward caused a famine in 1959–61 that killed tens of millions; estimates range from about 15 to 45 million. The Cultural Revolution (1966–76) brought further chaos.
Deng's reforms

From 1978 Deng Xiaoping let farmers sell surplus crops, allowed private businesses and opened Special Economic Zones to foreign investment. His slogan was that it doesn't matter whether a cat is black or white, as long as it catches mice.
The results

Shenzhen, next to Hong Kong, grew from a town of tens of thousands to a megacity of electronics and tech companies. China became the "world's factory", and since 2010 the world's second-largest economy.
New tensions
China's rise has brought trade disputes and rivalry with the USA, concern over Taiwan and the South China Sea, and debate in Europe over dependence on Chinese goods.
China's reforms produced the biggest and fastest escape from poverty in history, without political freedom.
Macau, Portuguese for over 400 years, was handed back to China in 1999, two years after Hong Kong.

cards.title: Globalização
cards.text: O transporte em contentores, os voos mais baratos, os acordos comerciais e a internet ligaram as economias. Os produtos são feitos com peças produzidas em muitos países.

deep.x: Globalisation means the world's economies becoming tied together through trade, money, people and information. It has happened before, but after 1945, and especially after 1990, it went further and faster than ever.
The humble box

In 1956 American trucker Malcom McLean shipped goods in standard steel **containers**. They could move from ship to train to lorry without unpacking. Loading costs fell dramatically, ports were automated, and shipping became so cheap that distance hardly mattered.
Supply chains

A phone may be designed in California, use chips from Taiwan, rare metals from Africa and be assembled in China or India. Cars made in Portugal, such as at Autoeuropa in Palmela, use parts from across Europe.
The pandemic and the war in Ukraine exposed how fragile long supply chains can be. Many governments now talk of bringing production closer to home, and tariffs have risen again.
Globalisation made goods cheaper and lifted billions, but its gains and pains were spread very unevenly.
About 80% of world trade by volume still travels by sea; Sines is Portugal's biggest container port.

cards.title: A pobreza extrema diminui
cards.text: A percentagem de pessoas em pobreza extrema caiu de cerca de metade da humanidade em 1950 para menos de 10% antes da pandemia, uma das grandes conquistas da história, embora o progresso seja desigual.

deep.x: The World Bank counts people as extremely poor if they live on less than about $3 a day, adjusted for local prices (the line was updated in 2025). Measured this way, extreme poverty used to be the normal human condition.

v.unit: share of world in extreme poverty (approx. %)

deep.x: What drove it down

x: Economic growth, especially in China, India and East Asia
Better farming: the "Green Revolution" in seeds and fertilisers
Schools, vaccines, clean water and cheaper mobile phones and banking

deep.x: The other numbers
In 2020 the pandemic pushed about 70 million people back into extreme poverty, the first big rise in decades. Progress has since slowed.
Today about two-thirds of the extremely poor live in sub-Saharan Africa, often in countries affected by conflict.
Ending most extreme poverty is one of humanity's biggest achievements, but the last few hundred million are the hardest to reach.

deep.w: The world keeps getting poorer
deep.r: The share of very poor people fell from about half to under a tenth in 70 years

cards.title: 11 de setembro de 2001
cards.text: Os atentados terroristas em Nova Iorque e Washington mataram quase 3000 pessoas e levaram às guerras do Afeganistão e do Iraque e a uma atenção global ao terrorismo.

deep.x: On the morning of 11 September 2001, 19 al-Qaeda hijackers seized four passenger planes in the USA. Two struck the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center in New York, which collapsed; one hit the Pentagon near Washington. On the fourth, passengers fought back and it crashed in a field in Pennsylvania.
Wars that followed

The USA and allies invaded Afghanistan in October 2001 to remove the Taliban, who sheltered al-Qaeda. In 2003 a US-led coalition invaded Iraq, claiming it had weapons of mass destruction; none were found. Both wars cost hundreds of thousands of lives, and in 2021 the Taliban took back power in Afghanistan as Western troops left.
Everyday changes

x: Much tighter airport security, including limits on liquids since 2006
More surveillance of phones and internet traffic
Debates about how much freedom to trade for security

deep.x: The 9/11 attacks reshaped wars, alliances and daily life far beyond New York.
Before the Iraq war, the leaders of the USA, UK and Spain met at the Lajes base in the Azores in March 2003, hosted by Portugal's prime minister.

cards.title: A crise financeira

steps: Rebenta a bolha imobiliária dos EUA

cards.text: O crash de 2008, que começou com os créditos à habitação nos EUA, provocou uma recessão global e, na Europa, uma crise da dívida que levou aos resgates da Grécia, da Irlanda e de Portugal.

deep.x: In the 2000s US banks lent heavily to homebuyers with weak finances ("subprime" mortgages). These loans were bundled into complex securities and sold worldwide, often rated as safe. When house prices fell, the losses spread through the whole financial system.
September 2008

Lehman Brothers, a major US investment bank, went bankrupt on 15 September 2008. Banks stopped trusting each other; governments rescued banks with huge sums and central banks cut interest rates to almost zero. In 2009 the world economy shrank for the first time in decades.
The euro crisis
Countries with high debts or banking problems found that markets would only lend to them at very high interest rates. Unlike before, they could not devalue their own currencies.
Portugal's troika years
Wages and pensions were cut, taxes rose and about 100,000 people a year emigrated at the peak. The economy recovered after 2014, helped by tourism and exports.
A problem in US housing loans became a global recession and a crisis that tested whether the euro could survive.

deep.w: The crisis hit only reckless countries
deep.r: It began in banks and spread through markets to countries with very different problems

cards.title: Pandemia

events.l: a OMS põe fim à emergência

cards.text: A COVID-19 espalhou-se pelo mundo a partir do início de 2020, causando milhões de mortes, confinamentos e o desenvolvimento de vacinas mais rápido da história.

deep.x: In December 2019 a new coronavirus, SARS-CoV-2, was identified in Wuhan, China. It spread through the air, often before people felt ill, and by March 2020 the WHO declared a pandemic. Hospitals filled and countries closed schools, shops and borders.
Record-speed vaccines

Chinese scientists published the virus's genetic code in January 2020. Within days, companies had designed vaccines. The first was approved in December 2020, using **mRNA** technology developed over decades of research.
Why so fast

x: Decades of earlier research on mRNA and coronaviruses
Trial stages run in parallel rather than one after another
Governments paid for production before approval

deep.x: Portugal's campaign
Led by Vice-Admiral Henrique Gouveia e Melo, Portugal's vaccination task force achieved one of the highest vaccination rates in the world by late 2021.
COVID-19 showed both how vulnerable a connected world is and how fast science can respond.
Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman won the 2023 Nobel Prize in Medicine for the mRNA work that made the vaccines possible.

cards.title: Alterações climáticas
cards.text: Desde os anos 1980 que os cientistas alertam para o aquecimento global causado pelos gases com efeito de estufa. O Acordo de Paris de 2015 fixou o objetivo de limitar o aquecimento a bem menos de 2 °C.

deep.x: Scientists have known since the 19th century that carbon dioxide traps heat. In 1958 Charles Keeling began measuring it on Mauna Loa in Hawaii; his curve has risen every year since. By the 1980s warming was measurable, and in 1988 the UN set up the IPCC to assess the science.

v.unit: CO₂ in the air, parts per million

deep.x: The agreements

In Paris almost every country agreed to keep warming "well below 2 °C" and to try for 1.5 °C, each setting its own targets. The USA has left the agreement twice, most recently with effect from January 2026.
Where we are

Warming is measured against 1850–1900. 2024 was the first calendar year about 1.5 °C warmer than pre-industrial times, though the Paris goal refers to long-term averages. Consequences include heatwaves, drought, fiercer fires and rising seas.
Portugal's stake

x: Southern Europe is a warming and drying hotspot
The 2017 fires killed over 100 people
About 70% of Portugal's electricity came from renewables in 2024

deep.x: Climate change is a slow-building crisis caused by burning fossil fuels, and the solutions now exist but must be scaled fast.

deep.w: Scientists only recently noticed warming
deep.r: The physics was known in the 1800s and warnings were clear by the 1980s

quiz.q: Quando foi Nelson Mandela eleito presidente da África do Sul?
O que aconteceu à pobreza extrema entre 1950 e 2019?
options: Caiu de cerca de metade da humanidade para menos de 10%

quiz.q: Que objetivo fixou o Acordo de Paris de 2015?
options: Limitar o aquecimento a bem menos de 2 °C

lessons.title: A revolução digital
lessons.summary: Dos computadores do tamanho de uma sala aos smartphones e à IA.

cards.title: Os primeiros computadores
cards.text: A decifração de códigos e os cálculos de guerra impulsionaram os primeiros computadores eletrónicos. O ENIAC (1945) ocupava uma sala, pesava 27 toneladas e usava cerca de 18 000 válvulas.

deep.x: Before machines, a "computer" was a person, often a woman, who did calculations by hand. The Second World War needed far more calculations than people could do: code-breaking, artillery tables and the atomic bomb.
Colossus and ENIAC

At Bletchley Park, Tommy Flowers built Colossus to break German high-command codes; it was kept secret until the 1970s. In the USA, ENIAC was built at the University of Pennsylvania to calculate shell trajectories.
Rewiring to program

ENIAC was programmed by plugging cables and setting switches, which could take days. Six women, including Kay McNulty and Jean Bartik, worked out how to program it, though they were long left out of the history books.
The stored program

The big idea came next: store the program in memory just like data, so you can change it without rewiring. The Manchester Baby ran the first stored program in June 1948. Every computer since works this way.
Early computers were built for war, but the idea of a programmable machine that stores its own instructions changed everything.
Vacuum tubes failed so often that ENIAC's engineers learned to leave it switched on, because most failures happened when it was turned on or off.

cards.title: O transístor e o chip
cards.text: O transístor (1947) e o circuito integrado (1958) tornaram os computadores mais pequenos, mais baratos e mais fiáveis. O 4004 da Intel (1971) pôs um processador inteiro num só chip.

deep.x: Vacuum tubes were big, hot and fragile. In December 1947 John Bardeen, Walter Brattain and William Shockley at Bell Labs built the first **transistor**: a tiny switch made from a semiconductor. They won the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics.
Many switches on one slice

In 1958 Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments put several components on one piece of material; months later Robert Noyce at Fairchild made a practical silicon version. This **integrated circuit**, or chip, could be printed rather than wired by hand.
Moore's law
In 1965 Gordon Moore noticed that the number of transistors on a chip doubled regularly, later about every two years. That trend held for about 50 years.

x: Intel 4004 (1971): 2,300 transistors
Doubling every 2 years for 50 years = 2²⁵ ≈ 33 million times
≈ 77 billion, close to today's biggest chips

deep.x: Who makes chips
The transistor turned computing from rooms of glowing tubes into billions of microscopic switches on a fingernail of silicon.
Silicon Valley got its name in the early 1970s from the many chip makers around Palo Alto in California.

cards.title: Os computadores pessoais
cards.text: No final dos anos 1970 e nos anos 1980, os computadores entraram nas casas e nos escritórios: o Apple II (1977), o IBM PC (1981), o Macintosh (1984) e o Microsoft Windows. Em Portugal, o ZX Spectrum (Timex) foi enormemente popular.

deep.x: In the 1960s computers belonged to governments, universities and big companies. Cheap microprocessors made it possible for hobbyists to build their own: the Altair 8800 kit (1975) inspired Bill Gates and Paul Allen to found Microsoft, and Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak to found Apple.
From typing to clicking

Early PCs used text commands. Ideas from Xerox's research lab in California, windows, icons and a mouse, were brought to the mass market by the Macintosh (1984) and later Windows. Pointing and clicking made computers usable by almost anyone.
Why the PC won

x: Spreadsheets like VisiCalc and Lotus 1-2-3 gave businesses a reason to buy
IBM used standard parts, so other firms made cheaper "clones"
Microsoft licensed its software to all of them

deep.x: In Portugal

The Sinclair ZX Spectrum was a cheap home computer that loaded games from cassette tapes. Timex, which had a factory in Portugal, sold its own versions here. A generation of Portuguese programmers started on it.
The PC turned the computer from an institution's machine into a personal tool for work, play and creativity.
In 2008 Portugal gave cheap "Magalhães" laptops to primary schoolchildren, one of the first national schemes of its kind.

cards.title: A internet
cards.text: A ARPANET ligou computadores de investigação dos EUA em 1969. O TCP/IP (1983) permitiu juntar as redes numa só internet. Portugal ligou-se à internet no início dos anos 1990, através das universidades.

deep.x: In 1969 the US Defense Department's research agency, ARPA, linked four university computers in **ARPANET**. The first message, sent from UCLA to Stanford in October 1969, was meant to be "LOGIN"; the system crashed after "LO".
Packets
The key idea was **packet switching**: a message is cut into small packets that travel separately and are reassembled at the end. If one route is busy or broken, packets go another way.
One network of networks

Other networks appeared, and they could not talk to each other. Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn designed TCP/IP, a shared set of rules. On 1 January 1983 ARPANET switched to it, and any network could join the "inter-net".
Portugal joins
The .pt domain was created in 1988. Portugal's universities connected to the internet in the early 1990s through the national research network run by FCCN, and home access spread later in the decade.
The internet is a network of networks that works because everyone agreed to speak the same simple language, TCP/IP.

deep.w: The internet was designed to survive a nuclear war
deep.r: ARPANET was built to share expensive computers; that research only influenced it

cards.title: A World Wide Web
cards.text: No CERN, em 1989–91, Tim Berners-Lee inventou a web: páginas, ligações e navegadores por cima da internet. E ofereceu-a gratuitamente.

deep.x: At CERN, the physics lab near Geneva, thousands of scientists struggled to share documents across incompatible computers. In March 1989 Tim Berners-Lee, a British computer scientist, wrote a proposal for linked information. His boss called it "vague but exciting".
Three inventions
He also wrote the first browser and the first web server, on a NeXT computer. The first website went online in 1991, explaining what the web was.
Free for all

On 30 April 1993 CERN released the web software into the public domain. Anyone could build on it without paying. The Mosaic browser (1993), with pictures on the page, and then Netscape (1994) made the web popular.
Hyperlinks
The link was the heart of it: any page could point to any other, anywhere, without permission. Search engines, online shops and Wikipedia all grew from that idea.
Berners-Lee's real gift was not just the web but making it free, so anyone could build on it.

deep.r: The internet is the network; the web is one service that runs on it, like email

cards.title: Pesquisa e redes sociais
cards.text: O Google (1998) organizou a web; o Facebook (2004), o YouTube (2005) e o Twitter (2006) fizeram de toda a gente um editor, mudando as notícias, a política e a amizade.

deep.x: By the late 1990s the web had millions of pages and finding things was hard. Larry Page and Sergey Brin, students at Stanford, ranked pages by how many other pages linked to them, weighted by those pages' own importance. Their search engine, Google, launched in 1998.
The business model
Most of these services are free to use. They earn money from advertising, targeted using what they learn about users. That gives them a strong reason to keep people scrolling.
Everyone a publisher
Anyone could now post text, photos and video to millions. Social media helped protests such as the 2011 Arab Spring, but also spread misinformation, harassment and polarised debate.
Rules arrive

x: The EU's GDPR (2018) gave people rights over their personal data
The EU's Digital Services Act requires big platforms to tackle illegal content
Australia banned social media accounts for under-16s from December 2025, and other countries are debating age limits

deep.x: Search and social media made information and publishing free, and paid for it with our attention and data.
Facebook has around 3 billion monthly users, more than a third of everyone on Earth.

cards.title: Telemóveis
cards.text: Os telemóveis espalharam-se depressa nos anos 1990; Portugal teve uma das taxas de adesão mais altas da Europa. O iPhone (2007) e o Android transformaram os telemóveis em computadores de bolso.

deep.x: On 3 April 1973 Motorola engineer Martin Cooper made the first handheld mobile call in New York, on a phone weighing about 1 kg. Early mobiles were car phones or expensive "bricks" for business people.
Europe's standard
European countries agreed on one digital standard, **GSM**, so a phone could work across borders. Text messages (SMS) were added almost as an afterthought and became hugely popular.
Portugal's fast start

Portugal's operators launched GSM in 1992, and TMN's prepaid "Mimo" card in 1995 was one of the first prepaid mobile services anywhere. With no contract, almost anyone could own a phone, and adoption soared.
Pocket computers
The iPhone (2007) put a touchscreen, a real web browser and, from 2008, an app store into a phone. Google's Android, used by many makers, brought smartphones to billions.
Mobile phones became the most widely owned computers in history, and for many people the only one they have.
There are more mobile phone subscriptions in the world than people.

cards.title: Multibanco
cards.text: A rede Multibanco, lançada em Portugal em 1985, foi um dos sistemas de caixas automáticas mais avançados do mundo, permitindo pagar contas, carregar telemóveis e comprar bilhetes muito antes de isso ser comum noutros países.

deep.x: In 1983 Portuguese banks set up a shared company, SIBS, to run a common network of cash machines and payment terminals. Multibanco opened in 1985. Unlike in many countries, where each bank had its own machines, a card from any Portuguese bank worked in every ATM from the start.
More than cash

Portugal's ATMs soon did much more than give money. You could pay utility bills using an "entidade" and "referência", top up a mobile phone, buy concert or train tickets and pay taxes, all from the same machine.
Why Portugal led

x: Banks cooperated on one system instead of competing with many
Late arrival meant it was built on newer technology
The state and utilities adopted Multibanco references early

deep.x: MB WAY
The same network now runs MB WAY (2015), which lets people send money or pay with a phone number and is used by millions in Portugal.
Multibanco shows how cooperation between competitors can create a service better than any could build alone.
Many online shops in Portugal still let you pay with a "referência Multibanco", a method almost unknown abroad.

cards.title: Nuvem e dados
cards.text: Desde os anos 2000, a computação passou para enormes centros de dados. As empresas alugam servidores à medida (AWS 2006, Azure 2010), e os dados tornaram-se um dos recursos mais valiosos.

deep.x: For decades every company ran its own servers in a back room. In 2006 Amazon Web Services began renting computing power and storage over the internet, paid by the hour. Microsoft Azure (2010) and Google Cloud followed. This is **cloud computing**.
Layers of the cloud
Data as a resource

Every click, purchase and journey produces data. Companies use it to recommend products, set prices, detect fraud and train AI. Whoever holds the most useful data has a big advantage, which is why privacy laws such as the EU's GDPR matter.
The physical cloud
The cloud is not in the sky. It lives in enormous buildings full of servers that need lots of electricity and water for cooling.

items.l: firms hold most of the market

deep.x: Portugal is attracting large data centres, notably at Sines, where submarine internet cables land and renewable power is available.
The cloud turned computing into a utility, like electricity, rented on demand from a few giant providers.

deep.w: The cloud is weightless and green
deep.r: It runs on physical data centres that use roughly as much electricity as all of France

cards.title: A era da IA

events.l: assistentes de IA por todo o lado

cards.text: A aprendizagem profunda (2012), o Transformer (2017) e o ChatGPT (2022) abriram um novo capítulo: computadores que compreendem e geram linguagem, imagens e código.

deep.x: The term "artificial intelligence" was coined in 1956. For decades AI used hand-written rules and repeatedly disappointed, leading to "AI winters". The breakthrough came from **machine learning**: systems that learn patterns from huge amounts of examples instead of being told the rules.
Why it took off in 2012

In 2012 a neural network called AlexNet easily won an image-recognition contest by running on graphics chips. In 2017 Google researchers published the **Transformer**, a design that handles language very well and scales with more data and computing power.
Language models

Large language models learn by predicting the next word across vast amounts of text. ChatGPT, released in November 2022, reached about 100 million users in two months, then the fastest-growing app ever. Systems such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini now write, translate, summarise and code.
Rules and recognition

x: The EU AI Act (2024) is the first broad AI law, applied in stages to 2027
AlphaFold predicted the shapes of most known proteins; its creators shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry
Data centres for AI are driving new demand for chips and electricity

deep.x: Modern AI learns from data rather than rules, and in a decade it went from labs to everyday tools.

deep.r: Today's models find statistical patterns; they can be fluent yet confidently wrong
